EGY.short: Egypt adopted a Cloud First Policy in 2024, in force since August 2024; no source found says where public bodies must host under it.
EGY.summary: The Supreme Council of Digital Society adopted the Cloud First Policy on 13 March 2024. The policy entered into force on 22 August 2024. It requires data classified top secret or secret to be hosted only within Egypt. In the last twelve months the ICT ministry told a cabinet meeting on 20 September 2026 that it is preparing a national data-centre strategy with other ministries and bodies. No source found names a government cloud or data centre that public bodies must use. Operating would need the government to name where public bodies must host.

ERI.short: A 2022 World Bank record shows no government cloud policy in Eritrea; nothing newer is held, so no stage is set.
ERI.summary: No stage is set. No government hosting or cloud policy or draft has been found for Eritrea, and no source dated in the last three years says the government has neither. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Absent would need a source from the past three years saying the government has no hosting or cloud policy and none is being written.

ETH.short: Federal directives tell public bodies to leave their own server rooms for shared national hosting; the national cloud data centre was unfinished in 2026.
ETH.summary: In November 2026 the innovation minister restated existing federal directives for public institutions to move off their own server rooms. They are to use shared national infrastructure instead. In the last twelve months, in May 2026, the security agency INSA held a forum on a proposed National Cloud Security Governance Framework. The National Cloud Data Center at the ICT Park in Addis Ababa is to host government services and was still under construction in November 2026. Operating would need the government to name where public bodies must host.

GAB.short: Nothing found says Gabon has a government hosting or cloud policy, or says it has none, so no stage is set.
GAB.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a government hosting or cloud policy, or says there is none.

GHA.short: Ghana held a validation workshop on a cloud and data centre framework in 2024; no source found says whether the framework has been adopted.
GHA.summary: On 26 June 2024 Smart Africa and the National Information Technology Agency held a validation workshop in Accra to gather stakeholders' input for an enhanced regulatory framework for cloud and data centres, the Ministry of Communications reported. After the workshop the minister said the government is working to have all its data held in other countries hosted in Ghana. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found says a government hosting or cloud policy is adopted and in force. Establishing would need a hosting or cloud policy adopted and in force.

GIN.short: Nothing found says Guinea has a government hosting or cloud policy, or says it has none, so no stage is set.
GIN.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a government hosting or cloud policy, or says there is none.

GMB.short: The Gambia has a government cloud policy and strategy dated 2023; no source found says where public bodies must host under it.
GMB.summary: The Gambia has a Government Cloud Policy, with a strategy and an implementation plan, dated 2023, which the Ministry of Communications and Digital Economy lists among its policies. The ministry says the Government Cloud Strategy for 2023 to 2027 builds on the cloud policy and aims to modernise government service delivery through cloud adoption. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found names a government cloud or data centre the policy tells public bodies to use, or a list of approved providers. Operating would need the government to name where public bodies must host.

KEN.short: Kenya's Cloud Policy took effect in May 2025 and gives State bodies 24 months to migrate; the list of approved providers is not yet published.
KEN.summary: The Kenya Cloud Policy, 2025 was signed on 7 April 2025 and took effect on 2 May 2025. It requires sensitive, secret and restricted government data to be stored in Kenya, and State organs have 24 months to migrate systems that are not exempted. In the last twelve months, in August 2026, applications to be an accredited government cloud provider were open. The Cabinet Secretary said in August 2026 that institutions must buy only from accredited providers. No list of approved providers has been published. Operating would need the government to name where public bodies must host.

LBR.short: Nothing found says Liberia has a government hosting or cloud policy, or says it has none, so no stage is set.
LBR.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a government hosting or cloud policy, or says there is none.

LBY.short: Libya had a national cloud computing policy out for consultation in 2026; no source found says whether it has been adopted.
LBY.summary: The General Information Authority held a consultative meeting to review the proposed National Cloud Computing Policy, reported in January 2026. ESCWA reports a further consultative workshop on the draft on 30 December 2025. In the last twelve months these two consultations are the only dated steps toward the policy that have been found. The meeting agreed to incorporate the feedback into its final version. No source found says a government hosting or cloud policy is adopted and in force. Establishing would need a hosting or cloud policy adopted and in force.

LSO.short: Nothing found says Lesotho has a government hosting or cloud policy, or says it has none, so no stage is set.
LSO.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a government hosting or cloud policy, or says there is none.

MAR.short: Morocco made cloud the mandatory default for public-administration technology spending in 2025; no source found says where public bodies must host.
MAR.summary: Morocco has a Cloud First Policy under Digital Morocco 2030, the ministry's director of cloud infrastructure said in 2025. The policy makes cloud the mandatory default for all public-administration technology investments. In the last twelve months, the minister told parliament in December 2025 that it would become the default progressively. No source found names a government cloud or data centre the policy tells public bodies to use, or a list of approved providers. Operating would need the government to name where public bodies must host.

MDG.short: Nothing found says Madagascar has a government hosting or cloud policy, or says it has none, so no stage is set.
MDG.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a government hosting or cloud policy, or says there is none.

MLI.short: Nothing found says Mali has a government hosting or cloud policy, or says it has none, so no stage is set.
MLI.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a government hosting or cloud policy, or says there is none.

MOZ.short: Mozambique said in 2025 it is drafting a new framework for cloud adoption; no source found says whether one has been adopted for public bodies.
MOZ.summary: In December 2025 the Minister of Communications and Digital Transformation said the government is drafting an updated regulatory framework for cloud adoption, to replace current legal restrictions. A Cloud Computing Regulation approved by Decree No. 72/2025 of 31 December 2025 licenses cloud providers. In the last twelve months these are the dated steps found. The law firm's account of the December 2025 decree describes the licensing of providers and no rule on where public bodies host. Establishing would need a hosting or cloud policy adopted and in force.

MRT.short: Mauritania's data-protection authority has required its authorisation for cloud services abroad since 2025; no source found says where public bodies must host.
MRT.summary: On 30 July 2025 Mauritania's data-protection authority issued deliberation 005/2025 on the minimum conditions for using cloud services abroad. Public and private data controllers must obtain its authorisation before processing personal data on foreign cloud services. In the last twelve months, the authority's meeting of 29 April 2026 had amendments to some of the deliberation's articles on its agenda. The amended text of the deliberation was published on 30 April 2026. No source found names a government cloud or data centre public bodies must use. Operating would need the government to name where public bodies must host.

MUS.short: A 2020 procurement directive names the Government Online Centre as government hosting; no source found says which bodies have moved onto it.
MUS.summary: The Procurement Policy Office's Directive No. 53 took effect on 15 December 2020. The directive names the Government Online Centre as the hosting for common-use ICT solutions. Other data centres or clouds may be used only with the ministry's approval. It has no end date, and no change has been found in the last twelve months. No recent source names the bodies that moved onto the Government Online Centre, or counts them. Mature would need a dated source naming or counting bodies moved onto it.

MWI.short: Malawi had no cloud policy enacted in June 2025, and no source found says whether one is being written, so no stage is set.
MWI.summary: No stage is set. No government hosting or cloud policy or draft has been found for Malawi. No source since October 2023 says the government has no hosting or cloud policy and none is being written. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Absent would need a source from the past three years saying the government has no hosting or cloud policy and none is being written.

NAM.short: Nothing found says Namibia has a government hosting or cloud policy, or says it has none, so no stage is set.
NAM.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a government hosting or cloud policy, or says there is none.

NER.short: Nothing found says Niger has a government hosting or cloud policy, or says it has none, so no stage is set.
NER.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a government hosting or cloud policy, or says there is none.

NGA.short: Nigeria's 2026 cloud policy names Galaxy Backbone as government's cloud, and the postal service hosts its postcode database there; no source found reports other moves.
NGA.summary: On 17 August 2026 the Federal Ministry of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy released the National Digital Cloud Policy. In the last twelve months it supersedes the Nigeria Cloud Computing Policy 2019, the policy that first introduced Cloud First. Galaxy Backbone is state-owned. It will aggregate government cloud demand from registered providers and negotiate framework agreements, with buying through a National Digital Marketplace on which NITDA registers providers. In November 2026 the postal service NIPOST said its postcode database is hosted and managed by Galaxy Backbone under the policy. No source found counts the ministries or agencies that have moved onto Galaxy Backbone.

RWA.short: Rwanda has required critical government systems to be hosted in the National Data Center since 2012; no source found says which bodies have moved recently.
RWA.summary: Rwanda's Ministerial Instructions N° 001/2012, issued by the Minister in the Office of the President in Charge of ICT, have been in force since 12 March 2012. Article 17 of the instructions requires all government IT systems and applications that process, store or provide critical government data to be hosted in the National Data Center. Article 18 requires institutions with data centres of their own to arrange disaster recovery from it. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Nothing found from the last three years names or counts public bodies moved onto the named hosting. Mature would need a dated source naming or counting bodies moved onto it.

SDN.short: Nothing found says Sudan has a government hosting or cloud policy, or says it has none, so no stage is set.
SDN.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a government hosting or cloud policy, or says there is none.

SEN.short: Senegal's president instructed in 2021 that all state data move to the Diamniadio national data centre; no source found says which bodies have moved.
SEN.summary: Commissioning the Diamniadio National Datacenter in June 2021, President Macky Sall instructed the government to migrate all state data and platforms to it. He also told it to repatriate national data hosted outside the country. The centre is managed by the state IT agency ADIE. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Nothing found from the last three years names or counts public bodies moved onto the named hosting. Mature would need a dated source naming or counting bodies moved onto it.

TCD.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a government hosting or cloud policy, or says there is none.

TGO.short: Nothing found says Togo has a government hosting or cloud policy, or says it has none, so no stage is set.
TGO.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a government hosting or cloud policy, or says there is none.

TUN.short: Tunisia's 2024 Cloud First circular sets hosting tiers, and labelled providers were listed in 2026; no source found says which bodies have moved.
TUN.summary: A ministerial order of 13 September 2023 requires public bodies' software, platforms and infrastructure to be hosted in-house or with cloud providers according to four tiers. Any other arrangement needs the cybersecurity agency's approval. Circulaire n° 16 of 22 July 2024 sends sensitive internal systems to a private cloud or to national or sectoral government cloud centres. In the last twelve months the cybersecurity agency published its list of labelled providers on 17 September 2026, with six N-Cloud entries. Nothing found from the last three years names or counts public bodies moved onto the named hosting. Mature would need a dated source naming or counting bodies moved onto it.

TZA.short: Tanzania approved hosting standards for public institutions in February 2026; the approved hosting environments are not named.
TZA.summary: The e-Government Authority's Data Center Standards and Guidelines for Public Institutions, version 2.0, was approved by its board chairperson on 18 February 2026. The standard rests on section 25 of the Act, which requires a public institution to host its systems in a government-approved hosting environment. In the last twelve months this standard is the dated step found. No source found names a government cloud or data centre the policy tells public bodies to use, or a list of approved providers. Operating would need the government to name where public bodies must host.

UGA.short: Cloud-first guidelines of 2018 require ministries and agencies to host classified information in the government data centre; no source found says how many have moved.
UGA.summary: NITA-U issued the National Guidelines on Cloud Computing for Government, Ministries, Departments and Agencies in October 2018. The same guidelines require those bodies to host information assets classed Official, Secret and Top Secret in the Government Cloud, the National Data Center run by NITA-U. The document gives no end date. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Nothing found from the last three years names or counts public bodies moved onto the named hosting. Mature would need a dated source naming or counting bodies moved onto it.

ZAF.short: South Africa gazetted its National Policy on Data and Cloud in May 2024; no government cloud or list of providers is named.
ZAF.summary: On 31 May 2024 the communications department gazetted the National Policy on Data and Cloud, covering national and provincial government and organs of state. It says government data shall be stored in unified, cloud-enabled data centres in designated locations. It names the State Information Technology Agency as the body that sources cloud services for government. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No government cloud or data centre that public bodies must use has been found, and no list of approved providers. Operating would need the government to name where public bodies must host.

ZMB.short: A 2023 regulation requires public bodies to store personal data in Zambia; no source found says which hosting they must use.
ZMB.summary: Statutory Instrument No. 43 of 2023, the Electronic Government (General) Regulations, was gazetted on 6 October 2023 under the Electronic Government Act 2021. Regulation 8 requires every public body to store the personal data it processes on infrastructure domiciled in Zambia. The regulations also require all public bodies to integrate their services with the Government Service Bus. They do not say which hosting to use. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Operating would need the government to name where public bodies must host.

ZWE.short: Zimbabwe announced a government cloud policy in 2026; no source found says whether it has been adopted.
ZWE.summary: At the first workshop of government ICT directors in May 2026, the ICT minister, Tatenda Mavetera, set out a Zimbabwe Government Cloud as a companion policy to a cloud-first and mobile-first direction. It is to end ministries buying their own servers and to consolidate the state's infrastructure. In the last twelve months this announcement is the only step toward a policy that has been found. No adopted policy, circular or regulation has been found. Establishing would need a hosting or cloud policy adopted and in force.

AGO.short: Angola's central bank published mobile money complaint counts in 2025; its rules for payment providers date from 2016 and 2017, so no stage is set.
AGO.summary: No stage is set. In September 2017 Banco Nacional de Angola's Aviso 7/17 set transparency, information and contract rules for payment service users. In September 2016 Aviso 12/2016 set rules for marketing financial products and services, payment-service providers' included. The bank's ranking put Afrimoney, a mobile money platform, at 1,138 complaints in the second quarter of 2025, up 180% on the first quarter. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found since October 2023 says consumer-protection rules for digital financial services are drafted or in force. Establishing would need such rules in force.

BDI.short: Nothing found since 2023 names consumer-protection rules for digital finance, so no stage is set.
BDI.summary: No stage is set. Nothing has been found since October 2023 that says whether consumer-protection rules apply to digital financial services in Burundi. No rule, draft or complaints body for digital finance has been found. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Absent would need a source from the past three years saying that no consumer-protection rules apply to digital financial services.

BEN.short: Benin's financial services observatory has taken complaints, e-money included, since 2025; no source found says whether consumer rules cover digital finance, so no stage is set.
BEN.summary: No stage is set. A 2020 decree created the OQSF, an observatory that mediates for financial-sector clients. The client may obtain mediation through the OQSF, operational since October 2024. On 29 July 2025 the OQSF presented an online portal for complaints from financial-sector clients, and it covers e-money issuers' customers. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found since October 2023 says consumer-protection rules for digital finance are drafted or in force. Establishing would need such rules in force.

BFA.short: A financial mediator took complaints, e-money included, in 2024; no source found reports enforcement figures since 2023.
BFA.summary: The OQSF-BF, created by decree in December 2022, offers financial mediation in disputes between users and providers. E-money issuers are among the providers. BCEAO Instruction n°001-01-2024 requires e-money issuers to run complaint-handling systems for clients and merchants. In 2025 the observatory was merged into the national financial-inclusion agency, ANPFI. In the last twelve months, in October 2026 the OQSF-BF, housed in ANPFI, said it mediates free of charge in disputes with e-money issuers and other providers. No source found reports a fine, a sanction or complaint figures after 2022. Mature would need such figures or a sanction under these rules.

BWA.short: Consumer-protection rules for digital finance were in force in 2026; no source found reports a complaints body.
BWA.summary: The Bank of Botswana says the Electronic Payment Services (Amendment) Regulations, 2026, took effect on 2 April 2026. They include market conduct obligations to enhance consumer protection. The regulations took effect in the last twelve months, and no earlier consumer rule for digital finance has been found. No source found since October 2023 says a financial ombudsman or complaints unit takes complaints. Operating would need a financial ombudsman or a regulator's complaints unit that takes complaints about digital financial services.

CAF.short: Nothing found names consumer-protection rules for digital finance or says there is none, so no stage is set.
CAF.summary: Not found. Nothing found says whether consumer-protection rules apply to digital finance.

CIV.short: A body took complaints about digital financial services in 2025; enforcement is not reported.
CIV.summary: In June 2025 the OQSF-CI's secretary said the observatory handles complaints about e-money issuers among others. Consumers can complain to the OQSF-CI by green line, email or website. In the last twelve months, from 2 November 2026 the regional central bank capped fees on PI-SPI instant transfers. Transfers are free up to 8,000 CFA francs a day, and the fee is 0.8 per cent above that. On 4 November 2026 a National Assembly committee adopted a banking bill covering fintech and e-money institutions. It provides for complaints handling, mediation and a deposit guarantee. No fine or sanction under these rules has been found. Mature would need a fine, sanction, licence withdrawal or complaint figures for digital financial services.

CMR.short: Regional consumer-protection rules covered payment institutions in 2026; no source found reports a complaints body for digital finance.
CMR.summary: CEMAC Regulation 01-20 of 3 July 2020 protects consumers of banking services. It provides for complaint services and mediation. In the last twelve months, in October 2026 the consumer observatory OBS-CC said the regulation also applies to payment institutions. OBS-CC added that Regulation 04/18 requires a permanent complaints mechanism for payment services. No source found since October 2023 says a financial ombudsman or regulator's complaints unit in Cameroon takes digital finance complaints. Operating would need such a body to take them.

COD.short: Nothing found names consumer-protection rules for digital finance or says there is none, so no stage is set.
COD.summary: Not found. Nothing found says whether consumer-protection rules apply to digital finance.

COG.short: Nothing found since 2023 names consumer-protection rules for digital finance, so no stage is set.
COG.summary: No stage is set. The nearest instruments found are Décret n° 2024-86 du 28 février 2024 portant institution de la médiation financière and Règlement N° 01/20/CEMAC/UMAC/COBAC du 3 juillet 2020 (protection des consommateurs de produits et services bancaires). Nothing found since October 2023 says whether consumer-protection rules apply to digital finance in Congo. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Establishing would need consumer-protection or conduct rules covering digital financial services in force.

COM.short: Nothing found names consumer-protection rules for digital finance or says there is none, so no stage is set.
COM.summary: Not found. Nothing found says whether consumer-protection rules apply to digital finance.

CPV.short: Cabo Verde's payment-services law is applied to digital banking, and the central bank handles and counts internet-banking complaints.
CPV.summary: The central bank's 2024 conduct report applies Decree-Law 8/2018, the legal regime for payment services and electronic money. Under it banks refunded clients for unauthorised card and internet-banking transactions. A Banco de Cabo Verde official said in March 2025 that the central bank handles complaints about digital payment systems. No change has been found in the last twelve months. In 2024 the central bank recorded 10 internet-banking complaints among 169 against banks, and banks refunded complainants 3.25 million escudos.

DJI.short: Nothing found names consumer-protection rules for digital finance or says there is none, so no stage is set.
DJI.summary: Not found. Nothing found says whether consumer-protection rules apply to digital finance.

DZA.short: Central bank rules of August 2025 make payment providers ring-fence customer funds and disclose fees; no complaints body has been found.
DZA.summary: Bank of Algeria Instruction 06-2025 of 17 August 2025 requires payment service providers to keep customer funds in segregated escrow accounts. It also requires a bank guarantee or liability insurance, and that users accept a contract setting out fees and dispute procedures before an account opens. In October 2024 the Bank of Algeria said it was drafting a regulation to protect consumers of financial services, notably digital ones. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No financial ombudsman or central bank complaints unit for digital financial services has been found. Operating would need one that takes complaints about digital financial services.

EGY.short: Consumer-protection rules for digital finance were in force in 2024; no source found reports a complaints body.
EGY.summary: The Central Bank of Egypt's instructions of 7 May 2024 set minimum requirements for complaint handling by banks, covering complaints about banks, outsourcing providers, payment service providers and agents contracted by the bank. On 19 February 2019 the CBE issued customer-rights instructions for banks and providers such as mobile payment companies, Shalakany says. Compliance was due by February 2020. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found since October 2023 says a financial ombudsman or a regulator's complaints unit takes complaints about digital financial services. Operating would need such a body.

ERI.short: Nothing found names consumer-protection rules for digital finance or says there is none, so no stage is set.
ERI.summary: Not found. Nothing found says whether consumer-protection rules apply to digital finance.

ETH.short: A financial consumer protection directorate took complaints in 2026; enforcement on digital financial services is not on record.
ETH.summary: In March 2026 the National Bank of Ethiopia said its Financial Consumer Protection Directive No. FCP/01/2020 requires financial institutions to tell customers about fraud risks. In the last twelve months, an assessment of the second National Financial Inclusion Strategy was reported by The Reporter in October 2026. It says the strategy set up a dedicated financial consumer protection directorate that handles complaints. The same auditors cautioned that consumer safety mechanisms remain ill-equipped for digital fraud, scams and social-engineering risks. No source found reports a fine, sanction, licence withdrawal or complaint figures for digital financial services. Mature would need such a report.

GAB.short: Consumer rules covering payment institutions and mobile money were in force in 2025; no source found reports a working complaints body.
GAB.summary: CEMAC Regulation 01/20 of 3 July 2020, a decree of 21 March 2024 and two ministerial orders of 7 January 2025 set Gabon's financial mediation framework. It covers payment institutions and mobile money disputes. UNCDF's November 2023 diagnostic said a new regulation on digital financial consumer protection was expected. In the last twelve months, the mediation scheme was due to launch on 26 October 2026. No source found says it has begun taking complaints. Operating would need a financial ombudsman or a regulator's complaints unit that takes complaints about digital financial services.

GHA.short: The central bank shut down over 400 illegal online lenders in 2025 and reports complaints against payment service providers.
GHA.summary: The Bank of Ghana says the Directive for Digital Credit Service Providers (September 2025) is in force. Its Second Deputy Governor said it requires digital credit providers to be licensed, disclose loan terms and follow consumer protection rules. In October 2025 the Bank said it had shut down more than 400 illegal online lending operators. Its 2023 complaints report counts 23 complaints against payment systems and service providers. In the last twelve months, on 17 November 2026 the Bank of Ghana named 19 loan apps operating in breach of the directive.

GIN.short: Consumer-protection standards covered e-money clients in 2026; no source found reports a complaints body.
GIN.summary: The central bank's instruction I/DGSIF/DSIMF/006/2018 sets consumer-protection standards for inclusive financial institutions, e-money institutions among them. Fees must be displayed, contracts written and language plain. Clients have access to their own data. In the last twelve months the instruction was cited and not changed. In August 2026 the lawyer Fodé Mourana Soumah described what the standards give clients of e-money services and other institutions. No source found since October 2023 names a financial ombudsman or a regulator's complaints unit. Operating would need such a body to take complaints about digital financial services.

GMB.short: The consumer-protection Acts were being revised for digital markets in 2025; no government source shows rules in force.
GMB.summary: In April 2025 the Ministry of Trade was revising the Competition and Consumer Protection Acts, working with a consultant, the GCCPC and Commonwealth support. The revision addresses digital markets, including e-commerce and digital financial platforms. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found since October 2023 says consumer-protection rules for digital financial services are in force. Establishing would need consumer-protection or conduct rules covering digital financial services or digital lending in force.

GNB.short: Nothing found names consumer-protection rules for digital finance or says there is none, so no stage is set.
GNB.summary: Not found. Nothing found says whether consumer-protection rules apply to digital finance.

GNQ.short: Nothing found names consumer-protection rules for digital finance or says there is none, so no stage is set.
GNQ.summary: Not found. Nothing found says whether consumer-protection rules apply to digital finance.

KEN.short: The competition authority reported 355 complaints about digital lenders in the year to June 2025, five times the year before.
KEN.summary: The Competition Authority of Kenya received 355 complaints from borrowers about digital lenders in the year to June 2025. The year before there were 67. Amendments to the CBK Act brought non-deposit-taking digital lenders under Central Bank of Kenya supervision. By September 2026, 281 digital credit providers were licensed. In the last twelve months, seven Kenyan regulators issued a draft Financial Consumer Protection Framework, with comments due 28 April 2026. The Central Bank of Kenya says its draft National Payment System Bill, 2026 aims to secure consumer and data protection.

LBR.short: Nothing found since 2023 names consumer-protection rules for digital finance, so no stage is set.
LBR.summary: No stage is set. Nothing found since October 2023 says whether consumer-protection rules apply to digital finance in Liberia. The nearest items found are Liberia Telecommunications Authority consumer protection services and MTN Mobile Money. No rule, complaints unit or complaint figure for digital financial services has been found. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Absent would need a source from the past three years that says no consumer-protection rules apply to digital financial services.

LBY.short: Libya's central bank opened a complaints platform in 2025, but the e-payment consumer rules date from 2020, so no stage is set.
LBY.summary: No stage is set. In March 2020 the National Payments Council issued an e-payment services regulation under the Central Bank of Libya. Its consumer protection chapter requires e-payment and mobile-wallet providers to give clear written service information, honest advertising and call-centre support. In June 2025 the Central Bank of Libya launched the website of its instant payment service, LYPay, with a platform for submitting complaints and inquiries. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found since October 2023 says consumer-protection rules for digital finance are drafted or in force. Establishing would need such rules in force.

LSO.short: The central bank's consumer protection division handled financial complaints in 2026; no source found reports enforcement on digital financial services.
LSO.summary: In February 2026 a Central Bank of Lesotho official said the Financial Consumer Protection Act of 2022 requires providers to lend responsibly and safeguard customer information. The Central Bank of Lesotho's Financial Consumer Protection Division handles and resolves financial complaints. In May 2025 the government told a parliamentary committee that the Payment Systems Bill, 2025 enforces consumer protection measures for payments. In the last twelve months, in February 2026 the market conduct framework was still being finalised. No source found since October 2023 reports a fine, a sanction or complaint figures for digital financial services. Mature would need such a report.

MAR.short: Morocco's banking mediation centre took 5,536 complaints in 2024, payment institutions included; no consumer rules for digital finance are known, so no stage is set.
MAR.summary: No stage is set. In 2024 Al Wassit Albanki, the banking mediation centre set up under Bank Al-Maghrib, received 5,536 complaint files. Payment institutions and money transfer companies were among the institutions concerned. The mediation rules of the Centre Marocain de Médiation Bancaire, of 23 March 2023, bind its members, payment institutions among them. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found since October 2023 says consumer-protection rules for digital finance are drafted or in force. Establishing would need such rules in force.

MDG.short: Consumer-protection rules for digital finance were in force in 2026; no source found reports a complaints body.
MDG.summary: Under the 2020 banking law the CSBF regulates e-money institutions, ensures user protection and can sanction breaches up to withdrawal of licence. E-money institutions are legally required to run a 24/7 customer service handling complaints on loss, theft, fraud and unauthorised transactions, per 2424.mg. Oral complaints must be confirmed in writing within five working days. In the last twelve months the law was cited and not changed: in August 2026 Newsmada reported the CSBF's role over e-money institutions. No source found since October 2023 says a financial ombudsman or a regulator's complaints unit takes complaints about digital financial services. Operating would need such a body.

MLI.short: Central bank rules capping fees on some electronic payments came into force in November 2026; no source found says a body takes complaints.
MLI.summary: Since 2 November 2026 new tariff rules of the regional central bank cap the fees on some electronic payment operations, APA reports. In the last twelve months, the Malian e-money issuer SAMA Money made receiving instant transfers free in November 2026. The fee rules come from the regional central bank, and no earlier consumer rule for digital finance in Mali has been found. No source found says an ombudsman or a regulator's unit takes complaints about digital financial services in Mali. Operating would need such a body.

MOZ.short: The central bank reported 44 complaints against mobile money providers in the first half of 2026.
MOZ.summary: The instant payment system (SPIM) regulation took effect on 2 March 2026. It sets a complaints procedure with an electronic portal. In April 2025 Banco de Moçambique put out for consultation a revision of its notice protecting mobile money customer funds. In the last twelve months, in the first half of 2026 the bank received 44 complaints about mobile money. Of these, 26 were against Vodafone M-Pesa and 18 against M-Mola. Across all complaints in that half-year the bank issued directives for correction. They included the refund of MZN 73,243,072 in improperly charged fees.

MRT.short: A pilot financial complaints line was announced in 2026; no source found reports rules and a working complaints body, so no stage is set.
MRT.summary: No stage is set. In the last twelve months, the central bank announced a pilot week of its complaints call centre for April 2026. Nothing found shows it taking complaints. Nothing found names rules for digital finance, a regulator's complaints unit for digital financial services, or complaint figures. Absent would need a source from the past three years that says no consumer-protection rules apply to digital financial services.

MUS.short: Nothing found names consumer-protection rules for digital finance or says there is none, so no stage is set.
MUS.summary: Not found. Nothing found says whether consumer-protection rules apply to digital finance.

MWI.short: The central bank counted nearly 47,000 complaints about failed digital financial services in 2024.
MWI.summary: The Reserve Bank of Malawi issued a directive setting complaint-handling procedures for banks and other providers. It sets resolution within 2 to 30 days and penalties up to K50 million per institution. The Reserve Bank says its fintech regulatory framework is meant to ensure consumer protection. No change has been found in the last twelve months. The Deputy Governor said 36,481 complaints about digital payments were recorded from April 2023 to March 2024. The 2024 annual report counts 46,969 banking-sector complaints linked to failed digital financial services.

NAM.short: Consumer-protection rules for digital finance were in force in 2026; no source found reports a complaints body.
NAM.summary: The Bank of Namibia's determination PSD-1 took effect on 6 January 2026. It carries user protection requirements for payment service providers, at paragraphs 10.4 and 16 of its arrangement of paragraphs. The determination took effect in the last twelve months, and no earlier consumer rule for digital finance has been found. No source found since October 2023 says a financial ombudsman or complaints unit takes complaints. Operating would need a financial ombudsman or a regulator's complaints unit that takes complaints about digital financial services.

NER.short: A 2024 source says no consumer-protection rules apply to digital financial services.
NER.summary: In January 2024 UNCDF said Niger's consumer protection texts do not cover digital finance. It said they need updating. It also said practically no legal recourse exists for consumers of digital financial services. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found since October 2023 says consumer rules for digital finance are being drafted. Preparing would need consumer-protection rules for digital financial services to be drafted.

NGA.short: Enforcement of consumer protection in digital finance was reported in 2026.
NGA.summary: The FCCPC's Digital, Electronic, Online or Non-Traditional Consumer Lending Regulations 2025 have been in force since 21 July 2025. They set consumer-protection rules for all digital lenders. The FCCPC invites consumers to report unlawful or unregistered digital lenders to its complaint portal. In the last twelve months, on 21 January 2026 the FCCPC began enforcement, withdrawing conditional approval from digital lenders that missed the compliance deadline. TechCabal reports MTN suspended its airtime lending in April 2026 under a regulatory suspension linked to the FCCPC's new requirements. The Federal High Court upheld the regulations on 20 July 2026.

RWA.short: A body took complaints about digital financial services in 2026; enforcement is not reported.
RWA.summary: NBR says customers with unresolved eKash problems may complain to the National Bank of Rwanda through the Intumwa chatbot. They can reach it by SMS, WhatsApp, website and social media. In the last twelve months, in August 2026 NBR took eKash complaints through its Intumwa chatbot. Governor Hakuziyaremye says the consumer-protection framework requires failed transfers to be refunded in a timely manner. No source found since October 2023 reports a fine, sanction or complaint figures. Mature would need a fine, sanction, licence withdrawal or complaint figures for digital financial services.

SDN.short: Consumer-protection rules for digital finance were in force in 2026; no source found reports a complaints body.
SDN.summary: Central Bank of Sudan Circular 7/2026 sets binding minimum rules for USSD financial services. They cover fee disclosure, no debit on failed transactions, free SMS confirmations, 24-hour support and complaint resolution within 48 hours. In the last twelve months, in July 2026 the central bank revoked the e-payment licence of Al-Asjad Digital and Smart Solutions, acting under its licensing standards and not under the consumer rules. No source found since October 2023 names a financial ombudsman or a regulator's unit that takes complaints about digital financial services. Operating would need such a body.

SEN.short: Fee caps protect users of instant transfers from 2026 and a mediator takes financial complaints; no source found reports enforcement on digital finance.
SEN.summary: The Observatoire de la qualité des services financiers settles disputes between users and providers by mediation. It has been under the Ministry of Finance since 2009. It handled 475 new disputed files in 2025, against 379 in 2024. These figures cover all financial services. In the last twelve months, from 2 November 2026 the regional central bank capped fees on PI-SPI instant transfers. Transfers are free up to 8,000 CFA francs a day, and the fee is 0.8 per cent above that. No source found reports a fine, sanction, licence withdrawal or complaint figures for digital financial services. Mature would need such a report.

SLE.short: The telecoms regulator proposed consumer rules for digital financial services in July 2025; no source found shows them in force.
SLE.summary: In July 2025 the National Communications Authority presented a proposed quality-of-service framework for digital financial services, to be applied jointly with the Bank of Sierra Leone. Its consumer provisions set timeframes for resolving complaints and require disclosure of service terms. The Bank of Sierra Leone's 2022–2026 financial inclusion strategy says its Consumer Protection Section tracks complaints, and that mobile money providers report complaints to the bank. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found since October 2023 says consumer-protection rules for digital financial services are in force. Establishing would need such rules in force.

SOM.short: Consumer-protection rules for digital finance were being drafted in 2025; none in force is on record.
SOM.summary: In November 2025 the House of the People passed the National Payment System Bill. The bill is stated to ensure consumer protection. It awaits the Senate. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found since October 2023 says consumer-protection rules for digital financial services are in force. Establishing would need consumer-protection or conduct rules covering digital financial services or digital lending in force.

SSD.short: Consumer-protection rules for digital finance were in force in 2026; no source found reports a complaints body.
SSD.summary: In September 2025 the Bank of South Sudan issued a consumer protection notice that covers banks, microfinance institutions and digital financial service providers. It requires clear fee and loan disclosure and complaint contacts, and bars harassment and fraudulent deductions. In the last twelve months, in September 2026 consumer protection rules took effect under the amended Electronic Money Regulation, and they cover banks and non-bank e-money issuers. No source found since October 2023 says a financial ombudsman or complaints unit takes complaints. Operating would need a financial ombudsman or a regulator's complaints unit that takes complaints about digital financial services.

STP.short: Nothing found since 2023 names consumer-protection rules for digital finance, so no stage is set.
STP.summary: No stage is set. Nothing has been found since October 2023 that says whether consumer-protection rules apply to digital financial services in Sao Tome and Principe. No rule, draft or complaints body for digital finance has been found. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Absent would need a source from the past three years saying that no consumer-protection rules apply to digital financial services.

SWZ.short: The central bank's ombudsman took complaints, mobile money included, in 2026; enforcement on digital financial services is not on record.
SWZ.summary: Since 5 March 2019 a Central Bank of Eswatini practice note has set rules for mobile money providers, covering fee disclosure, written customer contracts and complaints handling. In October 2024 the World Bank called these consumer-protection requirements limited and said banks and mobile money providers generally comply with them. The Central Bank of Eswatini says consumers can escalate complaints to the CBE's Ombudsman. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found reports a fine, sanction, licence withdrawal or complaint figures for digital financial services. Mature would need such a report.

SYC.short: The central bank published complaint figures for payment service providers for 2025.
SYC.summary: From 1 January 2025 the Financial Consumer Protection (Complaint Handling) Regulations 2024 apply to all financial services providers in the Act's Schedule. Digital finance is not named. The Financial Consumer Protection Act came into force on 1 May 2022, with a six-month transition. No change has been found in the last twelve months. In 2025 the Central Bank received 50 complaints directly from customers of banks and payment service providers. The Central Bank of Seychelles reports that payment service providers received 25 complaints in 2025, 14 in the first half and 11 in the second.

TCD.short: Consumer-protection rules for digital finance were in force in 2026; no source found reports a complaints body.
TCD.summary: In July 2026 leconomie.info set out the CEMAC payment-institution rules Moov Money Tchad must meet to keep its licence. It must ring-fence client funds and meet solvency norms, and it must also run regular cybersecurity audits. The report dates from the last twelve months, and no earlier position has been found. No source found since October 2023 says a financial ombudsman or complaints unit takes complaints. Operating would need a financial ombudsman or a regulator's complaints unit that takes complaints about digital financial services.

TGO.short: Nothing found names consumer-protection rules for digital finance or says there is none, so no stage is set.
TGO.summary: Not found. Nothing found says whether consumer-protection rules apply to digital finance.

TUN.short: Consumer-protection rules for digital finance were in force in 2024; no source found reports a complaints body.
TUN.summary: Central Bank of Tunisia Circular No. 2024-2 is dated 29 January 2024. It governs the information given to clients on the marketing and pricing of financial products and services, and it covers remote operations. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found since October 2023 says a financial ombudsman or complaints unit takes complaints, or reports a fine, sanction or complaint figures. Operating would need a financial ombudsman or a regulator's complaints unit that takes complaints about digital financial services.

TZA.short: The central bank barred 69 digital lending apps in 2024 for breaching its consumer protection guidance.
TZA.summary: The Bank of Tanzania Financial Consumer Protection (Amendment) Regulations, GN No. 298 of 2025, are dated 23 May 2025. Kemi Advocates reports they set fee disclosure, fraud-loss refund and complaint-handling rules for all providers the bank supervises, mobile money included. The bank's financial consumer protection department takes unresolved complaints about banks, microfinance institutions and mobile money providers. It received over 1,500 complaints in 2024. On 21 November 2024 the Bank of Tanzania named 69 digital lending apps as unlicensed and in breach of its guidance note. In the last twelve months, in April 2026 the finance minister said fees on interoperability transfers between wallets and bank accounts are capped at 5,000/- for amounts above 500,000/-.

UGA.short: Regulators took complaints about mobile money and digital lenders in 2024; no source found reports enforcement on digital financial services.
UGA.summary: In March 2024 the Uganda Microfinance Regulatory Authority launched its Digital Lending Guidelines, which set conduct rules for online lenders on confidentiality, interest limits, harassment and complaints redress. Since September 2022 payment licensees have followed conduct, disclosure and complaint rules under the National Payment Systems (Consumer Protection) Regulations. The Bank of Uganda's Financial Consumer Empowerment Mechanism takes complaints about supervised financial institutions left unresolved for 21 days. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Mature would need a fine, sanction, licence withdrawal or complaint figures for digital financial services under these rules.

ZAF.short: Credit rules bound digital lenders and the financial ombud took digital banking complaints in 2026; no fine or sanction under them is on record.
ZAF.summary: The National Credit Act's affordability assessment applies to credit providers, digital lenders among them, a Financial Regulation Journal article said in February 2026. Debt review and findings of reckless lending are the remedies. The National Financial Ombud's banking division reports that mobile banking and internet banking fraud generated the most complaints in 2025, 39% of all cases received. The ombud closed 3,651 fraud cases in 2025, most of them in mobile and digital banking. In the last twelve months the credit rules were cited and not changed. No fine, sanction or licence withdrawal for digital financial services has been found. Mature would need one under these rules.

ZMB.short: The consumer protection commission handled mobile money complaints in 2024; no source found reports enforcement of the e-money fee rules.
ZMB.summary: Directives in force since 2 August 2024 ban listed e-money wallet fees and cap others. On 14 September 2024 the Bank of Zambia issued directives against unwarranted e-money charges, and an e-money institution in breach faces a fine of up to K200,000 or up to two years' imprisonment. The Competition and Consumer Protection Commission resolved 1,477 complaints in 2024, and the main ICT complaint was delayed or unreversed mobile money transactions. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found since October 2023 reports a fine or sanction under the e-money directives. Mature would need a fine, sanction, licence withdrawal or complaint figures for digital financial services under these rules.

ZWE.short: Fee rules covering mobile banking were in force in 2026; no source found reports a complaints body.
ZWE.summary: The Consumer Protection Commission said in October 2024 that the Consumer Protection Act gives consumers the right to choose how they pay. In the last twelve months, the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe directed banks and deposit-taking microfinance institutions to cap cash withdrawal fees at 2% and POS charges at 1.5% by 31 March 2026. From 1 April 2026 POS charges on local and international cards were capped at 1.5% of the transaction, up to US$20. In February 2026 the governor said the bank continued to receive complaints from the public about the cost of banking. No source found since October 2023 names a financial ombudsman or a regulator's complaints unit for digital finance. Operating would need such a body.

AGO.short: Finance, tax and payroll systems in use, with a new civil-service human-resources system launched in 2026; no published map of government systems is known.
AGO.summary: On 30 October 2026 the finance ministry issued the 2027 budget proposal's allocation by organ of state from SIGFE, the state's integrated financial management system. A September 2026 paper by CIAT authors says the tax authority's SIGT handles taxpayer registration, declarations, assessment and payment. In the last twelve months, on 29 October 2026 the public-administration ministry launched SINGERH as the civil service's new integrated human-resources system. No source found says the government has published an enterprise architecture or an inventory of its systems. Mature would need such an architecture or inventory to be published.

BDI.short: No source found from 2023 or later says the government's financial system is in use, so no stage is set.
BDI.summary: No stage is set. No source found from 2023 or later says the government's financial management system is in use. In the last twelve months, a source found named SIGFP_BI without saying that it is in use. Two further sources name the same system, and neither says it runs. Preparing would need a source from 2023 or later that says the government budgets, accounts and pays through a computer system.

BEN.short: Benin's tax office has run tax on an online platform since 2022; nothing found covers finance or payroll systems, so no stage is set.
BEN.summary: No stage is set. The tax directorate rolled out its SIGIBé platform for large and medium taxpayers in 2022. It extended the platform to small businesses in 2024. Electronic payments exceed 96% for most taxes, according to the directorate's 2025 activity report. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Nothing found says whether the budget, accounts and payments or the payroll run on a computer system. Preparing would need a source from 2023 or later that says the government budgets, accounts and pays through a computer system.

BFA.short: Nothing found says whether the government's finance, tax or payroll systems are in use, so no stage is set.
BFA.summary: Not found. Nothing found says whether the government's finance, tax or payroll systems are in use.

BWA.short: The government budgets and pays through a computer system by 2025; no source found says whether tax and payroll do too.
BWA.summary: Botswana's Minister of Communications and Innovation told Parliament on 18 March 2025 that the Government Accounting and Budgeting System (GABS) was fixed in December 2024. Technical faults had disrupted payments across all ministries, departments and agencies. The Minister said it has since run at full capacity for over 20,000 users. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found from 2023 or later says the tax authority's system or the civil-service payroll runs on a computer system. Establishing would need tax collection and the civil-service payroll to run on computer systems, shown by sources from 2023 or later.

CAF.short: The government budgets and pays through a computer system by 2025, and tax runs online; no source found says whether the payroll does too.
CAF.summary: In June 2025 the IMF noted the adoption of the integrated financial information system at the treasury directorate and in line ministries. The tax directorate's director general said in January 2025 that the e-Tax system's registration and e-filing modules were fully operational. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Nothing found from 2023 or later says how the civil-service payroll is run. The finance ministry's March 2025 plan lists an integrated human resources management system as still to be set up. Establishing would need the civil-service payroll to run on a computer system, shown by a source from 2023 or later.

CIV.short: The state budget was executed on a computer system in 2026; no source found says whether tax and payroll are.
CIV.summary: In July 2026 SNDI's deputy director general described budget execution at Katiola, where every actor in it, the prefecture included, executes and tracks its budget over a satellite network. SNDI is the state's IT company. Its chief executive said in 2014 that SIGFIP, the public finance system it built, was used across government. In the last twelve months, the July 2026 account is the only newer description of budget execution on a computer system. No source found from 2023 or later says the tax system or the civil-service payroll is in use. Establishing would need both to run on computer systems, shown by sources from 2023 or later.

CMR.short: No source found from 2023 or later says the government's financial system is in use, so no stage is set.
CMR.summary: No stage is set. No source found from 2023 or later says the government's financial management system is in use. The same holds for the tax system. Sources found name SIGIPES, ANTILOPE, SYDONIA and AIGLES, which do not answer that. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Preparing would need a source from 2023 or later that says the government budgets, accounts and pays through a computer system.

COD.short: Nothing found says whether the government's finance, tax or payroll systems are in use, so no stage is set.
COD.summary: Not found. Nothing found says whether the government's finance, tax or payroll systems are in use.

COG.summary: Not found. Nothing found says whether the government's finance, tax or payroll systems are in use.
