EGY.short: The country had a cybersecurity strategy by 2026; no incident response by a national body is known since 2023.
EGY.summary: An NTRA vice president and a deputy minister said in September 2026 that the National Cybersecurity Strategy 2023-2027 is being implemented. He said Egypt established the Supreme Cybersecurity Council. He also said NTRA monitors cyber threats around the clock. In the last twelve months, the Council was reported in November 2026 to have started work on a third edition of the strategy. No incident handled or public alert issued by the national body has been found since October 2023. Establishing would need the national body to have handled a cyber incident or issued a public alert in the past three years.

ERI.short: No source found says whether the country has a cybersecurity strategy or a national cyber body, so no stage is set.
ERI.summary: No stage is set. No source found says whether Eritrea has adopted a cybersecurity strategy or created a national cyber body. None says it has neither. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found mentions an incident response team, a designation of critical information infrastructure or a count of incidents handled. Absent would need a source from the past three years that says Eritrea has no cybersecurity strategy and no national cyber body or response team.

ETH.short: The national cyber body published an account of incidents it dealt with for a period to 2026.
ETH.summary: INSA's Director General said Ethio-CERT identified, responded to and reported more than 71,000 cyberattacks in the Ethiopian year 2018 E.C.. INSA said it thwarted more than 50,000 attacks in the first nine months of 2025/26. In the last twelve months, Proclamation No. 1426/2026 identified 12 critical infrastructure sectors, including ICT, finance, transport, health and energy. It requires owners and operators to meet 18 cybersecurity obligations. The latest dated fact is that on 29 September 2026 INSA was stated to co-chair a newly established Financial Sector Cybersecurity Forum, with the National Bank of Ethiopia.

GAB.short: The country had a national cyber body by 2026; no incident response by a national body is known since 2023.
GAB.summary: The ANINF (Agence nationale des infrastructures numériques et des fréquences) offers security-event analysis and forensics, Gabonreview reported in September 2026. Its support covers isolation and restoration. Public bodies are stated to have approached it for audits and investigations in recent months. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No incident handled or public alert issued by the national body has been found since October 2023. No designation of critical information infrastructure has been found. Establishing would need the national body to have handled a cyber incident or issued a public alert in the past three years.

GHA.short: The national cyber body published an account of incidents it dealt with for a period to 2026.
GHA.summary: The communications minister said Ghana has 13 designated Critical Information Infrastructure sectors. About 200 institutions are identified as owners, and compliance is mandatory. In the last twelve months, the Cyber Security Authority's CERT-GH responded to 3,363 cybersecurity incidents between January and June 2026, per the Communications Minister. The Authority presented counts of 4,938 incidents for January to September 2026 and 4,604 for the whole of 2025. The latest dated fact is that on 22 October 2026 the Authority and NITA issued a joint alert on two critical PHP vulnerabilities.

GIN.short: The country had a national cyber body by 2026; no incident response by a national body is known since 2023.
GIN.summary: ANSSI Guinée, the national agency for information-system security and incident response, signed a performance contract with the digital economy ministry in July 2026. Its remit covers risk assessment, crisis management and incident response. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No incident handled or public alert issued by the national body has been found since October 2023. No designation of critical information infrastructure has been found. Establishing would need the national body to have handled a cyber incident or issued a public alert in the past three years.

GMB.short: The country had a national cyber body by 2026; no incident response by a national body is known since 2023.
GMB.summary: GmCSIRT, the Gambia Computer Security Incident Response Team, describes itself as the national CSIRT. It is a government agency founded in 2020, advising operators of critical information infrastructure. The ministry's presentation lists a Gambia National Cybersecurity Strategy and policy for 2020-2026 among the country's existing policies and strategies. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No incident handled or public alert issued by the national body has been found since October 2023. Establishing would need the national body to have handled a cyber incident or issued a public alert in the past three years.

GNB.short: The country had a cybersecurity strategy by 2025; no incident response by a national body is known since 2023.
GNB.summary: In September 2025 the Council of Ministers approved the National Cybersecurity Strategy of Guinea-Bissau at its ordinary meeting, ANG reports. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No incident handled or public alert issued by a national body has been found since October 2023. No designation of critical information infrastructure has been found, and no duty on operators to report incidents. No count of incidents handled has been found. Establishing would need the national body to have handled a cyber incident or issued a public alert in the past three years.

GNQ.short: The country had a national cyber body by 2024; no incident response by a national body is known since 2023.
GNQ.summary: Article 21 of Ley 7/2024 of 23 December 2024 creates the National Agency for Cybersecurity and Critical Infrastructures (ANCIC). It is an autonomous public body under the Presidency of the Government. Its functions are to manage cybersecurity through coordinated CERT/CSIRT teams, issue alerts on cyber incidents and respond to them. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No incident handled or public alert issued by the national body has been found since October 2023. Establishing would need the national body to have handled a cyber incident or issued a public alert in the past three years.

KEN.short: The national cyber body published an account of incidents it dealt with for a period to 2026.
KEN.summary: Kenya promulgated regulations on critical information infrastructure in early 2024, says the Communications Authority's director general. The National KE-CIRT/CC states it issued 20,748,489 cyber threat advisories in April-June 2026. In the last twelve months, the centre and State House ICT restricted access to the defaced president.go.ke site to contain the attack detected on 18 July 2026. A National Cybersecurity Agency was set up under Legal Notice No. 89 of 2026, and its board was inaugurated on 2 November 2026. The latest dated figure is that for July to September 2026 the Authority counted about 2.6 billion threat events.

LBR.short: The country had a cybersecurity strategy by 2026; no incident response by a national body is known since 2023.
LBR.summary: The March 2026 National Data Governance Policy lists the National Cybersecurity Strategy among the policy instruments Liberia has adopted. In October 2026 a senator cited the strategy as a step that strengthened Liberia's policy framework. Both sources have it running to 2029. In the last twelve months it was cited and not changed. The same policy proposes a national CERT. No incident handled or public alert issued by a national body has been found since October 2023. Establishing would need the national body to have handled a cyber incident or issued a public alert in the past three years.

LBY.short: The country had a national cyber body by 2026; no incident response by a national body is known since 2023.
LBY.summary: On 20 September 2026 a meeting chaired by the minister of state discussed drawing up an integrated national cybersecurity plan. The head of the General Authority for Cybersecurity and Digital Sovereignty attended. So did the head of the National Authority for Information Security and Safety. Both are stated as existing national bodies. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No incident handled or public alert issued by a national body has been found since October 2023. Establishing would need the national body to have handled a cyber incident or issued a public alert in the past three years.

LSO.short: The country had a national cyber body by 2026; no incident response by a national body is known since 2023.
LSO.summary: In March 2023 an Oxford capacity review found Lesotho had no national cybersecurity strategy and no national CSIRT. In the last twelve months, by September 2026 the government had designated the Lesotho Communications Authority to host the national CSIRT. This came ahead of the Cybersecurity Bill 2026. In November 2026 the Authority said its LC-CSIRT now serves as the interim national CERT while a permanent body is prepared. No incident handled or public alert issued by the national body has been found since October 2023. Establishing would need the national body to have handled a cyber incident or issued a public alert in the past three years.

MAR.short: Morocco's DGSSI issues alerts and publishes yearly figures, and vital-importance infrastructures must declare incidents to it.
MAR.summary: Decree 2-11-509 of 21 September 2011 created the DGSSI. Of 879 attacks recorded in 2025, 109 needed direct intervention by its centre. Decree 2-15-712 of 2016 requires vital-importance infrastructures to declare incidents to the national centre, a white paper by the IT users' association AUSIM says. In the last twelve months, a DGSSI study found these infrastructures' compliance above average. The latest dated fact is that on 12 November 2026 the DGSSI issued a critical alert on attacks on ScreenConnect users.

MDG.short: The country had a national cyber body by 2026; no incident response by a national body is known since 2023.
MDG.summary: Madagascar's Computer Incident Response Team (CIRT) is stated to exist and operate, with a Director General, Eric Rakotomaniraka. He spoke for it at the inaugural Cybersecurity Symposium in Antananarivo on 22-23 June 2026. The CIRT is described as taking part in the December 2025 strategy launch workshop. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No incident handled or public alert issued by the national body has been found since October 2023. Establishing would need the national body to have handled a cyber incident or issued a public alert in the past three years.

MLI.short: The country had a national cyber body by 2026; no incident response by a national body is known since 2023.
MLI.summary: Decree No. 2026-0097/PT-RM of 25 February 2026 adopted the National Cybersecurity Strategy and its action plan for 2026-2030. In the last twelve months, on 10 June 2026 the Council of Ministers adopted the texts creating ANSSI, the national information systems security agency. Then Ordinance No. 2026-031 of 25 September 2026 created it. The transitional parliament ratified the ordinance on 19 November 2026. No incident handled or public alert issued by the national body has been found since October 2023. Establishing would need the national body to have handled a cyber incident or issued a public alert in the past three years.

MOZ.short: Critical information infrastructure designated by 2026; the national body publishes no recent account of incidents it dealt with that is known.
MOZ.summary: Law 13/2026, in force from 29 September 2026, makes INTIC the National Cybersecurity Authority. Critical information infrastructure operators must register with it and notify the national CSIRT of significant incidents, with fines for failing to. In the last twelve months, INTIC's chairman said the national CSIRT detected 5,654 ransomware infection attempts from January to July 2026. The Prosecutor-General said the national CSIRT logged 182,031 incidents in 2024. No account of how the body dealt with incidents in the past year has been found. Mature would need the national body to publish evidence of dealing with incidents, responding, containing or notifying and not only recording them, for a quarter or more ending within the past year.

MRT.short: The country had a cybersecurity strategy by 2026; no incident response by a national body is known since 2023.
MRT.summary: Ecofin says an April 2024 decree created the National Agency for Cybersecurity and Electronic Certification to protect national cyberspace. A government presentation of November 2024 dates the agency to 23 April 2024 and gives it the task of setting up CERT Mauritanie. The National Cybersecurity Strategy 2022-2025, which includes a planned national CERT/CSIRT, is still being implemented. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No incident handled or public alert issued by the national body has been found since October 2023. Establishing would need the national body to have handled a cyber incident or issued a public alert in the past three years.

MUS.short: The national cyber body responded to an incident or issued an alert in 2026; no critical infrastructure designation is known.
MUS.summary: The Cybersecurity and Cybercrime Act of 2021 created CERT-MU, the national response team. In the last twelve months, on 22 October 2026 CERT-MU rated the PHP2Shell flaws critical in a security bulletin. On 13 November 2026 it classed the Microsoft 365 outage as high level in a security alert. Regulations gazetted in June 2026 let the National Cybersecurity Committee designate critical information infrastructure. No source found says any system has yet been designated. Operating would need the country to designate its critical information infrastructure, or to bind the operators of critical systems to report incidents to the national body.

MWI.short: The national cyber body responded to an incident or issued an alert in 2026; no critical infrastructure designation is known.
MWI.summary: Malawi CERT is a specialised unit under MACRA. It is the national focal point for coordinating cybersecurity incidents and threat responses. In the last twelve months, Malawi CERT, through MACRA, publicly warned of exploited MikroTik router flaws in September 2026, and advised patching. MACRA said in March 2026 that the Malawi Computer Emergency Response Team currently operates under the regulator. Work is under way to make it an independent institution. No designation of critical information infrastructure has been found. Operating would need the country to designate its critical information infrastructure, or to bind the operators of critical systems to report incidents to the national body.

NAM.short: Critical information infrastructure designated by 2026; the national body publishes no recent account of incidents it dealt with that is known.
NAM.summary: In October 2024 the ICT ministry said a register of critical information infrastructure had been developed. CRAN and NAM-CSIRT have since issued National Cybersecurity Incident Management Guidelines. In the last twelve months, NAM-CSIRT confirmed unauthorised activity on the Ministry of Defence and Veterans Affairs network in September 2026. On 22 October 2026 it warned of new PHP flaws. Its newsletter for July to September 2026 counted 506,143 vulnerabilities and 163,053 cyber events. Mature would need the national body to publish evidence of dealing with incidents, responding, containing or notifying and not only recording them, for a quarter or more ending within the past year.

NER.short: The country had a national cyber body by 2025; no incident response by a national body is known since 2023.
NER.summary: On 11 October 2025 the Council of Ministers adopted the decrees creating the Centre National de Cybersécurité (CNAC). The decrees make it a public administrative establishment and approve its statutes. It is to coordinate national cybersecurity strategy, including critical systems. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No incident handled or public alert issued by the national body has been found since October 2023. No designation of critical information infrastructure has been found. Establishing would need the national body to have handled a cyber incident or issued a public alert in the past three years.

NGA.short: Critical information infrastructure designated by 2026; the national body publishes no recent account of incidents it dealt with that is known.
NGA.summary: At a workshop on 11 August 2026 the NCC Executive Vice-Chairman said telecommunications and fibre-optic infrastructure has been designated Critical National Information Infrastructure. In the last twelve months, NgCERT, hosted by the Nigerian Communications Commission, issued advisory ngCERT-2026-050005 on 24 September 2026. It is a critical-rated warning on WhatsApp vulnerabilities. An op-ed states the 2024 Designation and Protection of Critical National Information Infrastructure Order provides a policy foundation. No account of how the body dealt with incidents in the past year has been found. Mature would need the national body to publish evidence of dealing with incidents, responding, containing or notifying and not only recording them, for a quarter or more ending within the past year.

RWA.short: The country had a national cyber body by 2026; no incident response by a national body is known since 2023.
RWA.summary: The National Cyber Security Authority issued Application Software Security Directives on 16 April 2026. In the last twelve months, in October 2026 the Authority signed partnerships with Airtel Rwanda and MTN Rwanda on cybersecurity capacity. No incident handled or public alert issued by the national body has been found since October 2023. No designation of critical information infrastructure has been found, and no duty on operators to report incidents. No count of incidents handled has been found. Establishing would need the national body to have handled a cyber incident or issued a public alert in the past three years.

SDN.short: The national cyber body responded to an incident or issued an alert in 2025; no critical infrastructure designation is known.
SDN.summary: A decree of 5 November 2025 set up the Sudanese Cybersecurity Authority under the digital ministry. The authority runs Sudan-CERT, the national incident response centre. On 1 November 2025 Sudan-CERT issued a high-level warning of a ransomware wave hitting small businesses. In the last twelve months, the authority announced its official launch in January 2026. No designation of critical information infrastructure has been found. Operating would need the country to designate its critical information infrastructure, or to bind the operators of critical systems to report incidents to the national body.

SEN.short: The country had a national cyber body by 2026; no incident response by a national body is known since 2023.
SEN.summary: In 2022 the state digital operator said its cybersecurity work followed the national strategy, SNC2022. The DCSSI sets the course and norms for cybersecurity. In the last twelve months, in October 2026 the DCSSI co-organised the second cybersecurity providers forum. No incident handled or public alert issued by the national body has been found since October 2023. A bill creating a national cybersecurity authority and naming critical information infrastructure was adopted on 20 August 2026, and is not stated promulgated. Establishing would need the national body to have handled a cyber incident or issued a public alert in the past three years.

SLE.short: The national cyber body responded to an incident or issued an alert in 2026; no critical infrastructure designation is known.
SLE.summary: SierraLoaded reports that NC3, the National Cybersecurity Coordination Centre, acts through the national computer security incident response team, SL-CSIRT. In the last twelve months, NC3, through SL-CSIRT, issued a critical alert reported on 24 October 2026 on two PHP remote-code-execution flaws. NatCA, the telecom regulator, issued a public notice on 30 July 2026 acknowledging ongoing cybersecurity incidents. With the ICT ministry, NC3 developed draft critical information infrastructure protection plans, presented for validation on 26 August 2026. No designation of critical information infrastructure has been found. Operating would need the country to designate its critical information infrastructure, or to bind the operators of critical systems to report incidents to the national body.

SOM.short: The country had a national cyber body by 2026; no incident response by a national body is known since 2023.
SOM.summary: The Prime Minister inaugurated the Somalia Computer Incident Response Team (SOMCIRT) on 7 March 2026. It was created under the January 2026 Cybersecurity Law. In the last twelve months, the National Communications Authority states that the law, approved by the House of the People on 26 January 2026, establishes the team. No incident handled or public alert issued by the national body has been found since October 2023. No designation of critical information infrastructure has been found. Establishing would need the national body to have handled a cyber incident or issued a public alert in the past three years.

SSD.short: The country had a national cyber body by 2026; no incident response by a national body is known since 2023.
SSD.summary: The Cybercrime and Computer Misuse Act 2026, signed 18 February 2026, designates the authority as lead national responder to cyber threats. It requires the authority to establish a National Computer Incident Response Team Coordination Centre (SS-CIRT/CC). In the last twelve months, Diplo's 2026 profile says the National Communication Authority has created the South Sudan Computer Incident Response Team. No incident handled or public alert issued by the national body has been found since October 2023. Establishing would need the national body to have handled a cyber incident or issued a public alert in the past three years.

STP.short: The country had a cybersecurity strategy by 2025; no incident response by a national body is known since 2023.
STP.summary: AGER states that implementation of the National Cybersecurity Strategy of Sao Tome and Principe (2024-2028) is under way. AGER submitted both the strategy and its annexed action plan to a 30-day public consultation. In November 2025 AGER listed a National Cybersecurity Strategy for 2024-2029 among the country's actions. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No incident handled or public alert issued by the national body has been found since October 2023. Establishing would need the national body to have handled a cyber incident or issued a public alert in the past three years.

SWZ.short: The national cyber body responded to an incident or issued an alert in 2025; no critical infrastructure designation is known.
SWZ.summary: The Computer Crime and Cybercrime Act of 2022 made the Eswatini Communications Commission (ESCCOM) the national cybersecurity agency. In July 2025 ESCCOM investigated ransomware attacks on public bodies, among them the Eswatini Water Services Corporation. In the last twelve months, in November 2026 SzCIRT, the national response team, issued a high-severity advisory on an attack on the Optimizely platform. A World Bank project paper noted that no critical information infrastructure framework yet existed. No source found says any system has since been designated. Operating would need the country to designate its critical information infrastructure, or to bind the operators of critical systems to report incidents to the national body.

SYC.short: The country had a national cyber body by 2026; no incident response by a national body is known since 2023.
SYC.summary: The Seychelles Department of ICT launched the newly established National Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-SC). It is the country's frontline for monitoring cyber threats and coordinating national responses. In the last twelve months, CERT-SC designed and delivered the third National Cyberdrill in October 2026, which the Department of ICT hosted. No incident handled or public alert issued by the national body has been found since October 2023. No designation of critical information infrastructure has been found. Establishing would need the national body to have handled a cyber incident or issued a public alert in the past three years.

TCD.short: The country had a national cyber body by 2026; no incident response by a national body is known since 2023.
TCD.summary: Ordinance 001/PR/2026 of 22 January 2026 reformed ANSICE, extending its missions, powers and operational capacity. In the last twelve months, ANSICE presented its record and six recommendations to the CESCE on 12 August 2026. They include operationalising a national CERT and a security operations centre. The 2026 budget volume lists ANSICE with a 400,000,000 FCFA transfer line, at that figure for the third year. No incident handled or public alert issued by the national body has been found since October 2023. Establishing would need the national body to have handled a cyber incident or issued a public alert in the past three years.

TGO.short: The national cyber body responded to an incident or issued an alert in 2026; no critical infrastructure designation is known.
TGO.summary: Law 2018-026 created ANCy in December 2018, and the law makes ANCy the national authority for the security of essential infrastructure. ANCy presented the National Cybersecurity Strategy 2024-2028 in Lomé in October 2024. More than 333,000 incidents were handled between 2021 and 2024, per ANCy's director-general. In the last twelve months, in September 2026 ANCy was touring the country to raise awareness. No designation of critical information infrastructure has been found. Operating would need the country to designate its critical information infrastructure, or to bind the operators of critical systems to report incidents to the national body.

TUN.short: Tunisia's national cyber body issued alerts and handled incidents in 2025 and 2026; no source found reports the decree designating critical information infrastructure.
TUN.summary: For the first half of 2026 the ANCS published 336 tunCERT advisories and 657,540 incidents reported to those affected. For 2025 the counts were 563 advisories and 557,793 incidents. In the last twelve months, ANCS published a list of N-Cloud entries on 17 September 2026, showing the national agency operating. La Presse says a national information systems security strategy for 2026-2030 is in place, after a first cycle covering 2020-2025. No designation of critical information infrastructure has been found. The 2023 decree-law leaves the list to a decree not found issued. Operating would need the country to designate its critical information infrastructure, or to bind the operators of critical systems to report incidents.

TZA.short: Tanzania has a cybersecurity strategy and a national response team; no source found reports an incident handled or alert issued since October 2023.
TZA.summary: TZ-CERT was set up within TCRA, the communications regulator, under the Electronic and Postal Communications Act, 2010. Tanzania launched a National Cybersecurity Strategy for 2023-2028. In the last twelve months, Government Notice No. 147 of 19 June 2026 designated 25 categories of computer systems as critical information infrastructure. No incident handled or public alert issued by the national body has been found since October 2023. Establishing would need the national body to have handled a cyber incident or issued a public alert in the past three years.

UGA.short: Critical information infrastructure designated by 2026; the national body publishes no recent account of incidents it dealt with that is known.
UGA.summary: CERT.UG, operated under NITA-U, is Uganda's national computer emergency response team. On 24 July 2025 CERT.UG/CC issued a critical advisory on the SharePoint 'ToolShell' flaw chain. In the last twelve months, the 2026 information security policy became mandatory for operators of critical information infrastructure, and requires them to report security breaches to CERT.UG. No count of incidents handled for a quarter or more has been found. Mature would need the national body to publish evidence of dealing with incidents, responding, containing or notifying and not only recording them, for a quarter or more ending within the past year.

ZAF.short: The country had a national cyber body by 2026; no incident response by a national body is known since 2023.
ZAF.summary: The Cybersecurity Hub, South Africa's National CSIRT, was set up in 2015 by the then Department of Telecommunications and Postal Services. Its mandate is the National Cybersecurity Policy Framework, passed by Cabinet in March 2012. On 13 September 2018 a SADC statement said South Africa had an established and operational national CIRT. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No incident handled or public alert issued by the national body has been found since October 2023. Establishing would need the national body to have handled a cyber incident or issued a public alert in the past three years.

ZMB.short: The country had a national cyber body by 2025; no incident response by a national body is known since 2023.
ZMB.summary: The Cyber Security Act, 2025 (Act No. 3 of 2025) establishes the Zambia Cyber Security Agency in the Office of the President (s.3). The Act commenced on 12 May 2025. The Agency constitutes the Zambia Cyber Incident Response Team (s.6) to handle incidents and issue alerts. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No incident handled or public alert issued by the national body has been found since October 2023. No designation of critical information infrastructure has been found. Establishing would need the national body to have handled a cyber incident or issued a public alert in the past three years.

ZWE.short: The national cyber body responded to an incident or issued an alert in 2025; no critical infrastructure designation is known.
ZWE.summary: POTRAZ, the telecom regulator, set up a Computer Incident Response Team to handle security incidents in the country. The team handled incident reports through 2025, a third of them fraud. A Cybersecurity and Monitoring Centre also operates under the Office of the President. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No designation of critical information infrastructure has been found, and no duty on operators to report incidents. Operating would need the country to designate its critical information infrastructure, or to bind the operators of critical systems to report incidents to the national body.

AGO.short: Angola's new cybersecurity law and Law 7/17 of 2017 are in force as of October 2026; no use of either is known.
AGO.summary: Novo Jornal reported on 23 January 2026 that a UNITA deputy called Law 7/17 of 16 February part of the current legal order. The law covers the protection of computer networks and systems. In the last twelve months the Assembly adopted the new cybersecurity law on 12 August 2026, which the deputy said would repeal Law 7/17. Angola's minister said it has entered into force, as SADC reported on 16 October 2026. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty has been found in the last three years. Operating would need a dated arrest, charge, prosecution or conviction, or a penalty.

BDI.short: A 2022 cybercrime law is in force and was cited as applied in 2026; no use against anyone is known.
BDI.summary: Burundi's cybercrime law is Law No. 1/10 of 16 March 2022 on the prevention and repression of cybercrime. In the last twelve months it was cited and not changed. At a workshop in Bujumbura in February 2026 a government delegate called it adopted and in application. Participants discussed its gaps against the Malabo Convention. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty has been found in the last three years. Operating would need a dated arrest, charge, prosecution or conviction, or a penalty.

BEN.short: The 2018 Code du numérique is in force; no arrest or prosecution naming it is on record.
BEN.summary: Benin's Loi n° 2017-20 of 20 April 2018, the Code du numérique, treats illegal access to and penetration of an information system as offences in its Livre VI. No change to the code has been found in the last twelve months. Benin's Centre national d'investigations numériques reported over 6,500 digital-offence complaints in 2025, and INTERPOL's Operation Sentinel led to 106 arrests in Benin between 27 October and 27 November 2025. Neither source names the code. Operating would need a dated arrest, charge, prosecution or conviction naming the law, or a penalty.

BFA.short: A 2024 information-security law is in force; no arrest or prosecution naming it is on record.
BFA.summary: Burkina Faso's Loi n°014-2024/ALT of 9 July 2024 sets rules to control and protect information systems, with licensing and fines. In the last twelve months the Council of Ministers of 30 July 2026 adopted decrees applying it. One categorises critical-infrastructure bodies, and the other sets security audits and auditor accreditation. The cybercrime brigade arrested two people in August 2025 and 22 people in October 2025. Neither source names the 2024 law. Operating would need a dated arrest, charge, prosecution or conviction naming the law, or a penalty.

BWA.short: A 2025 cybersecurity act awaits commencement and the 2018 cybercrime act stays in force until then; no use of either is known.
BWA.summary: Botswana's Cybersecurity Act, 2025 (Act No. 21 of 2025) was assented to on 5 November 2025 and gazetted on 11 November 2025. It repeals and replaces the Cybercrime and Computer Related Crimes Act 2018, and takes effect on a date the Minister appoints by Order. In the last twelve months it was cited and not brought into force: in March 2026 the communications minister said it was expected to come into force in April. No order appointing a date has been found. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty has been found in the last three years. Operating would need a dated arrest, charge, prosecution or conviction, or a penalty.

CAF.short: A cybercrime law, Loi 24.002 of February 2024, is in force; a 2026 opinion piece says police and prosecutors use it. No case is known.
CAF.summary: The telecoms regulator ARCEP's index lists Loi 24.002 of 21 February 2024 on cybersecurity and the fight against cybercrime among the country's laws. The National Assembly had voted the bill by acclamation on 25 January 2024. No change to the law has been found in the last twelve months. An opinion piece of 18 August 2026 refers to it as wielded by the prosecutor's office and police. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty has been found in the last three years. Operating would need a dated arrest, charge, prosecution or conviction, or a penalty.

CIV.short: The 2013 cybercrime law is in force; a man was prosecuted under it in October 2025.
CIV.summary: Côte d'Ivoire's cybercrime law is law no. 2013-451 of 19 June 2013, amended by law no. 2023-593 of 7 June 2023. In October 2025 a man was prosecuted under the 2013 law for threatening to spread sexual images. The national information-security agency's platform received and handled 12,100 files in 2024, and the report as relayed does not name the law. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found shows the law in regular use in the last two years. Mature would need sources from the past two years that show it used again and again.

CMR.short: A cybercrime law from December 2010 is in force and was reviewed at a June 2026 workshop; no use against anyone is known.
CMR.summary: Cameroon's cybercrime law is Law no. 2010/012 of 21 December 2010, which a June 2026 Le Jour report treats as the existing law. In the last twelve months it was cited and not changed. A workshop in Yaounde on 8 and 9 June 2026 reviewed its articles. A Nkafu brief of 4 September 2026 called for it to be revised. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty has been found in the last three years. Operating would need a dated arrest, charge, prosecution or conviction, or a penalty.

COD.short: A digital code has been in force since 2023, and in August 2026 police were told to enforce it; no case is known.
COD.summary: The Democratic Republic of the Congo's cybercrime provisions sit in the Code du numérique, Ordonnance-loi n° 23/010 of 13 March 2023. In the last twelve months, on 17 August 2026 the Attorney General at the Court of Cassation told judicial police officers to take up offences under the Digital Code on their own initiative. In November 2026 ACP reported seven ministerial orders drafted to put the Code into effect. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty has been found in the last three years. Operating would need a dated arrest, charge, prosecution or conviction, or a penalty.

COG.short: Cybersecurity and cybercrime laws of 2020 are in force; no arrest or case under them is known.
COG.summary: The Republic of the Congo has two laws of 5 June 2020, loi n° 26-2020 on cybersecurity and loi n° 27-2020 on the fight against cybercrime. The Journal officiel of 18 June 2026 prints a decree of 6 May 2026 that cites both as in force. In the last twelve months they were cited and not changed. In its 2025 assessment, UNESCO says their application still has to be strengthened, and it cites no arrest, prosecution or conviction under either. Operating would need a dated arrest, charge, prosecution or conviction, or a penalty.

COM.short: Cybercrime offences are in the Penal Code in force since 2021; a separate cybersecurity law was only a draft; no use is known.
COM.summary: The Comoros promulgated its new Penal Code by decree on 16 February 2021, according to the national digital agency ANADEN. It is loi n°20-38/AU of 29 December 2020, and its articles 449 to 505 set out cybercrime offences. ANADEN's publication of 4 March 2021 lists a specific cybersecurity law as drafted and not yet adopted. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No case brought has been found in the last three years. Operating would need a dated arrest, charge, prosecution or conviction, or a penalty.

CPV.short: A 2021 cybersecurity decree-law is in force; no case under it is known.
CPV.summary: Cabo Verde has Decreto-lei n.º 9/2021, its cybersecurity regime, with Decreto-Regulamentar n.º 1/2021, which creates the national CSIRT. The 2026 State Budget law cites them as in place. No change to either decree has been found in the last twelve months. The NOSi plan for 2024 lists them among existing texts, and neither document records a case brought under the law. Operating would need a dated arrest, charge, prosecution or conviction, or a penalty.

DJI.short: A cybersecurity and cybercrime law has been in force since 2014; no source found says whether it has been used.
DJI.summary: Law n°66/AN/14/7ème L of 20 July 2014 on cybersecurity and the fight against cybercrime is cited by Djibouti's 2023 law ratifying the Malabo Convention. The National Assembly passed a Digital Code on 30 June 2025, with Book VI on cybersecurity and cybercrime, and its legislative section still awaited promulgation. No change to the 2014 law has been found in the last twelve months. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under either text has been found in the last three years. Operating would need a dated arrest, charge, prosecution or conviction, or a penalty.

DZA.short: A 2009 law on offences linked to information technology is treated as in force by a 2020 decree; no use of it is known.
DZA.summary: Algeria's Law 09-04 of 5 August 2009 sets rules on preventing and fighting offences linked to information and communication technologies. Presidential decree 20-05 of 20 January 2020 lists it among the laws it rests on. In the last twelve months, in March 2026 the director general of the security agency ASSI announced a draft cybersecurity bill. It would make security measures mandatory for institutions. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty has been found in the last three years. Operating would need a dated arrest, charge, prosecution or conviction, or a penalty.

EGY.short: A 2018 information technology crimes law is in force; in November 2025 courts convicted a series of content creators under it.
EGY.summary: Egypt's cybercrime law is Law 175 of 2018 on combating information technology crimes. An Economic Court ruling of November 2025 applies the law and its executive regulations, Prime Ministerial Decree 1699 of 2020. In the last twelve months, on 29 November 2025 the Cairo Economic Court sentenced video blogger Mohamed Abdel Aaty to two years and a fine under the law. It sentenced Qamar El-Wekala to six months. An MP's bill of 22 April 2026 would tighten the law's provisions. A second MP's bill would raise its penalties.

ERI.short: Eritrea's Penal Code, read in 2020, covers computer offences in place of a cybercrime act; no use of it is known.
ERI.summary: Eritrea has no separate cybercrime act. The Council of Europe cybercrime office's legal profile, in its version of 5 May 2020, maps the Penal Code to the Budapest Convention's offence articles. Article 374 covers unauthorized use of a computer, including access, interception, and data and system interference, and Article 298 covers violation of privacy. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty has been found in the last three years. Operating would need a dated arrest, charge, prosecution or conviction, or a penalty.

ETH.short: A 2016 computer crime law is in force; a court convicted a YouTube host under it in 2024. No regular use is on record.
ETH.summary: Ethiopia's cybercrime law is Computer Crime Proclamation No. 958/2016. The Federal High Court applied it in November 2024 to find Meskerem Abera guilty on two counts over two YouTube programmes. In the last twelve months, Birr Metrics reported in December 2025 that Yohanis Daniel faced an added charge under the law over a TikTok live stream. Proclamation No. 1426/2026 on critical infrastructure was signed on 21 July 2026 and takes effect in July 2027. No source found shows the law in regular use in the last two years. Mature would need sources from the past two years that show it used again and again.

GAB.short: A cybersecurity and cybercrime law, numbered 027/2023, was in force in 2025; no use of it against anyone is known.
GAB.summary: Gabonreview, on 1 June 2025, presented law no. 027/2023 on cybersecurity and the fight against cybercrime as a national law. ANINF's SecBOM tool must comply with it. In the last twelve months, a law ratifying the ordinance on social networks was promulgated by decree 0436/PR of 5 October 2026. It sets five years' imprisonment and a fine of FCFA 5 to 20 million for using another person's identifying details to deceive users. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty has been found in the last three years. Operating would need a dated arrest, charge, prosecution or conviction, or a penalty.

GHA.short: A cybersecurity law is in force; in 2026 the authority fined a state registry and a private firm under it.
GHA.summary: Digital Policy Alert says Ghana's Cybersecurity Act of 2020 sets measures for critical infrastructure, cybercrime prevention and incident response. It created the Cyber Security Authority. In the last twelve months, in December 2025 the communications minister said over 272 comments had come in on a draft amendment bill. On 13 August 2026 the Graphic reported that the Authority fined the Office of the Registrar of Companies GH¢240,000 under Section 92. It also fined Purpleline Solutions Limited GH¢120,000. No source found shows the law in regular use in the last two years. Mature would need sources from the past two years that show it used again and again.

GIN.short: A cybersecurity law is in force; in 2025 the media regulator said it will be used against web media. No case is known.
GIN.summary: Guinea has had a law on cybersecurity and personal data protection since 2016, mainly aimed at cybercrime, according to the director of ANSSI's alert centre. In the last twelve months, on 13 August 2026 ANSSI held a consultation workshop on draft texts on cybersecurity and cybercrime. They were prepared with SOCSLAWYERS to update the 2016 framework. On 26 July 2025 the media regulator's president said the law will be applied to web media that break the rules. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty has been found in the last three years. Operating would need a dated arrest, charge, prosecution or conviction, or a penalty.

GMB.short: A 2009 act with cybercrime offences is in force and a cybercrime bill was still pending in 2026; no use of either is known.
GMB.summary: The Gambia's Information and Communications Act, 2009 (No. 2 of 2009) entered into force on 29 May 2009. Its Part III of Chapter III, on computer misuse and cyber crime, creates offences such as unauthorised access to computer data. Parliament introduced a Cybercrime Bill in March 2024. In the last twelve months the Oxford Institute of Technology and Justice stated that, as at June 2026, it has not been enacted, and in November 2026 the bill was reported still under debate. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty has been found in the last three years. Operating would need a dated arrest, charge, prosecution or conviction, or a penalty.

GNB.short: No source found names a cybercrime or cybersecurity law or bill, so no stage is set.
GNB.summary: Not found. Nothing names a cybercrime or cybersecurity law or bill for Guinea-Bissau, or says there is none.

GNQ.short: Ley 7/2024 is in force; in September 2026 the vice-president's lawyers filed four complaints under it, which await the court. No charge is known.
GNQ.summary: On 1 July 2026 the Government stated that Ley 7/2024 is fully in force. The law dates from 23 December 2024 and covers social networks, computer crimes and cybercrime. In the last twelve months, on 16 September 2026 lawyers for vice-president Teodoro Nguema Obiang Mangue lodged four private criminal complaints under it at a Malabo court. They await the court. No arrest, prosecutor's charge or court decision has been found. Operating would need a dated arrest, charge, prosecution or conviction, or a penalty.

KEN.short: The Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act is in force; dozens of social media users have been arrested or prosecuted under it since 2024.
KEN.summary: Kenya's Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act of 2018 stands. The Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes (Amendment) Act, 2025 amended it from 4 November 2025. In the last twelve months, in March 2026 the Court of Appeal struck down sections 22 and 23, its false-publication offences, and upheld the rest. CPJ reports that journalist Peter Mwita was charged in a Mombasa court in February 2026 and pleaded not guilty. On 3 September 2026 Kenya launched an official guide to prosecuting 76 listed cyber offences under the Act.

LBR.short: Cybercrime law in force since 2026; used in September 2026 to arrest a commentator over images of the Vice President.
LBR.summary: President Boakai approved Liberia's Cybercrime Act on 3 July 2026. The House had passed it in 2023 and the Senate in November 2025. In the last twelve months, in September 2026 police arrested the commentator Jerry Nyantee Wrato over AI-generated images of the Vice President. The Inspector General's letter of 21 September resolved to prosecute him under sections 10.1, 15.1, 18.1 and 19.1 of the Act. A court ordered him released on habeas corpus on 22 September. No source found shows the law in regular use in the last two years. Mature would need sources from the past two years that show it used again and again.

LBY.short: A 2022 cybercrime law was cited as in force in July 2026; no use of it is known.
LBY.summary: On 15 November 2026 a House committee discussed gaps in Libya's Law No. 5 of 2022 on combating cybercrime. Cabinet Decision 358 of 15 July 2026 cites it among its legal bases for a new National Authority for Cybersecurity and Digital Sovereignty. In the last twelve months a wider cybersecurity law has been in preparation. On 15 July 2026 a House committee met National Security Council officials in Benghazi to work on the bill. No arrest, charge or conviction under the 2022 law has been found. Operating would need a dated arrest, charge, prosecution or conviction, or a penalty.

LSO.short: Cybercrime and cybersecurity bills were still awaiting Parliament in September 2026; no law in force is known, and no use of one.
LSO.summary: Cabinet split the 2024 bill into a Cybercrime Bill 2026 and a Cybersecurity Bill 2026. The Lesotho Times reports that a 2021 version was withdrawn from Parliament. It says the 2024 bill was referred but not enacted. In the last twelve months a draft was circulated in August 2026. That month the Director General of ICT said both bills were ready and waiting for approval by the National Assembly. No cybercrime or cybersecurity law in force has been found. Establishing would need a cybercrime or cybersecurity law in force, as an act of its own or as part of a penal or digital code.

MAR.short: Morocco's 2020 cybersecurity law is in force; no case or penalty naming it is on record.
MAR.summary: Morocco's Loi n° 05-20 on cybersecurity was promulgated by dahir n° 1-20-69 of 25 July 2020 and published on 6 August 2020. Décret n° 2-24-921, applying article 25, was in force by the Bulletin officiel of 20 February 2025. In the last twelve months, in November 2026 the National Defence Administration was working on a revision of the law. The DGSN counted 13,643 cybercrime cases in 2025 and 415 arrests. Neither figure names the 2020 law. Operating would need a dated arrest, charge, prosecution or conviction naming the law, or a penalty.

MDG.short: A 2014 cybercrime law is in force; in January 2026 the Presidency cited it announcing prosecutions for online insults. No source found reports regular use.
MDG.summary: Madagascar's cybercrime framework still rests in part on loi n°2014-006, adopted in June 2014. In the last twelve months, on 8 January 2026 the Presidency said prosecutions were under way for online insults. It recalled article 20 of that law. The Council of Ministers adopted a bill recasting the law on 7 July 2026. In November 2026 the government withdrew it from the Assembly's agenda. No source found shows the 2014 law in regular use in the last two years. Mature would need sources from the past two years that show it used again and again.

MLI.short: Cybercrime provisions in force since December 2024 are in regular use: three journalists were detained under them in 2026.
MLI.summary: IPI states that Mali amended its Penal Code in December 2024, incorporating provisions previously in the 2019 cybercrime law. In the last twelve months, Human Rights Watch reports that editor Youssouf Sissoko was arrested on 5 February 2026 under the 2019 law. RSF says he was sentenced on 23 March 2026 to two years in prison. The criminal chamber of the cybercrime pole had 4 cases involving 8 accused on 21 May 2026. Journalist Chahana Takiou was sentenced on 3 August 2026 to 12 months, 6 suspended. The trial of commentator Mohamed Youssouf Bathily began on 10 August 2026.

MOZ.short: Cybersecurity and cybercrime laws were signed in 2026. No use of the law is known.
MOZ.summary: INTIC says Law 13/2026 on cybersecurity and Law 14/2026 on cybercrime entered into force on 29 September 2026. Before them, the Penal Code (Law 24/2019, amended by Law 17/2020) also defined cybercrimes. In the last twelve months, Parliament unanimously approved the Cyber Security Law in April 2026, and President Chapo promulgated it in June 2026. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the laws has been found in the last three years. Operating would need a dated arrest, charge, prosecution or conviction, or a penalty.

MRT.short: A cybercrime law has been in force since 2016. No use of the law is known.
MRT.summary: Mauritania's Law no. 2016-007 on cybercrime was adopted by the National Assembly and the Senate and promulgated by the President of the Republic. It has 52 articles covering offences, search and interception powers, and international cooperation. No change to the law has been found in the last twelve months. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty has been found in the last three years. Operating would need a dated arrest, charge, prosecution or conviction, or a penalty.

MUS.short: A cybercrime and cybersecurity law has been in force since 2021; no case naming it is on record.
MUS.summary: Mauritius's Cybersecurity and Cybercrime Act 2021 was assented to on 24 November 2021 and proclaimed in force on 10 December 2021. In the last twelve months, regulations designating critical information infrastructure came into operation under it in June 2026. On 10 November 2026 the ministry said amendments had gone to the Attorney-General's Office for vetting. The police Cybercrime Unit handled 930 cases from January 2023 to January 2026, with 130 arrests. The source does not name the Act. Operating would need a dated arrest, charge, prosecution or conviction naming the law, or a penalty.

MWI.short: Malawi's 2016 cyber law is in force; a man was charged under it in 2026 for hacking phones. No regular use is on record.
MWI.summary: Malawi's Electronic Transactions and Cyber Security Act, Act 33 of 2016, was gazetted on 4 November 2016 and commenced on 1 June 2017. In the last twelve months, in October 2026 the Justice Minister said a new cybercrime bill should go to Parliament in the February to April 2027 session. Nyasa Times reports that Collins Magalasi was charged in court in September 2026 under section 83(1), read with section 89. The charge is aiding the hacking of the President's phone. In August 2024 police charged a Mzuzu man with cyber spamming under section 91. Mature would need sources from the past two years that show it used again and again.

NAM.short: Only a cybercrime bill is known, under consultation in 2026; no law in force is known, so no use of one.
NAM.summary: In December 2024 the regulator CRAN said Namibia lacks dedicated cybercrime legislation. Namibia's proposed cybercrime law is the Cybercrime Bill. In the last twelve months, a draft bill was presented to stakeholders in Windhoek on 18 February 2026, and in April 2026 the final draft was circulated ahead of a validation workshop, before it goes to Parliament. No cybercrime or cybersecurity law in force has been found. Establishing would need a cybercrime or cybersecurity law in force, as an act of its own or as part of a penal or digital code.

NER.short: A 2019 cybercrime law is in force; it was used against journalists in 2025 and a lawyer in 2026. No source found reports regular use.
NER.summary: Niger's cybercrime law is law no. 2019-33 of 3 July 2019. It was amended on 12 June 2024 to set penalties for online defamation, insults and harmful data. In the last twelve months, on 3 December 2025 the State Court upheld journalist Samira Sabou's 2020 conviction and ruled that the law applied. On 13 October 2026 the Niamey High Court convicted the lawyer Lirwana under Article 31. It sentenced him to two years and a 2 million CFA franc fine. No source found shows the law in regular use in the last two years. Mature would need sources from the past two years that show it used again and again.

NGA.short: A cybercrime law is in force and in regular use against journalists, activists and critics, among them Omoyele Sowore in 2026.
NGA.summary: Nigeria's Cybercrimes (Prohibition, Prevention, etc.) Act is an enacted law of 2015. The President signed an amendment in February 2024, after the Senate passed it in December 2023 and the House on 14 February 2024. In December 2024 activist Olamide Thomas was arrested and charged over a Facebook post. In the last twelve months the Department of State Services has been prosecuting activist Omoyele Sowore. On 30 August 2026 its Director-General said the prosecution would wait until after the 2027 election. On 15 October 2026 the Southern Africa Litigation Centre said that section 24 is repeatedly used to arrest journalists.

RWA.short: A cybersecurity law is in force, and the Supreme Court upheld one article in June 2025. No source found says whether it has been used.
RWA.summary: On 5 June 2025 Rwanda's Supreme Court upheld the constitutionality of Article 39 of the 2018 Cybercrime Law, CIVICUS Monitor reports. The article criminalises publishing rumours through digital platforms. In the last twelve months the law was cited and not changed: a commentary of 30 July 2026 in the East African Policy Observer says that Rwanda's binding legal instruments include cybersecurity law. The ruling records no arrest, charge or conviction under the law, and none has been found in the last three years. Operating would need a dated arrest, charge, prosecution or conviction, or a penalty.

SDN.short: A cybercrime law is in force and was used repeatedly in 2025 and 2026, including 17 arrest warrants against journalists in July 2026.
SDN.summary: A rights group says Sudan's Cybercrime Law was amended in 2018, 2020 and 2022. It says the Cabinet approved a further draft amendment on 13 October 2025. In the last twelve months, on 21 July 2026 the Red Sea State cybercrime prosecutor issued 17 arrest warrants, RSF reports. They name 15 journalists and two news sites. In August 2026 a criminal court in El Obeid sentenced pharmacist Ahmed Suleiman Ahmed Al-Waqi to six years, three of them under the law. On 1 November 2026 the Council of Ministers approved a draft Cybersecurity Regulation Bill 2026.

SEN.short: A cybercrime law has been in force since 2008; a man was sentenced in 2024 for an insult made through a computer system.
SEN.summary: Senegal's cybercrime law is Law 2008-10 of 25 January 2008. A 2018 practitioner source says no separate cybersecurity act had been adopted. In the last twelve months, in August 2026 the Ministry of Telecommunications and Digital Economy submitted a bill to the National Assembly's Intercommission. It would set up a National Cybersecurity Authority and CERTs. Senegal's national police recorded 3,902 cybercrime complaints in 2024 and referred 194 people to prosecutors. No source found shows the law in regular use in the last two years. Mature would need sources from the past two years that show it used again and again.

SLE.short: A cybercrime law has been in force since 2021; people were charged under it in 2024 and 2025. No regular use is on record.
SLE.summary: Sierra Leone's Cyber Security and Crime Act, 2021 was published as a supplement to the Gazette dated 25 November 2021. It sets up a response coordination centre, an advisory council and a fund, and defines offences. No change has been found in the last twelve months. A Freetown councillor was charged at Pademba Road Court in November 2025 with cyberstalking and cyberbullying, and Joseph Sesay was arraigned at the same court on 5 August 2025. No source found shows the law in regular use in the last two years. Mature would need sources from the past two years that show it used again and again.

SOM.short: Cybersecurity and cybercrime bills have moved through parliament since 2025; no law in force is known, and no use is known.
SOM.summary: The National Communications Authority states that the House of the People approved the Cybersecurity Law on 26 January 2026. In the last twelve months, the House concluded first reading of the Cybercrimes Bill on 8 December 2025. On 29 August 2026 the Senate held first reading of a 33-article cybersecurity bill, which still needs second and third readings. No cybercrime or cybersecurity law in force has been found. Establishing would need a cybercrime or cybersecurity law in force, as an act of its own or as part of a penal or digital code.

SSD.short: A cybercrime law was signed in February 2026 and put into operation in July 2026; no case under it is known.
SSD.summary: Radio Tamazuj reports that President Kiir signed South Sudan's Cybercrime and Computer Misuse Act 2026 on 18 February 2026 and that it came into force on signature. Parliament had passed the bill on 25 November 2025. In the last twelve months, Eye Radio reports that the government announced it was putting the Act into effect in July 2026. The National Cyber-Security Task Force held its first operational meeting on 16 July 2026. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law has been found. Operating would need a dated arrest, charge, prosecution or conviction, or a penalty.

STP.short: A cybercrime law has been in force since 2017; no case under it is known.
STP.summary: Sao Tome and Principe's Lei n.º 15/2017, the Lei sobre Cibercrime, was passed by the Assembleia Nacional on 28 June 2017, promulgated on 3 August 2017 and published on 6 October 2017. It creates computer-crime offences and procedural powers, and gives the Polícia Judiciária a contact point open twenty-four hours a day. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty has been found in the last three years. Operating would need a dated arrest, charge, prosecution or conviction, or a penalty.

SWZ.short: A cybercrime law has been in force since 2022; a court convicted a woman under it in 2025. No regular use is on record.
SWZ.summary: Eswatini's Computer Crime and Cybercrime Act, 2022 was published in the Government Gazette on 4 March 2022 and came into operation that day. In the last twelve months it was cited and not changed. In April 2026 the minister called it the legal groundwork, with its regulations at an advanced stage. A Mbabane woman was convicted by the Magistrates Court in August 2025 over a WhatsApp message. Two accused appeared in Manzini Magistrates Court in September 2025 on fraud charges, some under the Act. No source found shows the law in regular use in the last two years. Mature would need sources from the past two years that show it used again and again.

SYC.short: A cybercrime law has been in force since 2022 and was widened in December 2025; no case under it is known.
SYC.summary: Seychelles' Cybercrimes and Other Related Crimes Act 2021 (Act 59 of 2021) was assented on 15 December 2021 and repeals the Computer Misuse Act (Cap 254). In the last twelve months, Act 23 of 2025 amended it: the National Assembly passed the amendment on 15 December 2025 and the President assented on 22 December 2025. It widens the offences and adds search and interception powers. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty has been found in the last three years. Operating would need a dated arrest, charge, prosecution or conviction, or a penalty.

TCD.short: A cybercrime law from 2015 is listed among Chad's laws; no source found says whether it has been used.
TCD.summary: The sector regulator ARCEP's register of laws lists Loi N°009/PR/2015 on Cybersecurity and the Fight Against Cybercrime among Chad's laws. In the last twelve months, on 16 February 2026 the National Assembly approved, by 160 votes to 1, the ratification of Ordinance 001/PR/2026 of 22 January 2026. The ordinance reforms the agency ANSICE to modernise the legal framework on cybersecurity and cybercrime. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty has been found in the last three years. Operating would need a dated arrest, charge, prosecution or conviction, or a penalty.

TGO.short: A cybercrime law has been in force since 2018, amended in 2022; no case under it is known.
TGO.summary: Togo's Loi n° 2018-026 of 7 December 2018 on cybersecurity and the fight against cybercrime defines and punishes cybercrime offences. Loi n° 2022-009 of 24 June 2022 amends its articles 2, 3 and 6. No change has been found in the last twelve months. The visas of Décret n° 2022-094/PR of 9 September 2022 cite both laws as current. Operating would need a dated arrest, charge, prosecution or conviction, or a penalty.

TUN.short: Tunisia's cybercrime and cybersecurity decree-laws are in force; six journalists were prosecuted under Decree 54 in the year to April 2026.
TUN.summary: Tunisia's Decree-law no. 2023-17 of 11 March 2023 on cybersecurity sets audit, labelling, classification, incident-response and critical-infrastructure duties. Fines run from 50,000 to 100,000 dinars. Decree-law 54 of September 2022 makes spreading falsehoods by electronic means an offence. The journalists' union SNJT recorded six prosecutions of journalists under Decree 54 between April 2025 and April 2026. In the last twelve months, an amendment replacing jail with fines of 10,000 to 20,000 dinars for a first offence took effect on 30 September 2026.

TZA.short: A cybercrime law has been in force in Tanzania since 2015; no case under it is known.
TZA.summary: Tanzania's Cybercrimes Act, Chapter 443 in the Revised Edition 2023, originally Act No. 14 of 2015, commenced on 1 September 2015. It applies to Mainland Tanzania and Zanzibar. In the last twelve months it was cited and not changed. The ICT Minister said on 19 August 2026 that section 29 sets penalties for damaging critical ICT infrastructure. They are a fine of not less than 100m/- or three times the damage, imprisonment of at least five years, or both. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty has been found in the last three years. Operating would need a dated arrest, charge, prosecution or conviction, or a penalty.

UGA.short: The Computer Misuse Act is in force, and in 2026 police arrested three men over alleged fake news and personal data posts.
UGA.summary: Nilepost says Uganda's cyber-offence framework is anchored in the Computer Misuse Act, 2011 as amended in 2022, in an account dated 1 September 2026. The Constitutional Court struck down Sections 11, 23, 26, 27, 28 and 29 of the Act, leaving the rest standing. No other change has been found in the last twelve months. In September 2026 Kampala Metropolitan Police arrested and held three men over alleged fake news and unlawful disclosure of personal data on social media, and charges were not disclosed. No source found shows the law in regular use in the last two years. Mature would need sources from the past two years that show it used again and again.

ZAF.short: A cybercrime law has been in force since 2021; 37 cases under it were on court rolls in November 2024.
ZAF.summary: South Africa's Cybercrimes Act 19 of 2020 was signed on 26 May 2021 and came partly into operation on 1 December 2021. A parliamentary reply of 29 November 2024 put 37 cases with 88 charges under the Act on court rolls. In the last twelve months, the Acting Minister of Police told Parliament in October 2026 that the Hawks had registered eight cyber fraud, extortion and ransomware cases over three years. They had made one arrest. No separate cybersecurity act exists, and in October 2025 a Hawks cybercrime head said a Cybersecurity Bill was still to come.

ZMB.short: Two cyber laws passed in 2025 are in force; a journalist was arrested under one in August 2026; no regular use is on record.
ZMB.summary: Zambia has a Cyber Crimes Act and a Cyber Security Act, both of 2025. They replaced the 2021 Cyber Security and Cybercrime Act. The Global Network Initiative says the President signed both into law on 8 April 2025. In the last twelve months, Paradigm Initiative, citing the African Union's preliminary report, says ZNBC journalist MacPherson Mukuka was arrested under section 10 of the cybercrime law. He had recorded a private conversation during the August 2026 elections. No source found shows the law in regular use in the last two years. Mature would need sources from the past two years that show it used again and again.

ZWE.short: Cybercrime offences in the criminal code, amended 2021, are in force, and officials describe a wider law in 2026; no case of use is known.
ZWE.summary: On 24 January 2026 the Director General of POTRAZ stated that Zimbabwe has no standalone cyber crimes act. Cybercrime offences are in force instead in sections 163 to 168 of the Criminal Law (Codification and Reform) Act, which was amended in 2021. In the last twelve months, on 15 October 2026 a POTRAZ official described a Cybersecurity Act as holding cybercrime definitions alongside cybersecurity provisions in one law. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty has been found in the last three years. Operating would need a dated arrest, charge, prosecution or conviction, or a penalty.

AGO.short: A data centre ran on dedicated power lines from the substation in 2025; no source found reports power set aside for data centres.
AGO.summary: Raxio Group runs data centres in Angola. In December 2025 its chief technology officer said Raxio builds medium-voltage lines direct from the substation to each of its facilities. He said it always uses two power lines, each able to carry the load, plus diesel generators. No earlier position has been found, so no change is recorded in the last twelve months. No PUE and no water figure has been found for a data centre in Angola. Establishing would need power set aside for data centres: a signed supply contract, a plant built for them, or a tariff or zone in force.

No source found says power is set aside for data centres. In the last twelve months, in December 2025, he said Raxio always uses two such lines, plus diesel generators, in every market. That repeats the design and does not change it. CMR.summary: ST Digital's Douala01 data centre has two utility feeds, one power transformer and three backup generator sets. The operator gives these figures, and a design and yearly PUE both under 1.5, in its 2024 OCP Ready self-assessment. No change has been found in the last twelve months. COG.summary: On 27 October 2026 the regulator ARPCE said nationwide power cuts and scarce diesel were badly disrupting data centres. In the last twelve months, on 22 September 2026, the government said works on the national data centre stood at 82%. The 12 MW Kintelé solar farm is being built to keep its power stable and is not yet in service. No power usage effectiveness (PUE) of 1.6 or less has been found for any data centre in service, nor a figure for water use or cooling that uses no water. ZAF.summary: CPT1 in Cape Town takes wheeled solar power under an agreement signed in March 2023. Teraco's CEO reported an average yearly PUE of 1.43 for 2025, and Teraco gives its water use as 0.04 litres per kWh in 2024, down from 0.10 in 2023. Both figures are Teraco's own. In the last twelve months, Teraco says the first wind power from its own producer reached its Cape Town data centres in September 2026.

AGO.short: Two data centres for hire at Tier III or above in service by 2026.
AGO.summary: In July 2026 AFR-IX Telecom was deploying into Raxio's data centre in Luanda. Raxio says it is Tier III certified. Paratus Group says its two Luanda data centres are Tier III by design. Paratus Angola opened the second in 2019. In the last twelve months, the government inaugurated its National Data Centre and Cloud at Camama on 28 April 2026. Menos Fios reported in May that its 12 modules are certified Tier III. No global cloud region has been found in the country. Mature would need a global cloud provider to sell its services from a cloud region in the country.

BDI.summary: By 2020 the World Bank reported that Burundi Backbone System has one level-3 data center, built at a cost of USD 2 million. The operator uses it to offer hosting to customers, and other public agencies use it to back up their systems. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found states that a data centre for hire in Burundi is Tier III or above, and no global cloud region has been found. Establishing would need one data centre for hire at Tier III or above.

BEN.short: A data centre for hire in service by 2026, none found at Tier III or above.
BEN.summary: In April 2026 an ASIN official said Benin has several data centres, one of them run commercially by SBIN. MTN Benin rents servers and storage to businesses at its data centre. In the last twelve months, SBIN's Celtiis Business launched Celtiis Cloud in Cotonou on 31 July 2026, selling hosting, storage, backup and colocation. No source found states that a data centre for hire in Benin is Tier III or above, and no global cloud region has been found. Establishing would need one data centre for hire at Tier III or above.

BFA.summary: By 2025 BTW Media described the Virtix data centre of Virtual Technologies & Solutions in Ouagadougou as Tier III, with no certifying body named. It offers colocation, cloud and hosting services. In the last twelve months, IKA Solution launched IKA Cloud in Ouagadougou on 31 July 2026, selling web hosting, dedicated servers and server colocation to outside customers. No second data centre for hire at Tier III or above has been found, and no global cloud region. Operating would need two or more data centres for hire at Tier III or above.

He says it sells colocation, cloud, IaaS and disaster recovery to external customers. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No global cloud region has been found. Raxio says CIV1 is Uptime Institute Tier III certified and sells carrier-neutral colocation. In October 2025 the digital ministry said ST Digital's new Grand-Bassam data centre was built to Tier III norms. No change has been found in the last twelve months. CMR.summary: Orange Business Cameroun describes its data centre, open since May 2017 with 340 racks in two white rooms, as Tier III+. In the last twelve months, Camtel said in June 2026 that its Zamengoe data centre is certified Tier III by the Uptime Institute. In June 2025 ST Digital's chief executive had said Camtel's holds the Uptime Institute's Tier III design certificate. In August 2026 Camtel presented its hosting services to institutions and businesses. No global cloud region has been found. Mature would need a global cloud provider to sell its services from a cloud region in the country.

In October 2024 DatacenterDynamics reported both as Uptime Institute Tier III certified and described the OADC Texaf site as a colocation facility. In the last twelve months this was cited and not changed: in August 2026 Raxio described its DRC facility as Tier III certified and carrier-neutral. No global cloud region has been found. Mature would need a global cloud provider to sell its services from a cloud region in the country.

COG.short: Two data centres for hire at Tier III or above in service by 2026.
COG.summary: On 28 February 2024 the President commissioned the regulator ARPCE's Tier 3+ data centre at Pointe-Noire, which hosts data of the public administration and private firms. ARPCE gives the Tier on its own word, naming no certification. ST DIGITAL says its centres in seven countries, Congo among them, are Tier 3 facilities. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No global cloud region has been found. Mature would need a global cloud provider to sell its services from a cloud region in the country.

The same page says a separate neutral data centre is still under construction. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found states that a data centre for hire in the Comoros is Tier III or above, and no global cloud region has been found. Establishing would need one data centre for hire at Tier III or above.

CPV.summary: NOSi's 2024 accounts state that the Praia data centre holds Uptime Institute Tier III certification and report revenue from housing and IaaS services. NOSi, the state technology enterprise, operates secure data centres in Praia and Mindelo and offers cloud services to public and private entities. In the last twelve months, NOSi launched a solar power system for the Praia data centre on 16 February 2026. No second data centre for hire at Tier III or above has been found, and no global cloud region. Operating would need two or more data centres for hire at Tier III or above.

DJI.short: Two data centres for hire at Tier III or above in service by 2024.
DJI.summary: In November 2024 Wingu Africa launched its Tier 3 carrier-neutral data centre at the TO7 Technology Park, with a design capacity of 3 MW. Djibouti Telecom describes its Djibouti Data Center as Tier 3, with colocation for customers, and the IFC says it has been in service since 2013. In the last twelve months, a World Bank diagnostic of September 2026 found the two main data centres nearly full, Agence Ecofin reported. No global cloud region has been found. Mature would need a global cloud provider to sell its services from a cloud region in the country.

Iconsnet operates two data centres, in Algiers and Oran, offering cloud computing and off-site backup. In the last twelve months, the Mohammadia complex of the national digital services centre was inaugurated on 5 July 2026. Le Jeune Independant says it holds Tier III Design certification. A second data centre for hire at Tier III or above has not been found. Operating would need two or more data centres for hire at Tier III or above.

EGY.short: Two data centres for hire at Tier III or above by 2026, and a global cloud region in the country.

Telecom Egypt's Regional Data Hub at Smart Village holds Uptime Institute Tier III certification of design, facility and operation. Huawei announced it launched the Huawei Cloud Cairo Region on 21 May 2024, its first public cloud region in North Africa. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Commercial data centre capacity across Egypt stood at 28 MW in November 2026.

ERI.short: A data centre for hire in service by 2026, none found at Tier III or above.
ERI.summary: By 2026 Eritel Telecom Corporation's own service page offers paid Eritel Nextcloud private-cloud subscriptions in Silver, Gold and Platinum tiers of 100 to 500 GB. Eritel says they are hosted in its own datacenters. An operator data centre in Eritrea is therefore selling hosting to outside customers. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found states that a data centre for hire in Eritrea is Tier III or above. Establishing would need one data centre for hire at Tier III or above.

ETH.short: Two data centres for hire at Tier III or above in service by 2026.

In April 2024 Wingu Africa said its ICT Park data centre in Addis Ababa had met the criteria for the same certificate. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No global cloud region has been found. Mature would need a global cloud provider to sell its services from a cloud region in the country.

GAB.summary: On 3 July 2026 Gabon's first national data centre, run by ST Digital, opened at Nkok, and it hosts the data of the state, firms and citizens. TechAfrica News says it was built to Tier III international standards. The digital economy ministry calls it the Nkok Sovereign Tier III Datacenter. In the last twelve months, the Nkok opening is the only change found. A second data centre for hire at Tier III or above has not been found. Operating would need two or more data centres for hire at Tier III or above.
