In the last twelve months, on 8 May 2026 the secure titles agency ANATS and Airtel Tchad signed a partnership to identify mobile subscribers. ANATS is to verify Airtel's customer data, and the two systems are to be linked. No source found since October 2023 shows a service in use checking people against the ID system. Establishing would need a service in use checking people against the national ID, such as SIM registration or a bank's KYC.

TGO.short: Public services signed people in against the national identification number in 2026; no source found reports use in a second sector.
TGO.summary: A December 2024 decree requires telecom operators to record each subscriber's ANID identification number at SIM registration and to see the card, giving existing operators 12 months to comply. In the last twelve months, ANID's 2026 deck says the unique identification number is used through verification and authentication across the ecosystem. It is used to sign in to the public services portal. The deck also shows the identification number in use in microfinance institutions, without describing a check. Operating would need services in two or more sectors checking people against the national ID.

TUN.short: Services in two or more sectors checked people against the national ID in 2026; no source found reports volumes.
TUN.summary: E-Houwiya is open to banks for remote onboarding and KYC under Central Bank rules of February 2025. In the last twelve months, since 1 July 2026 the national business register's procedures have required a digital identity, Mobile ID for people. A September 2026 circular gives the agriculture ministry's bodies until 15 November 2026 to authenticate users through E-Houwiya. The 2026 playbook lists Tunisie Telecom, CNAM, CNSS, five banks, La Poste and insurers among its integrators, with no total. Mature would need a figure for verifications made against the ID, or a count of the services relying on it.

TZA.short: Use of the national ID by other services was reported with figures in 2026.
TZA.summary: In a 2025 presentation, NIDA counts 124 institutions integrated with its consent-based eKYC, 55 government and 69 private. The Ministry of Home Affairs counted 147 institutions connected to NIDA's system. It put 66 as public and 81 as private, with 17 added from July 2025 to April 2026. In the last twelve months, by August 2026 the government spokesman said 157 institutions, 72 government and 85 private, were linked to NIDA's system and could verify the people they serve.

UGA.short: Use of the national ID by other services was reported with figures in 2024.
UGA.summary: URSB's ICT commissioner said in 2025 that business registration has a real-time link with NIRA for identity verification. The Bank of Uganda reports 74 financial institutions with NIRA database access for KYC. In the last twelve months, NIRA says 10 of its 107 partner institutions were checking customers by NIN and biometrics through its new system by 28 October 2026. In October 2026 the gender ministry said 43,000 older people could not draw SAGE cash grants. The ages on their national ID cards made them ineligible.

ZAF.short: Use of the national ID by other services was reported with figures in 2026.
ZAF.summary: Banks, mobile networks and insurers use the population register check, among them Capitec, TymeBank, Vodacom and MTN, in a report of January 2026. In the last twelve months, SASSA biometrically verified 997,379 grant beneficiaries from September 2025 to March 2026. Home Affairs says the justice cluster alone runs over 180,000 checks a day through its service. In September 2026 the minister said voter registration is verified through an electronic interface with the population register.

ZMB.short: Farm-input vouchers and banks checked people against the national ID in 2026; no count of those checks is known.
ZMB.summary: The FISP e-Voucher farm-input subsidy uses eKYC checks to cut ghost beneficiaries. It ran in all 116 districts by January 2026. Developers were trained in 2025 to link the SmartCarePro health record to the ID. In the last twelve months, in May 2026 the Bank of Zambia said Home Affairs charges banks about 80 cents for each successful API check. The central bank is also building a central eKYC platform on the Home Affairs digital ID. No figure for checks against the ID has been found. Mature would need a source from the past three years giving a figure for verifications made against the ID, or counting the services relying on it.

ZWE.short: Mobile money providers and the Electoral Commission checked people against the Civil Registry in 2026; no source found says how many checks.
ZWE.summary: In June 2026 the Reserve Bank governor said all mobile money providers verify customers against the Civil Registry at onboarding and in later reviews. Ghost and duplicate wallets were shut down once the registry was linked to subscriber records. In the last twelve months, in July 2026 the Justice Minister said the Electoral Commission was already using the Registrar-General's population database to verify voters. Nothing found gives a figure for checks made against the Civil Registry. Mature would need a figure for verifications made against the ID, or a count of the services relying on it.

AGO.short: Angola has cables landing at two Luanda stations and a land link to Namibia (2026), and capacity is sold wholesale on SACS.
AGO.summary: Angola's submarine cables land in Luanda at two stations, Sangano and Cacuaco, Angola Telecom said in July 2026. Angola Cables runs the Sangano station for SACS, which has joined Luanda to Fortaleza in Brazil since 2018. In the last twelve months, Unitel opened its 2Africa landing station at Cacuaco in December 2025. Angola Telecom also reported a fibre link from Santa Clara to Ondjiva in Namibia, carrying both countries' operators' services. In September 2026 Ciena said Angola Cables sells wholesale capacity on SACS and its MONET cable.

BDI.short: Two independent fibre routes abroad by 2021; no cable of more than 100 Tbps is known to carry its traffic.
BDI.summary: In July 2021 the regulator ARCT said Burundi reaches the EASSy, SEACOM and TEAMS cables through its neighbours. It lists two fibre crossings each with Rwanda, the DRC and Tanzania. Burundi Backbone System joins Tanzania's backbone at Kabanga and Manyovu, under a contract renewed in February 2024. In the last twelve months, TTCL and Burundi Backbone System agreed in September 2026 to raise that link from 4 Gbps to 10 Gbps. No source found says a cable of more than 100 Tbps design capacity carries Burundi's traffic. Operating would need such a cable, such as 2Africa or Equiano, to carry the country's traffic.

BEN.short: Two independent fibre routes abroad by 2026; no source found says whether other operators buy capacity on them.
BEN.summary: The deal record states Maroc Telecom's West Africa submarine cable lands at Cotonou. Its south segment was operational in July 2021. In the last twelve months, Mobile Europe reported on 15 July 2026 that CSquared's architecture includes the Equiano cable, landing in Nigeria and Togo. It says the cable reaches Benin by terrestrial backbone. No source found says other operators buy capacity at the landing station or on the routes, or that they run on open-access or wholesale terms. Mature would need other operators to buy capacity at the landing station or on the cable, or the cable to run on open-access or regulated wholesale terms.

BFA.short: Two independent fibre routes abroad by 2026; no source found says whether other operators buy capacity on them.
BFA.summary: Maroc Telecom's 5,700 km transafrican terrestrial fibre cable runs from Morocco to Niger via Mauritania, Mali and Burkina Faso. The record gives 2022 as its year of completion. In the last twelve months, Agence Ecofin said on 17 August 2026 that Burkina Faso relies on Cote d'Ivoire, Ghana and Togo for submarine-cable capacity. Mobile Europe said on 15 July 2026 that Equiano reaches the country over CSquared's terrestrial backbone. No source found says other operators buy capacity on these routes, or that they run on open-access or wholesale terms. Mature would need other operators to buy capacity at the landing station or on the cable, or the cable to run on open-access or regulated wholesale terms.

BWA.short: Two independent fibre routes abroad by 2018; no source found says whether other operators buy capacity on them.
BWA.summary: BoFiNet counts three international submarine cable systems for Botswana: EASSy, WACS and Equiano, in its report to March 2025. Paratus Botswana opened its 840 km Kalahari fibre on 29 May 2024. It completed a route to Equiano at Swakopmund in Namibia. In the last twelve months, BoFiNet raised its capacity through two crossings into South Africa from 300 Gbit/s to 1 Tbit/s in September 2026. No source found says other operators buy capacity at the landing station or on the cable. Mature would need other operators buying capacity on the cable, or the cable on open-access or regulated wholesale terms.

CAF.short: Two independent fibre routes abroad by 2026; no cable of more than 100 Tbps is known to carry its traffic.
CAF.summary: Agence Ecofin said on 12 October 2026 that the Central African Republic has two terrestrial fibre links to neighbours, through Cameroon and through Congo-Brazzaville. They run on the Central African Backbone, about 935 km of fibre. In the last twelve months, a ministry official said on 30 August 2026 that the planned Congo-Brazzaville interconnection remains to be realised. No source found says a cable of more than 100 Tbps design capacity carries the country's traffic. Operating would need such a cable to carry the country's traffic.

CIV.short: Two or more fibre routes abroad by 2024; no source found says whether two are independent of each other.
CIV.summary: Five submarine cables land at Abidjan, the regulator ARTCI reported: SAT-3, ACE, WACS, MainOne and Maroc Telecom's West Africa cable. Developing Telecoms counts six, with 2Africa. MainOne's branch landed at Grand Bassam, near Abidjan, and entered service in December 2019. In the last twelve months, the 2Africa branch was back in service at the end of July 2026, after two days of outages. No source found says two of the routes land at different stations, or run through two different neighbours. Operating would need two routes that share no landing station, and a cable of more than 100 Tbps design capacity carrying the country's traffic.

CMR.short: Two independent fibre routes abroad by 2024; no cable of more than 100 Tbps is known to carry its traffic.
CMR.summary: A 2024 report of the regulator ART, quoted by Ecomatin, says Camtel has three landing stations, at Kribi, Limbe and Douala, for the SAT3, WACS, NCSCS and SAIL cables. The same report says Camtel's capacity lets it sell international transmission to national and sub-regional operators. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found says a cable of more than 100 Tbps design capacity carries Cameroon's traffic. Operating would need such a cable, such as 2Africa or Equiano, to carry the country's traffic, beside the routes already in service.

COD.short: Two independent fibre routes abroad by 2026, and other operators buy capacity on them.
COD.summary: WACS and 2Africa both land at Muanda on the Atlantic coast, Ecofin reported. WACS was connected in 2013, and 2Africa landed in September 2023. In the last twelve months, 2Africa went live in December 2025, and Airtel put it into service with 200 Gbps on 18 December 2025. Paratus switched on its 2,000 km G2M fibre from Goma to Mombasa on 9 February 2026, and says it carries traffic for its first wholesale customers. The WACS segment between the DRC and Congo was back in service on 16 November 2026 after repairs.

COG.short: Congo has two submarine cables and fibre links to five neighbours (2025); no source found says whether other operators buy capacity.
COG.summary: Congo has been on the WACS cable since 2012, and the President activated the 2Africa connection at Pointe-Noire on 28 February 2024. The minister said in May 2025 that Congo is linked by fibre to five neighbours. In the last twelve months, a cut on 2 January 2026 took out WACS, then the main international link. WACS was repaired on 12 February 2026. A further fault on 29 October 2026 sent Congo Telecom's traffic to backup links. Mature would need other operators buying capacity on the cable, or the cable on open-access or regulated wholesale terms.

COM.short: Two or more fibre routes abroad by 2024; no source found says whether two are independent of each other.
COM.summary: Digital Watch Observatory states Comoros is linked to regional and global fibre systems including EASSy, FLY-LION3 and 2Africa. The Comorian minister said 2Africa will be a fourth international submarine cable joining those already operational. Comores Câbles states on an undated page that 2Africa has been put into service. Huawei Marine announced it delivered the 260 km Avassa submarine cable between Grande Comore, Anjouan and Mayotte. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found says two of the routes land at different stations, or run through two different neighbours. Operating would need two routes that share no landing station, and a cable of more than 100 Tbps design capacity carrying the country's traffic.

CPV.short: Two or more fibre routes abroad by 2026; no source found says whether two are independent of each other.
CPV.summary: Caboverde24, citing Cabo Verde Telecom, reported in September 2026 that WACS, EllaLink and SHARE currently reach Praia, with direct routes to Lisbon, West Africa and Fortaleza in Brazil. All three land at Praia. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found says other operators buy capacity on these routes, or that they run on open-access or wholesale terms. No source found says two of the routes land at different stations, or run through two different neighbours. Operating would need two routes that share no landing station, and a cable of more than 100 Tbps design capacity carrying the country's traffic.

DJI.short: Two independent routes and a high-capacity cable by 2024, with over 50 operators buying capacity at the landing stations; no source found reports open-access terms.
DJI.summary: Djibouti Telecom runs two landing stations, YAC A and Haramous, with eight submarine systems between them. Djibouti Telecom says its cable stations serve more than 50 telecom operators, African Business reported in May 2024. In the last twelve months, the prime minister put the number of cables landing in Djibouti at 14 in March 2026. La Nation said in January 2026 that Djibouti Telecom holds the monopoly of international telecoms. The finance minister said in September 2026 that twelve cables land in Djibouti. No source found says capacity is sold on regulated wholesale terms.

DZA.short: Two independent fibre routes abroad by 2026; no cable of more than 100 Tbps is known to carry its traffic.
DZA.summary: Algeria is connected through four submarine cable systems, the minister told parliament in January 2026. Algerie Telecom's 2024 deck places them at three coastal cities: Oran and Algiers for the cables to Spain, Annaba for SEA-ME-WE 4. In the last twelve months, traffic moved to other cables during maintenance on the Algeria-Spain cable in October 2026, and service returned to normal on 27 October. No source found says a cable of more than 100 Tbps design capacity carries the country's traffic. Operating would need such a cable, such as 2Africa or Equiano, to carry the country's traffic.

EGY.short: Two independent fibre routes abroad by 2025, and other operators buy capacity on them.
EGY.summary: Telecom Egypt operates 10 landing stations on the Mediterranean and Red Sea coasts, among them Alexandria, Port Said, Ras Ghareb, Suez and Zafarana. 2Africa lands at Ras Ghareb and Port Said, Telecom Egypt said in November 2025. It completed SEA-ME-WE-6 landings at the same two stations in July 2025. Telecom Egypt runs WeConnect, an open and neutral platform for cross-connecting the cable systems at its landing stations. In the last twelve months, the minister said in September 2026 that 20 international subsea cables cross Egypt, carrying 90% of internet traffic between Europe and Asia.

ERI.short: A 2026 source says no submarine cable lands, and no land route abroad is on record.
ERI.summary: In August 2026 Mesob Journal said Eritrea is the only coastal African state without an operational submarine cable landing station. The same piece proposes a landing at Massawa or Assab and an exchange point in Asmara. In June 2024 Middle East Eye reported cable firms looking at Eritrea's waters as a route avoiding Yemen, and that the government did not reply to their requests. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found names a land link abroad, or says there is none. Preparing would need one fibre route to carry the country's internet traffic abroad: a submarine cable landing in the country, or a fibre link through a neighbour.

ETH.short: One fibre route abroad in service by 2026; no second route is known.
ETH.summary: La Nation's profile of Djibouti Telecom lists a terrestrial cable between Djibouti and Ethiopia in the operator's network, linking Ethiopia to Djibouti's submarine cable landings. This is the one international fibre route found in service. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found names a second international fibre route in service. Nothing has been found saying other operators buy capacity on this route, or that it runs on open-access or wholesale terms. Establishing would need a second international fibre route in service, even one that shares a landing station or a neighbour with the first.

GAB.short: Gabon has four submarine cables and fibre links to three neighbours (2026); no source found says whether other operators buy capacity.
GAB.summary: TM Africa said in September 2026 that Gabon lands four subsea cable systems: 2Africa, ACE, Maroc Telecom's West Africa cable and SAT-3/WASC. ACE Gabon operates the Libreville landing station. In the last twelve months, full ACE service was restored on 4 June 2026 after a fault on 27-28 May. In October 2026 SPIN's director-general said the national backbone links Gabon physically with Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea and Congo. He said cross-border traffic stays low. No source found says other operators buy capacity at the Libreville landing or on the land links. Mature would need other operators buying capacity at the landing station or on the cable, or the cable on open-access or regulated wholesale terms.

GHA.short: Ghana's cables land at Accra and a land link reaches a high-capacity cable in Togo (2026); no source found says whether other operators buy capacity.
GHA.summary: Ghana's regulator counts five submarine cable providers: SAT-3, MainOne, WACS, Glo and ACE. In the last twelve months, 2Africa was activated in late 2025, with MTN's Bayobab leading its landing in Ghana. CSquared said in July 2026 that its backbone carries Ghana's traffic to Equiano, which lands in Nigeria and Togo. The regulator's November 2024 authorisation template lets its holder provide capacity on a submarine cable to licensed operators. The template names no holder and no cable. Mature would need other operators buying capacity at the landing station or on the cable, or the cable on open-access or regulated wholesale terms.

GIN.short: One submarine cable is Guinea's only fibre route abroad in 2026; a second cable is planned, not in service.
GIN.summary: The ACE consortium says ACE landed at Conakry as Guinea's first international cable and entered service on 15 December 2012. In the last twelve months, the Medusa cable was signed in May 2026 to be Guinea's second. On 27 October 2026 the ministry's secretary general told MPs that Guinea depends on a single submarine cable, close to saturation. Actu7 wrote in August 2026 that the Medusa link is not yet in service. No source found names a second international fibre route in service, by sea or through a neighbour. Establishing would need a second international fibre route in service, even one sharing a landing station or a neighbour with the first.

GMB.short: Two independent fibre routes abroad by 2026; no cable of more than 100 Tbps is known to carry its traffic.
GMB.summary: GAMTEL states two international routes in service: the ACE cable, and a 28 Gbps backup link with Free in Senegal. It says traffic is rerouted automatically to the backup if ACE fails. In the last twelve months, the ACE cable station at Sukuta lost power on 4 June 2026, causing a nationwide outage, The Point reported. TechGriot wrote in September 2026 that The Gambia remains dependent on a single undersea cable, with terrestrial redundancy through Senegal still thin. No source found says a cable of more than 100 Tbps design capacity carries the country's traffic. Operating would need such a cable, such as 2Africa or Equiano, to carry the country's traffic.

GNB.short: One submarine cable is Guinea-Bissau's only fibre route abroad in 2024; no second route is known to be in service.
GNB.summary: Guinea-Bissau joined its first international submarine cable, ACE, in March 2023. Agence Ecofin says the country's international connectivity is confined to the coast. In June 2024 ECOWAS said the six countries of its Amilcar Cabral cable project, Guinea-Bissau among them, each have one landing station. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found names a second international fibre route in service. Establishing would need a second international fibre route in service, even one sharing a landing station or a neighbour with the first.

GNQ.short: Two independent fibre routes abroad by 2025; no cable of more than 100 Tbps is known to carry its traffic.
GNQ.summary: Ceiba-2, a 400 km cable linking Malabo, Bata and Kribi in Cameroon, was inaugurated on 4 June 2018 beside the ACE cable. On 10 November 2025 the national backbones of Gabon and Equatorial Guinea were joined at Meyo-Kyé and Ebebeyin. In the last twelve months, Ecofin said in October 2026 that the country still relies mainly on the ACE cable. GITGE's annual report, from about 2016, says it sells capacity to ISPs and government companies on open, non-discriminatory terms. No source found says a cable of more than 100 Tbps design capacity carries the country's traffic. Operating would need such a cable to carry the country's traffic.

KEN.short: Two or more fibre routes abroad by 2026; no source found says whether two are independent of each other.
KEN.summary: The Communications Authority's June 2026 figures put Kenya's international bandwidth at 28,950 Gbps over seven cable systems. They are SEACOM, TEAMS, EASSy, Lion2, DARE1, PEACE and 2Africa, all landing at Mombasa. In the last twelve months, Seacom opened a Nairobi-Kisumu-Kampala route in June 2026. Seacom says traffic moves inland from the Mombasa landing stations. No source names separate landing stations for any two cables. Operating would need two routes that share no landing station, and a cable of more than 100 Tbps design capacity carrying the country's traffic.

LBR.short: Two independent fibre routes abroad by 2025; no cable of more than 100 Tbps is known to carry its traffic.
LBR.summary: Orange Liberia's chairman said its fibre link to Cote d'Ivoire let Liberia keep 100% of its international internet traffic, during a four-day ACE cable outage. The LTA chairman said a second landing at Buchanan is sought but not yet built. In the last twelve months, TechAfrica News reported Liberian officials saying the country depends on a single international route, the ACE submarine cable. It lands at one point in Monrovia. No source found says a cable of more than 100 Tbps design capacity carries the country's traffic. Operating would need such a cable, such as 2Africa or Equiano, to carry the country's traffic.

LBY.short: One fibre route abroad in service by 2025; no second route is known.
LBY.summary: The Medusa submarine cable, 8,700 km and linking Libya to Mediterranean countries, was inaugurated on 10 May 2025 at Misrata, according to the state holding company LPTIC. Libya United International Company signed the connection contract in November 2023. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found names a second international fibre route in service. Nothing has been found saying other operators buy capacity on this route, or that it runs on open-access or wholesale terms. Establishing would need a second international fibre route in service, even one sharing a landing station or a neighbour with the first.

LSO.short: Two or more cable routes abroad, all through South Africa in 2026; no source found says whether other operators buy capacity on them.
LSO.summary: In November 2026 Capacity said Lesotho has no cable landing of its own. It said the country's international traffic reaches global networks over links across the border into South Africa. The regulator's sector review, on data collected in August 2016, found Lesotho's operators drew international bandwidth from the WACS, EASSy and SEACOM cables. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found says Lesotho's routes run through a neighbour other than South Africa. Operating would need two routes that share no landing station, and a cable of more than 100 Tbps design capacity carrying the country's traffic.

MAR.short: Two or more fibre routes abroad by 2026; no source found says whether two are independent of each other.
MAR.summary: The Conversation said in August 2026 that Morocco is connected to about ten submarine cables, Africa-1 and 2Africa among them. In the last twelve months, Orange Maroc announced the landing of the Medusa cable at Nador on 16 December 2025. Le Matin describes the station as the first open-access cable landing station in the kingdom. No source found says two of the routes land at different stations, or run through two different neighbours. Operating would need two routes sharing no landing station, and a cable of more than 100 Tbps design capacity carrying the country's traffic.

MDG.short: Madagascar's cables land at three stations, one a high-capacity cable (2024); no source found says whether other operators buy capacity.
MDG.summary: Madagascar is linked by four submarine cables, Madagascar Newsroom said in December 2024: Lion 1 and 2, EASSy, METISS and 2Africa. EASSy lands at Toliara in the south-west, METISS at Fort Dauphin in the south-east and 2Africa at Mahajanga in the north-west. Telma said in February 2023 that EASSy, LION and METISS reach the country through its national backbone. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found says other operators buy capacity at the landing station or on the cable. Mature would need other operators buying capacity at the landing station or on the cable, or the cable on open-access or regulated wholesale terms.

MLI.short: Two independent fibre routes abroad by 2021; no source found says whether other operators buy capacity on them.
MLI.summary: Afribone Mali says its international links run over optical fibre through Dakar and Abidjan to the ACE and MainOne submarine cables. In the last twelve months, the national fibre backbones of Mali and Senegal were interconnected and inaugurated on 5 October 2026 at Kidira-Diboli, the Malian government portal said. Agence Ecofin says the link gives landlocked Mali a route to the 2Africa, ACE and SAT-3 cables landing in Senegal. It describes the link as an additional corridor to an existing terrestrial axis. No source found says other operators buy capacity on these routes. Mature would need other operators buying capacity at the landing station or on the cable, or the cable on open-access or regulated wholesale terms.

MOZ.short: Two independent fibre routes abroad by 2025, and other operators buy capacity on them.
MOZ.summary: 2Africa lands at Maputo and Nacala, while EASSy and SEACOM both land at Maputo, Submarine Networks said in July 2025. Vodacom Mozambique says it built the landing station at Nacala, with direct links to Europe and the Americas. The research network MoRENet had 60 Gbps abroad by October 2025, over two routes. No change has been found in the last twelve months. WIOCC agreed on 23 July 2025 to deliver capacity on 2Africa East to the operator Tmcel, which is not the cable's owner.

MRT.short: One fibre route abroad in service by 2026; no second route is known.
MRT.summary: Mauritania has been connected to the ACE cable since 2011 and still depends on it, with no fully operational alternative, Ecofin said in May 2026. In the last twelve months, a second cable began coastal installation on 4 May 2026, with service expected in January 2027. On 1 May 2026 Moov Mauritel said it had put the West Africa cable into operation. Ecofin's report four days later still describes ACE as the single system. No source found names a second international fibre route fully in service. Establishing would need a second international fibre route in service, even one sharing a landing station or a neighbour with the first.

MUS.short: Two or more fibre routes abroad by 2026; no source found says whether two are independent of each other.
MUS.summary: Mauritius had five submarine fibre cables, Defimedia said in May 2024: SAFE, LION, EASSy, METISS and MARS. Mauritius Telecom had put a sixth, T3, into operation days earlier. Telecom Review Africa listed four systems in July 2025: SAFE, LION, LION2 and METISS. Mauritius Telecom's chief executive counted five cables in February 2026. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found says two of the routes land at different stations, or run through two different neighbours. Operating would need two routes sharing no landing station, and a cable of more than 100 Tbps design capacity carrying the country's traffic.

MWI.short: Two independent fibre routes abroad by 2025; no cable of more than 100 Tbps is known to carry its traffic.
MWI.summary: Airtel Malawi says it has increased its international connectivity from three to five fibre routes. It says these include new links through Tanzania and through Mozambique via Nacala. TNM says it acquired additional fibre routes into Malawi via Zambia and Mozambique, after subsea cable cuts left it only the Mchinji/Chipata link. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found says a cable of more than 100 Tbps design capacity carries the country's traffic. Operating would need such a cable, such as 2Africa or Equiano, to carry the country's traffic.

NAM.short: Namibia has two submarine cables and a land route to Johannesburg (2026), and other operators buy capacity on the Equiano cable.
NAM.summary: Telecom Namibia says WACS has served since 2011 and Equiano landed on 1 July 2022, both at Swakopmund. It activated capacity on Equiano at its new cable station on 31 July 2024. In the last twelve months, Paratus called its Trans-Kalahari fibre route from Windhoek to Johannesburg another route out of the country in October 2026, with onward access to east coast cables such as SEACOM. On 12 June 2026 Telecom Namibia agreed to give Angola Telecom 1 Tbps of dedicated capacity on Equiano. It will also host Angola Telecom's equipment at its landing station.

NER.short: One fibre route abroad in service by 2022; no second route is known.
NER.summary: Maroc Telecom's 5,700 km transafrican terrestrial cable runs from Morocco to Niger via Mauritania, Mali and Burkina Faso, and is recorded as completed in 2022. It lets Moov Africa Niger reach international bandwidth. In the last twelve months, the ministers of Niger and Algeria presided on 6 October 2026 at Assamaka over the official launch of operation of the trans-Saharan fibre backbone, which links Niger to Algeria. The report gives no capacity. It does not say Niger's traffic runs over it. No source found names a second international fibre route in service. Establishing would need a second international fibre route in service.

NGA.short: Two independent fibre routes abroad by 2025, and other operators buy capacity on them.
NGA.summary: Nigeria's cables land at two stations: most at Lagos, and 2Africa at Qua Iboe, the first landing outside Lagos. TechCabal states Nigeria has eight active subsea cable systems, with combined design capacity of about 370 Tbps. Equinix and MainOne provide the 2Africa landing facilities, middle-mile fibre and carrier-neutral data centre PR1, for network operators, cloud providers and enterprises. In the last twelve months, MainOne activated a multi-gigabit connection at Victor Attah airport, Uyo, on 8 August 2026.

RWA.short: Three fibre routes abroad through Tanzania and Kenya by 2024; no cable of more than 100 Tbps is known to carry its traffic.
RWA.summary: Rwanda has three international fibre routes to the SEACOM cable, through Tanzania and Kenya, the investment board's guidebook said in March 2024. The Internet Society lists land links to Burundi, the DR Congo, Tanzania and Uganda, and no submarine cable. In the last twelve months, Paratus switched on its 2,000 km fibre from Mombasa to Goma in February 2026, through Nairobi, Kampala and Kigali. It carries traffic for its first wholesale customers. No source found says a cable of more than 100 Tbps design capacity carries the country's traffic. Operating would need such a cable, such as 2Africa or Equiano, to carry the country's traffic.

SDN.short: Cables at Port Sudan and land links to four neighbours by 2024; no cable of more than 100 Tbps is known to carry its traffic.
SDN.summary: Sudan has land fibre links to Ethiopia, Egypt, South Sudan and Chad, beside submarine cables at Port Sudan, the Internet Society said in March 2024. A 1 Gbps undersea link for aid agencies opened at Port Sudan in August 2024, built with Sudatel. In the last twelve months, DCD said in February 2026 that Port Sudan connects several cables to the Middle East and Europe. It named none of them. Djibouti Telecom's chief executive said at a signing on 4 February 2026 that cables run between Port Sudan and Jeddah. No source found says a cable of more than 100 Tbps carries the country's traffic. Operating would need such a cable, such as 2Africa or Equiano, to carry it.

SEN.short: A land route and several cables, among them 2Africa, carried traffic abroad by 2025, and other operators reach the cables at a neutral facility.
SEN.summary: ACE, MainOne, SAT-3, SHARE and 2Africa were named in January 2025 among the submarine cables landing in Dakar. In May 2025 Phase 3 Telecom and Sonatel activated a 3,500 km land route from Lagos to Dakar, through Benin, Togo and Ghana. In the last twelve months, Sonatel said 2Africa entered service at its Senegal landing station in December 2025, with a nominal capacity of 180 Tbit/s. Onix runs a carrier-neutral data centre at that station. In 2023 it said the centre gives companies direct access to several subsea cables and backhaul routes on carrier-neutral terms.

SLE.short: One submarine cable is Sierra Leone's only fibre route abroad in 2024; a second landing is planned, not in service.
SLE.summary: The ACE cable has served Sierra Leone since 15 December 2012, landing at Freetown. In 2024 The Conversation said only one fibre cable comes into the country. In June 2024 ECOWAS said the six countries of its Amilcar Cabral cable project, Sierra Leone among them, each have one landing station. In the last twelve months, the government announced in November 2026 a National Cable Consortium to land a second cable, a 45 million dollar project. It is planned, not in service. No source found names a land route through a neighbour. Establishing would need a second international fibre route in service, even one sharing a landing station or a neighbour with the first.

SOM.short: Two independent fibre routes abroad by 2022, and other operators buy capacity on them.
SOM.summary: DatacenterDynamics lists Somalia's current landings as DARE1 at Mogadishu and Bosaso and Gulf2Africa at Bosaso and Berbera. Two cables therefore land at different stations. The same source reports that Hormuud Telecom's newly completed Somali cable landing station is open-access and will accommodate various submarine cables. In the last twelve months, The Star reported that Somcable Submarine Network operates two international subsea landings, 2Africa and PEACE, at the Port of Berbera. Its chief technology officer calls them two physically diverse routes.

SSD.short: One fibre route abroad in service by 2023; no second route is known.
SSD.summary: South Sudan has no submarine cable landing of its own and depends on land fibre links to its neighbours. In August 2025 ITWeb Africa reported that it still had only one fibre connection, a 200 km line from Uganda to Juba, with links from Kenya and Djibouti only planned. In the last twelve months, the regulator set up a committee to oversee the international gateway in January 2026. A World Bank plan of August 2026 names a land link across the border with Kenya. No source found names a second international fibre route in service. Establishing would need a second international fibre route in service, even one sharing a landing station or a neighbour with the first.

STP.short: One fibre route abroad in service by 2013; no second route is known.
STP.summary: The World Bank records that the ACE submarine cable landed in Sao Tome and Principe in November 2011, and that it was commercially launched in February 2013. The ACE consortium states the 17,000 km cable entered service on 15 December 2012. It lists a landing station at Sao Tome and Principe, where ACE is the first international submarine cable to land. The World Bank says the country's participation was on an open-access basis through STP-Cabo SARL. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found names a second international fibre route in service. Establishing would need a second international fibre route in service, even one sharing a landing station or a neighbour with the first.

SWZ.short: Two or more fibre routes abroad by 2023; no source found says whether two are independent of each other.
SWZ.summary: UASF states that EPTC's connectivity relied on an upstream provider in South Africa through its North, West and South routes. ESCCOM's investigation confirmed that Jenny Internet Eswatini used a direct cross-border fibre link at the Malutha Border Post, which bypassed EPTC's backbone. In the last twelve months, the Commission ordered Jenny to use EPTC backbone connectivity from 1 July 2026. No source found says two of the routes land at different stations, or run through two different neighbours. Operating would need two routes sharing no landing station, and a cable of more than 100 Tbps design capacity.

SYC.short: Two or more fibre routes abroad by 2026; no source found says whether two are independent of each other.
SYC.summary: Seychelles Cable Systems says PEACE is Seychelles' second submarine fibre cable landing, in service from 16 November 2022. It says PEACE runs alongside the SEAS cable commissioned over ten years earlier. The World Bank project information document says Seychelles has three submarine cables. No change has been found in the last twelve months. The source does not name the SEAS landing station. No source found says two of the routes land at different stations. Operating would need two routes sharing no landing station, and a cable of more than 100 Tbps design capacity carrying the country's traffic.

TCD.short: Two fibre routes through Cameroon to one landing station by 2026; no route avoiding Cameroon is known.
TCD.summary: Russell Southwood wrote in November 2026 that Chad has two routes to the Camtel landing station at Kribi, with a third planned. In March 2026 Chad told ITU-D that a 35 km fibre link to Cameroon is its only operational link. Chad's telecoms minister said in October 2026 that only one international access, through Cameroon, is active. In the last twelve months, the minister told the ITU Plenipotentiary Conference in November 2026 that three links with Cameroon and Sudan are completed. No source found says a route that avoids Cameroon is in service. Operating would need two routes sharing no landing station, and a cable of more than 100 Tbps design capacity.

TGO.short: Two or more fibre routes abroad by 2025; no source found says whether two are independent of each other.
TGO.summary: Lomé Data Centre states its own direct access to four submarine cables, ACE, 2Africa, WACS and Equiano, on a page dated 24 September 2025. Data Landscapers lists one cable landing station for CSquared, for the Equiano cable at Lomé. In the last twelve months, Mobile Europe reported on 15 July 2026 that CSquared's architecture includes Equiano, landing in Nigeria and Togo. It says the system reaches Benin, Ghana and Burkina Faso by terrestrial backbone. No source found says two of the routes land at different stations, or run through two different neighbours. Operating would need two routes sharing no landing station, and a cable of more than 100 Tbps design capacity carrying the country's traffic.

TUN.short: Two independent fibre routes abroad by 2026, and other operators buy capacity on them.
TUN.summary: The US ITA commercial guide says Tunisie Telecom, the leading international connectivity provider, manages three sub-sea cables. INT decision 165/2013 orders the national operator to offer alternative operators regulated, cost-oriented access to international capacity. In the last twelve months, Orange Tunisie announced on 24 June 2026 that MEDUSA is in operational service via the Bizerte landing station. It says MEDUSA carries its first international traffic and has four fibre pairs of 24 Tbps each. Medusa describes its system as carrier-neutral.

TZA.short: Two independent fibre routes abroad by 2025; no source found says whether other operators buy capacity on them.
TZA.summary: In June 2025 the ministry said three submarine cables are active: SEACOM, EASSy and 2Africa. They land in Dar es Salaam. In July 2025 the minister said the Horohoro route with Kenya gives Tanzania a land path to eight undersea cables through Kenya. In the last twelve months, a minister counted four submarine cable stations in July 2026, without naming them. No source found says other operators buy capacity at the landing station or on the cables. Mature would need other operators buying capacity at the landing station or on the cable, or the cable on open-access or regulated wholesale terms.

UGA.short: Two independent fibre routes abroad by 2025, through Kenya and Tanzania; no high-capacity cable is known to carry its traffic.
UGA.summary: Xalam Analytics wrote in July 2025 that Uganda's few routes abroad run mainly over the Seacom and EASSY cables, through Tanzania and Kenya. In the last twelve months, Seacom opened a Nairobi-Kisumu-Kampala route on 17 June 2026, with 1 Tbps lit. Paratus switched on its 2,000 km G2M route from Mombasa through Nairobi and Kampala to Goma in February 2026. ITWeb Africa reported in September 2026 that Liquid had added a third route from Mombasa to the Uganda border. No source found says a cable of more than 100 Tbps design capacity carries the country's traffic. Operating would need such a cable to carry the country's traffic.

ZAF.short: Two independent fibre routes abroad by 2024, and other operators buy capacity on them.
ZAF.summary: The Conversation Africa says southern Africa's internet comes largely through two landing stations in South Africa, at Melkbosstrand near Cape Town and Mtunzini in northern KwaZulu-Natal. Bayobab says 2Africa West is open for business with South African landings at Yzerfontein and Duynefontein. Teraco states its Cape Town campus is connected to all subsea cable systems landing in the Cape region: ACE, Equiano, SAT-3, SAFE, WACS and 2Africa. Xalam Analytics states South Africa's wholesale fibre regulatory regime is the most open in Africa. No change has been found in the last twelve months.

ZMB.summary: Zambia has fibre links to eight neighbouring countries, its technology minister, Felix Mutati, said in February 2026. In the last twelve months, Bayobab and Vodacom Mocambique opened a fibre interconnection at the Zambia-Mozambique border on 21 February 2026. It gives Zambia a route to subsea cables on the Indian Ocean coast, including direct connectivity to 2Africa. No source found says other operators buy capacity at the landing station or on the cable. Mature would need other operators buying capacity at the landing station or on the cable, or the cable on open-access or regulated wholesale terms.

The International Telecommunication Union's series put the share at 69.1 per cent in 2022, 69.5 per cent in 2023 and 70 per cent in 2024.
