AGO.short: Angola has an interoperability framework written and none adopted; no source found says whether public bodies will be required to follow it.
AGO.summary: The work began in March 2025 with Estonia's Digital Nation, funded by the World Bank. The Instituto de Modernização Administrativa's terms of reference of February 2026 say a seven-month study with 25 public institutions produced a Framework and Roadmap of Interoperability. In the last twelve months, a regional progress report says the institute completed the framework study and its platform roadmap in the first half of 2026. None of these sources names an instrument adopting the framework or gives a date for adoption. Establishing would need a framework for how government systems exchange data to be adopted and published.

BDI.short: A May 2024 notice sought a consultant to write Burundi's government interoperability framework; no source found says whether drafting has begun, so no stage is set.
BDI.summary: No stage is set. A May 2024 notice sought a consultant to write Burundi's government interoperability framework, and no later source says drafting began. Also found is the EAC Secure Data Sharing Framework (proposed regional cross-border data flow framework), a regional proposal. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No government interoperability framework has been found in drafting, adopted or required. Preparing would need a framework, standard or regulation for how government systems exchange data to be written or out for consultation.

BEN.short: Benin's interoperability framework, instituted by decree in 2020 and supervised by a national committee, governed more than 120 connected systems in 2025.
BEN.summary: The Cadre d'interopérabilité, published by the state digital agency, is instituted by decree 2020-209 of 18 March 2020. It sets four levels, juridical, organisational, semantic and technical, and five common infrastructure components. In May 2025 Benin told ID4Africa that more than 120 systems had been integrated through the exchange platform that runs under the framework. In the last twelve months, a new architecture policy for state information systems went to sectoral consultation in Cotonou on 30 June 2026. The agency's legal note of July 2026 treats the framework as in place. A national interoperability committee supervises.

BFA.short: Burkina Faso adopted a general interoperability framework by prime ministerial order in 2018; no source found says whether public bodies must follow it.
BFA.summary: Burkina Faso's Référentiel général d'interopérabilité, a normative document fixing the rules for compatibility between public administrations' information systems, was adopted by order of the Prime Minister on 23 May 2018. The account of the adoption is a news report of 15 October 2019. It names no body charged with enforcing the rules. In the last twelve months the framework was cited and not changed. In May 2026 the government told the World Health Assembly that its regulatory framework includes it. Operating would need a decree, law, regulation or circular that makes the framework compulsory and names the body that enforces it.

BWA.short: Botswana's 2025 Digital Services Act requires an information exchange framework, and one is being aligned with donor support; none is issued.
BWA.summary: Section 12 of Botswana's Digital Services Act, assented to in October 2025, requires the Digital Services Authority to establish a standardised Framework for Secure Exchange of Information. The Act comes into force by ministerial order. A European Union-funded project running from August 2024 to August 2027 is working with the government to improve and align the National Interoperability Framework. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found says the exchange framework has been issued, and no public body is reported as bound by either text. Establishing would need a framework for how government systems exchange data to be adopted and published.

CAF.short: Nothing found says Central African Republic has a government interoperability framework, or says it has none, so no stage is set.
CAF.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a government interoperability framework, or says there is none.

CIV.short: Cote d'Ivoire adopted a general interoperability framework by decree in 2021 and binds public bodies to it; the enforcing body is not named.
CIV.summary: Decree 2021-913 of 22 December 2021 adopts the Référentiel Général d'Interopérabilité des Systèmes d'Information, annexed to it, as the general framework of technical rules for the interoperability of information systems. Its third article binds public bodies to comply with the framework. The decree was made on the joint report of the ministers for the digital economy and for the public service, who are charged with carrying it out. It names no separate body that enforces compliance. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Operating would need a decree, law, regulation or circular that makes the framework compulsory and names the body that enforces it.

CMR.short: Cameroon's draft e-government law, validated by officials in November 2025, would set interoperability rules for public bodies; it is not adopted.
CMR.summary: A workshop at Ebolowa from 3 to 14 November 2025 gave technical validation to the draft e-government bill on access to public information and the digital transformation of the administration. The project that supports the reform says the bill provides that administrations must make their information systems compatible, with GovTech Cameroun setting the security and interoperability norms. No source found says the bill has been adopted. The account of 20 November 2025 gives no date for its passage through parliament. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Establishing would need a framework for how government systems exchange data to be adopted and published.

COD.short: DR Congo's government adopted draft public-sector digital norms, including an interoperability standard, in April 2022; no source found says whether any order makes them compulsory.
COD.summary: The government adopted the draft digital norms and standards for the public sector on 15 April 2022, in five books that include the Référentiel Général d'Interopérabilité. A workshop on 2-3 February 2022 had validated the books. The minister said the norms would be given legal force by ministerial order, and the article reports none as issued. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Operating would need a decree, law, regulation or order that makes the framework compulsory and names the body that enforces it.

COG.short: Congo said in September 2026 it is developing a national digital architecture as the reference for connecting public systems; none is adopted.
COG.summary: Congo's digital economy ministry said on its news page of 2 September 2026 that the country is committing to develop a National Digital Architecture built on the principles of digital public infrastructure. The page describes it as the reference framework for interconnecting public and private information systems. The page dates from the last twelve months, and no earlier position has been found. It cites no instrument adopting the architecture, gives no timetable and names no body that will hold it. Establishing would need a framework for how government systems exchange data to be adopted and published.

COM.short: Nothing found says Comoros has a government interoperability framework, or says it has none, so no stage is set.
COM.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a government interoperability framework, or says there is none.

CPV.short: The government told the World Bank's GovTech survey in 2025 that its interoperability framework is in draft; no adopted framework has been found.
CPV.summary: The government told the World Bank's GovTech survey in 2025 that its Public Administration Information Systems Interoperability Framework is in draft or planned. The survey line gives 2026 as the year. In the last twelve months, in December 2025, IMIJ reported about 62 public and private institutions connected to its national identification systems. NOSi runs PDEX, an API publication and subscription platform for the state. No source found says an interoperability framework is adopted and published. Establishing would need a framework for how government systems exchange data to be adopted and published.

DJI.short: Djibouti's state information systems agency issued a national interoperability framework in 2022; no source found says whether public bodies must follow it.
DJI.summary: The Agence Nationale des Systèmes d'Information de l'État issued the Cadre d'Interopérabilité de Djibouti as the national interoperability framework, setting out principles and four layers of interoperability. The document is dated 2022. A consultancy says it drafted the national interoperability framework for the agency in a project that ran from May 2022 to April 2023. Neither source names a decree or circular that makes the framework compulsory for ministries, and neither counts the public bodies that exchange data under it. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Operating would need a decree, law, regulation or circular that makes the framework compulsory and names the body that enforces it.

DZA.short: Algeria's decree of December 2025 makes a national interoperability system the only route for data exchange between public bodies; use is not yet reported.
DZA.summary: Executive decree 19-271 of 7 October 2019 set a national interoperability framework for information systems. In the last twelve months, the Journal officiel of 30 December 2025 carried presidential decree 25-320, which makes the national interoperability system the exclusive framework for data exchange between public institutions and administrations. The decree puts the system under the High Commission for Digitalisation. On 20 September 2026 the Council of Ministers ordered a further presidential decree on the secure digital interoperability plan between state bodies. No source names the bodies exchanging data under it. Mature would need a dated source that names or counts the public bodies that exchange data under the framework.

EGY.short: Egypt's 2024 Cloud First Policy says legislation on exchanging official data is being drafted; no adopted interoperability framework has been found.
EGY.summary: Egypt's Cloud First Policy, published in 2024, names the Supreme Council of Digital Society, its executive office and its specialised committees. It says they started developing national legislation on the classification, provision and exchange of official data and information. In the last twelve months, in July 2026, the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology reported 105 government bodies connected to its Government Digital Transformer. It also runs the Government-to-Government project with the Ministry of Interior. No adopted framework for how government systems exchange data has been found. Establishing would need a framework for how government systems exchange data to be adopted and published.

ERI.short: A 2022 index recorded no government interoperability framework in Eritrea; nothing dated since says whether one exists, so no stage is set.
ERI.summary: No stage is set. No framework or draft has been found on record for Eritrea. No source dated in the last three years says the government has neither a framework nor one being written. Also found are ASYCUDA World and the National identity card (new electronic card). No change has been found in the last twelve months. Absent would need a source from the past three years that says the government has no interoperability framework and none is being written.

ETH.short: Ethiopia approved a government interoperability framework by 2019; a 2023 assessment found the main services portal did not follow it.
ETH.summary: The Ministry of Innovation and Technology's library of guidelines and standards lists the Ethiopian Government Interoperability Framework of 2019 with the status Approved. Its e-government assessment of February 2023 refers to the approved framework. It found that the E-Services Portal offers no data interoperability features, a departure from the approved framework. In July 2024 the ministry was leading an interoperable digital government initiative, with a governance and compliance document for the framework attached. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Operating would need a decree, law, regulation or circular that makes the framework compulsory and names the body that enforces it.

GAB.short: Gabon's digital agency was drawing up a national interoperability framework in December 2025; no source found says whether it is adopted or required.
GAB.summary: A World Bank appraisal document of 15 June 2021 set a baseline of No for a common interoperability framework governing secure data exchange within government. In the last twelve months, as reported on 22 December 2025, the ANINF is drawing up a national interoperability framework under the Gabon Digital programme. The report lists interoperability of public systems among the remaining challenges. No source found says the framework is adopted and published, or that a text requires public bodies to follow one. Establishing would need a framework for how government systems exchange data to be adopted and published.

GHA.short: Ghana adopted an e-government interoperability framework in 2008; a 2022 draft update calls its implementation ineffectual.
GHA.summary: The National Information Technology Agency's draft update says the first Government of Ghana e-government interoperability framework, with the Government of Ghana Enterprise Architecture, was adopted in 2008. Version 2.0 of the framework is labelled a draft for stakeholder review, dated 2022. The draft says implementation of the 2008 framework was ineffectual and that the framework is out of date. No source found says version 2.0 has been approved or names an instrument that makes either version compulsory. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Operating would need a decree, law, regulation or circular that makes the framework compulsory and names the body that enforces it.

GIN.short: Guinea's digital agency lists interoperability rules at version 0.2.2, with no date and no adopting act, so no stage is set.
GIN.summary: No stage is set. No framework or draft is on record for Guinea, and no source dated in the last three years says the government has neither. Also found are the document Normes Procédures Règles d'Interopérabilité des SI v0.2.2, X-Road and GovStack. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Preparing would need a framework, standard or regulation for how government systems exchange data to be written or out for consultation.

GMB.short: The Gambia said in April 2026 that a national enterprise architecture framework governs interoperability; it was still being validated a month later.
GMB.summary: In April 2026 the Ministry of Communications and Digital Economy told a United Nations commission about a national enterprise architecture framework, led by the government ICT agency. It said the framework is ensuring interoperability across government systems through open standards, shared services and national governance. The statement dates from the last twelve months, and no earlier position has been found. It gives no date of adoption and names no ministry exchanging data under it. It cites no decree, regulation or circular that makes the framework compulsory. Establishing would need a framework for how government systems exchange data to be adopted and published.

GNB.short: Guinea-Bissau approved a national interoperability regulation by decree in October 2025; no source found says who enforces it.
GNB.summary: The government approved the regulation through Decree 27/2025, published in the Boletim Oficial of 31 October 2025. The Council of Ministers had approved the draft decree on the Regulation on Interoperability of Systems and Digital Platforms of Public and Private Services in July 2025. The regulation sets common technical standards so that systems can exchange data. In the last twelve months it was cited and not changed: in August 2026 the programme reported the national interoperability regulation as approved. The decree's text has not been found, and no source names the body that enforces it. Operating would need a decree, law, regulation or circular that makes the framework compulsory and names the body that enforces it.

GNQ.short: A 2024 World Bank diagnostic says Equatorial Guinea has no national interoperability framework; none is reported as being written.
GNQ.summary: A World Bank diagnostic of 2024 states that the government has no national interoperability framework and no government enterprise architecture framework. A report of July 2024 says the diagnostic recommends a national interoperability framework, describing it as currently absent. The diagnostic says public sector systems do not communicate with each other. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source dated since 2024 reports a framework being drafted, and none names a body charged with writing one. Preparing would need a framework, standard or regulation for how government systems exchange data to be written or out for consultation.

KEN.short: Kenya launched its interoperability framework in 2026, and every ministry, county and agency must now adopt it; no source found says how many have.
KEN.summary: The ICT Authority's published second edition of the Government Enterprise Architecture and Government Interoperability Framework sets out an interoperability charter and data, technical and metadata standards. It leaves its approval date blank. In the last twelve months, in April 2026, Kenya launched the ICT Authority Interoperability Framework, setting standards for government platforms to share data. Kenya's 2026/27 performance contract guidelines make every ministry, county, department and agency put the architecture and framework in place. Each sends its architecture to the State Department for ICT for approval and registers its systems and APIs. No source counts the bodies that have done so. Mature would need a dated source that names or counts the public bodies that exchange data under the framework.

LBR.short: An April 2026 executive order requires Liberia's new technology office to produce an interoperability framework; nothing says drafting has begun, so no stage is set.
LBR.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a government interoperability framework, or says there is none.

LBY.short: A regional commission proposed an interoperability framework for Libya in December 2025; nothing says drafting has begun, so no stage is set.
LBY.summary: No stage is set. No framework or draft is on record for Libya, and no source dated in the last three years says the government has neither. Also found are LyGIF and the National Directory of Government Data, both in one linked document. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Preparing would need a framework, standard or regulation for how government systems exchange data to be written or out for consultation.

LSO.short: Lesotho's finance minister in February 2025 and a consultancy in March 2026 said a government interoperability framework is being developed; no source found reports adoption.
LSO.summary: On 19 February 2025 the Minister of Finance and Development Planning told Parliament that the Government of Lesotho Enterprise Architecture and Interoperability Framework is being developed. The government had issued terms of reference for the Government of Lesotho Enterprise Architecture and a standalone e-Government Interoperability Framework, on a page dated 22 July 2024. In the last twelve months the position was repeated and not changed. In March 2026 a consultancy said it is supporting the Ministry of Information, Communications, Science, Technology and Innovation in developing the e-Government Interoperability Framework. No source found says the framework is adopted and published. Establishing would need a framework for how government systems exchange data to be adopted and published.

MAR.short: The World Bank's GovTech survey lists a general interoperability framework for Morocco as in draft or planned for 2026 in its 2025 round.
MAR.summary: The World Bank's GovTech survey, in its 2025 round, lists a General Interoperability Framework for Morocco as in draft or planned, with 2026 as the framework's year. Morocco's Agency for Digital Development owns an e-government interoperability platform built by Minsait, described in 2022. The same agency runs Jisr, which recorded 55 million data exchange operations in one year, reported in February 2024. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found says a government interoperability framework is adopted and published. Establishing would need a framework for how government systems exchange data to be adopted and published.

MDG.short: Madagascar published its interoperability framework in 2022 and made a decree on interoperability's institutions in 2025; no source found says whether it is compulsory.
MDG.summary: The digital governance unit published version 1.0.2 of the Cadre d'interopérabilité, described as the first official interoperability framework in Madagascar. It was validated on 10 November 2022 after drafts from December 2021. A decree followed: decree 2025-1959 on the institutional framework of interoperability in Madagascar is listed on a legal portal, by title only. In the last twelve months, an article of April 2026 said an exchange system is implemented within a legal framework reinforced by that decree. The decree's text has not been found. What it requires of public bodies is not stated. Operating would need a decree, law, regulation or circular that makes the framework compulsory and names the body that enforces it.

MLI.short: Nothing found says Mali has a government interoperability framework, or says it has none, so no stage is set.
MLI.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a government interoperability framework, or says there is none.

MOZ.short: Mozambique's 2017 decree binds all public bodies to its interoperability framework, with the ICT regulator enforcing; no source found says which bodies comply.
MOZ.summary: Decree 67/2017, approved by the Council of Ministers on 17 October 2017 and published on 1 December 2017, approves the Regulation of the e-Government Interoperability Framework. It applies to all public administration bodies, central and local. It obliges them to use a single interoperability platform and integrate their systems. In the last twelve months, a national workshop that opened on 11 June 2026 was the last consultation on the revised text before its final approval. On 23 October 2026 the national ICT institute presented the proposed revision, which raises the guiding principles from 10 to 15. Mature would need a dated source that names or counts the public bodies that exchange data under the framework.

MRT.short: Mauritania's digital ministry was drafting a framework of public digital service standards in March 2026; it is not adopted.
MRT.summary: A report of 27 March 2026 says the digital transformation ministry held a three-day workshop to develop a unified framework of standards for public digital services, to ensure greater interoperability. By September 2026 the ministry said a reference framework for the state's digital architecture standards had been drawn up. A Digital Architecture Council is planned to enforce it; the ministry did not say the framework was adopted. All of this dates from the last twelve months, and no earlier position has been found. The report names no decree, order or circular that would make the framework compulsory. Establishing would need a framework for how government systems exchange data to be adopted and published.

MUS.short: Mauritius issued an e-government interoperability framework in 2002; no source found says whether public bodies must follow it.
MUS.summary: The government issued version 1.0 of the Mauritius e-Government Interoperability Framework in November 2002, setting technical standards and specifications for interoperability across government information systems. The framework covers data exchange between public agencies. Only one source has been found on it, and no later version is named. No source says it has been replaced or withdrawn. None names a decree, regulation or circular that makes it compulsory, or the public bodies that exchange data under it. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Operating would need a decree, law, regulation or circular that makes the framework compulsory and names the body that enforces it.

MWI.short: Malawi's ICT ministry proposed a binding government data sharing regulation in June 2026; it is not adopted.
MWI.summary: A report of 11 June 2026 says the Ministry of ICT has proposed a Government Data Sharing Regulation. It would be a binding rule with a common digital standard so that government systems can communicate. It would route all government data exchange through the National Data Centre. The proposal dates from the last twelve months, and no earlier position has been found. The report gives no date for adoption, names no body that would enforce the rule and reports no ministry exchanging data under it. Establishing would need a framework for how government systems exchange data to be adopted and published.

NAM.short: Namibia drafted an interoperability framework in 2016 and updated the document in 2021-2022; nothing says the government adopted it.
NAM.summary: The exchange platform's supplier says that in 2014 it introduced an interoperability platform and a corresponding framework in Namibia. The Office of the Prime Minister drafted an Interoperability Framework for Namibia, modelled on Estonia's X-Road, and consulted stakeholders on it in 2016. The supplier adds that in a 2021-2022 project for the Office it helped Namibia update its interoperability framework document. None of these accounts says the government adopted or published the framework, or names an instrument making it compulsory. No source found is dated after 2024. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Establishing would need a framework for how government systems exchange data to be adopted and published.

NER.short: Nothing found says Niger has a government interoperability framework, or says it has none, so no stage is set.
NER.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a government interoperability framework, or says there is none.

NGA.short: Nigeria's IT agency took over a government enterprise architecture framework in March 2026; no source found says whether agencies must follow it.
NGA.summary: A governors' forum report of July 2025 rated Katsina State's alignment with the Nigeria e-Government Interoperability Framework as high. In the last twelve months, in March 2026, the national IT agency took over the Nigeria Government Enterprise Architecture framework from the Korean cooperation agency. The work took two and a half years. The report describes the framework as now operational and enabling data exchange across government agencies. It cites no instrument that makes the framework compulsory, and no source found says the agency enforces it. Operating would need a decree, law, regulation or circular that makes the framework compulsory and names the body that enforces it.

RWA.short: Rwanda approved a national data sharing policy for public institutions in May 2025; no source found says whether they must follow it.
RWA.summary: A news report says Rwanda approved its National Data Sharing Policy in May 2025, to provide a framework for data exchange between public institutions. Before the policy, a 2019 survey of eight public agencies found no common standards, guidelines, interoperability framework or enterprise architecture, and recommended publishing one. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source dated since the policy's approval names an instrument that makes it compulsory or a body that enforces it. The policy's text has not been found. Operating would need a decree, law, regulation or circular that makes the framework compulsory and names the body that enforces it.

SDN.short: Nothing found says Sudan has a government interoperability framework, or says it has none, so no stage is set.
SDN.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a government interoperability framework, or says there is none.

SEN.short: Senegal presented a national interoperability framework and a draft decree in 2026; neither is adopted.
SEN.summary: On 26 March 2026 a steering committee validated a national interoperability framework and a draft decree, the first phase's output. On 28 and 29 April 2026 it met the health ministry to build the framework's health version. On 5 May 2026 the digital ministry was to present the draft decree. All of this dates from the last twelve months, and no earlier position has been found. No source found says the decree or the framework has been adopted. In August the ministry said the inventory of state systems was still to be drawn up. Establishing would need a framework for how government systems exchange data to be adopted and published.

SLE.short: Sierra Leone's ICT ministry said in October 2025 it had developed a government enterprise architecture framework; it is not issued.
SLE.summary: The Ministry of Communication, Technology and Innovation said in October 2025 that a Government Enterprise Architecture Framework it developed will serve as a national guide for digital integration. It also trained over 100 ICT officers from ministries, departments and agencies in enterprise architecture. Its statement does not say the framework has been adopted or published. It cites no instrument that would make it compulsory, and names no body that would enforce it. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Establishing would need a framework for how government systems exchange data to be adopted and published.

SOM.short: Somalia held a workshop in October 2026 to validate a national framework for coordinating government systems; no source found reports its adoption.
SOM.summary: In August 2025 the Ministry of Communications and Technology's e-Government Strategy 2025-2029 said the federal government had no enterprise architecture or interoperability framework. In the last twelve months, on 27 October 2026, the Office of the Prime Minister and the ministry held a national workshop to validate the National Digital Coordination Framework. It covers the coordination, interoperability and alignment of federal government digital systems. No adopted text of the framework has been found, and no body has been found charged with enforcing one. Establishing would need a framework for how government systems exchange data to be adopted and published.

SSD.short: Nothing found says South Sudan has a government interoperability framework, or says it has none, so no stage is set.
SSD.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a government interoperability framework, or says there is none.

STP.short: Sao Tome and Principe's regulations list names an interoperability law from 2024; no source found says who enforces it and which bodies follow it.
STP.summary: The regulations list of the national innovation institute, INIC, names Lei 1/2024 Quadro Nacional de Interoperabilidade, though the text of the 2024 law is not posted. The national cybersecurity strategy has a final version dated 15 December 2023. It records that the Quadro Nacional de Interoperabilidade was published in November 2021. It also says that a Lei de Interoperabilidade was at the time a draft bill. In the last twelve months the law was cited and not changed. In October 2026 the justice minister cited the 2024 framework law among the country's legislative initiatives. No source found names a body that enforces the framework. Operating would need a decree, law, regulation or circular that makes the framework compulsory and names the body that enforces it.

SWZ.short: Eswatini published its e-Government Interoperability Framework v1.0 in March 2025; no source found says public bodies are required to follow it.
SWZ.summary: The Office of the Executive Secretary, e-Governance, in the Ministry of ICT published the Eswatini e-Government Interoperability Framework v1.0 in March 2025. It sets technical policies and standards for how government systems interconnect and exchange data. An IOM assessment from a mission in October 2022 had described a government interoperability framework as a submitted proposal. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found says a decree, law, regulation or circular makes the framework compulsory, or names the body that enforces it. Operating would need a decree, law, regulation or circular that makes the framework compulsory and names the body that enforces it.

SYC.short: Nothing found says Seychelles has a government interoperability framework, or says it has none, so no stage is set.
SYC.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a government interoperability framework, or says there is none.

TCD.short: A 2019 thesis quoting the 2017-2021 digital plan said no normative framework existed; nothing recent is known, so no stage is set.
TCD.summary: No stage is set. No framework or draft is on record for Chad, and no source dated in the last three years says the government has neither. Also found are the Integrated public finance management system (SIGFiP), the National biometric registry and the e-Visa. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Absent would need a source from the past three years that says the government has no interoperability framework and none is being written.

TGO.short: Togo's digital agency holds its common interoperability framework as a draft guide, version 1.0, as at September 2026.
TGO.summary: The Agence Togo Digital sets out the government's Cadre Commun d'Interopérabilité in its Guide de l'Architecture d'Entreprise. The guide's version-control page shows version 1.0 with the status Brouillon, meaning draft. It shows a blank version date and an empty revision history. The page was captured on 6 September 2026 and carries no date of its own. No change has been found in the last twelve months. It names no decree, order or circular adopting the guide or making it compulsory, and no body that would enforce it. Establishing would need a framework for how government systems exchange data to be adopted and published.

TUN.short: Tunisia set rules for electronic data exchange between public bodies by decree-law and decree in 2020; no source found says whether they are enforced.
TUN.summary: Decree-law 2020-31 of the Head of Government, published in the Official Journal of 10 June 2020, concerns electronic data exchange between public bodies and their users and between the bodies themselves. Government decree 2020-777 of 5 October 2020 sets the conditions and procedures for that exchange, implementing the decree-law. The decree defines a national interoperability operator and an interoperability system. No change has been found in the last twelve months. The passages found show titles and definitions and not the provisions that follow. No source says public bodies must use the system or that the operator enforces the rules. Operating would need a decree, law, regulation or circular that makes the framework compulsory and names the body that enforces it.

TZA.short: Tanzania's e-government agency approved an interoperability framework in 2016; no source found says whether public institutions must follow it.
TZA.summary: The e-Government Agency issued the e-Government Interoperability Framework, version 1.0, approved by its chief executive in February 2016. The framework sets common standards and technical guidelines for public institutions to exchange data. It is the agency's own document, and the only source found that states the rule. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found names a law, regulation or circular that makes the framework compulsory for public institutions, or says the agency enforces it or counts the institutions that comply. Operating would need a decree, law, regulation or circular that makes the framework compulsory and names the body that enforces it.

UGA.short: Uganda issued an e-government interoperability framework in 2021 and renewed it in 2026; no source found says whether public bodies must follow it.
UGA.summary: The published Uganda e-Government Interoperability Framework was issued by the ICT ministry and the national IT authority and dated 6 May 2021. It sets twelve principles and six interoperability layers for e-government systems. In the last twelve months, the framework's renewal was launched with a multi-agency workshop in Kampala in February 2026. By May 2026 the government had renewed the Government Enterprise Architecture and the framework, with World Bank support. No source names an instrument that makes the framework compulsory, counts the bodies following it, or names the body that enforces the renewed framework. Operating would need a decree, law, regulation or circular that makes the framework compulsory and names the body that enforces it.

ZAF.short: Government has published minimum interoperability standards, being updated in 2026; no source found says whether any rule makes them compulsory.
ZAF.summary: In a reply to a question of 28 August 2025, the Department of Public Service and Administration told Parliament it had published the Minimum Interoperability Standards. It presents them as guidance for departments. In the last twelve months, Operation Vulindlela's report for April to June 2026 says work progressed on updating them. The update was to be tested in priority digital services by September 2026. No instrument has been found that makes the standards compulsory or names who enforces them, and no department is reported following them. Operating would need public bodies to be required to follow the framework.

ZMB.short: Zambia issued a public service interoperability standard in 2019; no decree or law making it compulsory has been found.
ZMB.summary: The government, through the electronic government division in the Office of the President, issued the Public Service ICT Electronic Government Interoperability Standard, first edition, in a final version dated February 2019. The text describes itself as the electronic government interoperability framework for all ministries, provinces and spending agencies. The standard is a government-issued document and cites no decree or law behind it. It says of itself that the division enforces it. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source dated since 2019 names a law that makes it compulsory or counts the bodies checked against it. Operating would need a decree, law, regulation or circular that makes the framework compulsory and names the body that enforces it.

ZWE.short: Zimbabwe handed an enterprise architecture blueprint to government ICT directors in May 2026; nothing says it is published or binding.
ZWE.summary: A supplier says it completed an enterprise architecture framework, roadmap and change plan for the government, in a project that ran from September 2023 to September 2024. In the last twelve months, in May 2026, the Enterprise Architecture Model blueprint was officially handed over. The ICT minister said the blueprint was handed to the nation's ICT directors at a conference of 7 May 2026. A Herald column of November 2026 says the government is building a whole-of-government enterprise architecture that defines interoperability standards. No source names an instrument making the blueprint compulsory or says it has been published. Establishing would need a framework for how government systems exchange data to be adopted and published.

AGO.short: A 2018 presidential decree makes a national interoperability plan binding on public services; no source found says whether it requires them to share data.
AGO.summary: Angola's Presidential Decree 46/18 of 14 February 2018 approves a national plan for interoperability across central and local administration. It makes adherence to the plan mandatory for public administration services. In the last twelve months, a draft Digital Government Law went to public consultation on 6 May 2026. It has 107 articles and would frame interoperability between state institutions. The 2018 decree remains the instrument in force. No source found says it requires bodies to share data, to connect to an exchange platform, or to stop asking people for what the state already holds. Operating would need a law in force that requires public bodies to share.

BDI.short: Nothing found names a law or decree on public bodies sharing data for Burundi, or a draft, so no stage is set.
BDI.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data, or a draft of one. Nothing found says there is none.

BEN.short: A 2020 decree sets up the national data exchange platform; no source found says whether public bodies are required to use it.
BEN.summary: Benin's Decree 2020-209 of 18 March 2020 was issued by the Presidency. It sets up XRoad BJ, the national interoperability platform through which public bodies exchange data. No later text is recorded as amending or replacing it, and no change has been found in the last twelve months. Nothing found says the decree obliges ministries and agencies to connect to the platform or to exchange data through it. No public body is named as exchanging data because the decree requires it. Operating would need a law in force that requires public bodies to share data or to connect to the exchange platform.

BFA.short: A 2018 order of the Prime Minister sets interoperability rules for public administrations; no source found says whether it requires them to share data.
BFA.summary: Burkina Faso adopted its general interoperability reference, the Référentiel général d'interopérabilité, by an order of the Prime Minister dated 23 May 2018. The order fixes rules that make the information systems of public administrations compatible with each other. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Nothing recorded says the order obliges administrations to exchange data or to connect to a common platform. No administration is named as exchanging data because the order requires it. Operating would need a law in force that requires public bodies to share data, to connect to the exchange platform, or not to ask a person for what another body already holds.

BWA.short: A 2025 act tells public bodies not to collect what another body already holds; no rules made under it are recorded.
BWA.summary: Botswana's Digital Services Act, 2025 (Act No. 22 of 2025) was passed by the National Assembly on 14 August 2025 and assented to on 17 October 2025. It says a public or private body shall avoid collecting information that another body already holds. It starts on a date the minister sets by order in the Gazette. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No regulation, decree or order made under the Act has been found, and no public body is named as exchanging data because it requires them to. Mature would need such a rule, or public bodies named as exchanging data under the Act.

CAF.short: Nothing found names a law or decree on public bodies sharing data for Central African Republic, or a draft, so no stage is set.
CAF.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data, or a draft of one. Nothing found says there is none.

CIV.short: A 2017 ordinance binds every administrative authority to connect to the state's exchange platform; no source found says whether it has been applied since 2023.
CIV.summary: Cote d'Ivoire's Ordinance 2017-500 of 2 August 2017 was made by the President in the Council of Ministers. Its chapter on interoperability says the state sets up a platform to which every administrative authority is bound to connect. It also bars an authority from asking a user again for information the administration already holds. No repeal is recorded, and no change has been found in the last twelve months. No decree or order applying the ordinance since 2023 has been found. No authority is named as connected to the platform because the ordinance requires it. Mature would need such a decree or order, or authorities named as exchanging data because it requires them to.

CMR.short: A draft e-government law described in 2025 would have administrations share data; it has not been passed.
CMR.summary: In November 2025 the government's digital transformation project described a draft e-government law on access to public information and the digital transformation of the administration. The draft would require administrations to make their information systems compatible so that they share data securely. It was examined at a workshop in Ebolowa. No promulgation is recorded, and no change has been found in the last twelve months. No decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data has been found in force. Establishing would need a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data to be in force.

COD.short: Nothing found names a law or decree on public bodies sharing data for DR Congo, or a draft, so no stage is set.
COD.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data, or a draft of one. Nothing found says there is none.

COG.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data, or a draft of one. Nothing found says there is none.

COM.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data, or a draft of one. Nothing found says there is none.

CPV.short: A 2020 government resolution orders state bodies to share data and a law to be drafted; no source found says that law has passed.
CPV.summary: Cape Verde's Council of Ministers Resolution 54/2020 was approved on 19 March 2020 and took effect in March 2020. It orders a legal diploma on interoperability of public administration systems to be drafted. Measure g says state bodies must share the data a process needs, subject to data protection rules. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source says the diploma has been drafted or passed, and no law is reported to have followed the resolution. Establishing would need a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data to be in force.

DJI.short: Nothing found names a law or decree on public bodies sharing data for Djibouti, or a draft, so no stage is set.
DJI.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data, or a draft of one. Nothing found says there is none.

DZA.short: A December 2025 decree makes one national system the only channel for data exchange between public bodies; no order made under it is known.
DZA.summary: Algeria's Presidential Decree 25-320 of 30 December 2025 sets up a national data governance system with a national interoperability system. In the last twelve months it was published and, in September 2026, a further decree on a secure digital interoperability plan was reported as being drawn up. Before it, Executive Decree 23-316 of 6 September 2023 was the earlier measure; it remains in force. The 2025 decree makes the system the exclusive channel for exchange between public bodies. No order made under it has been found. Mature would need such an order, or bodies named as exchanging data because the decree requires it.

EGY.short: A bill on data exchange between government bodies was finished for parliament in December 2025; nothing is in force.
EGY.summary: In December 2025 the chair of Egypt's House ICT committee said the government had finished a 35-article bill on classifying and circulating information. The communications minister said that month the draft would go to Cabinet and then the House. In the last twelve months the bill went from a draft, which the deputy communications minister told the committee in February 2024 had been drafted, to a finished text. The bill has not been passed, and no law is in force. Establishing would need a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data to be in force.

ERI.short: Nothing found names a law or decree on public bodies sharing data for Eritrea, or a draft, so no stage is set.
ERI.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data, or a draft of one. Nothing found says there is none.

ETH.short: The Council of Ministers sent a draft data governance proclamation to parliament in September 2026; nothing is in force.
ETH.summary: On 28 September 2026 Ethiopia's Council of Ministers referred a draft National Data Governance Proclamation to the House of Peoples' Representatives. The same meeting is reported as approving a draft National Data Management Proclamation, meant to ease data sharing, interoperability and reuse. In the last twelve months these two drafts are the only ones found, and the House had not passed either by the end of September 2026. Neither report states whether it would oblige public bodies to share. No law, decree or regulation on sharing is in force. Establishing would need such a law, decree or regulation to be in force.

GAB.short: A 2025 ordinance makes it compulsory for administrations to interconnect and exchange information; no source found says whether it has been applied.
GAB.summary: Gabon's Ordinance 0006/PR/2025 regulating digitalisation was signed by the President on 12 August 2025 and published in the Official Journal on 30 August 2025. It makes it compulsory for administrations to interconnect, so that they exchange information, and puts interoperability of information systems at its centre. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No decree or order applying the ordinance has been found, and no administration is named as exchanging data because it requires it. Mature would need such a decree or order, or bodies named as exchanging data because the ordinance requires them to.

GHA.short: A data harmonisation bill went to public consultation in November 2025 and a data exchange act is proposed; nothing is in force.
GHA.summary: Ghana's National Information Technology Agency put its draft Data Harmonisation Bill 2025 out for public consultation on 19 November 2025. In the last twelve months, in May 2026 the bill was before Parliament and had not passed. In July 2026 a representative of the communications minister said a Data Exchange Act was also proposed. No law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data has been found in force. Establishing would need such a law, decree or regulation to be in force.

GIN.short: Only a 2019 arrêté on health and birth registration data between two ministries is held, a one-sector text, so no stage is set.
GIN.summary: No stage is set. The only text found is a 2019 arrêté between the health and territorial administration ministries on vaccination and birth certificates. It covers one sector, which a law for one sector cannot place. Nothing found names a law, decree or draft on public bodies sharing data in general. No change has been found in the last twelve months. An interoperability framework issued as a decree or regulation would count. Establishing would need a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data to be in force, however old.

GMB.short: Nothing found names a law or decree on public bodies sharing data for Gambia, or a draft, so no stage is set.
GMB.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data, or a draft of one. Nothing found says there is none.

GNB.short: A decree of October 2025 approved a national interoperability regulation; no source found says whether it requires public bodies to share data.
GNB.summary: Guinea-Bissau's national regulation on the interoperability of digital systems and platforms was approved by Decree 27/2025 and published in the Official Bulletin of 31 October 2025. In the last twelve months it was cited and not changed: the regional digital project announced the approval again in August 2026. Reports say it lets public bodies share information securely. They do not say it obliges bodies to share, to connect to a platform, or to stop asking people for what another body holds. Operating would need a law in force that requires public bodies to share.

GNQ.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data, or a draft of one. Nothing found says there is none.

KEN.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data, or a draft of one. Nothing found says there is none.

LBR.short: An executive order of April 2026 mandates interoperable government systems, with legislation due within a year; no law is in force.
LBR.summary: Liberia's Executive Order No. 163, signed by President Boakai on 22 April 2026, mandates interoperable digital systems across ministries, agencies and commissions. No earlier instrument on the subject has been found. In the last twelve months the order introduced a government interoperability framework, and says data sharing is governed by formal agreements on access, use and accountability. Draft legislation to make the arrangement permanent is due within twelve months of the order. No law is in force. Establishing would need a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data to be in force.

LBY.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data, or a draft of one. Nothing found says there is none.

LSO.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data, or a draft of one. Nothing found says there is none.

MAR.short: A framework bill covering interoperability between government institutions was under government review in November 2025; nothing is in force.
MAR.summary: Morocco's framework bill known as Digital X.0, which covers interoperability among other subjects, was under review by the General Secretariat of the Government in November 2025. In the last twelve months, on 30 June 2026 the minister said a bill on dematerialising administrative services was being drawn up, to base public services on data exchange between administrations. Neither bill had been passed by the end of September 2026. No law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data has been found in force. Establishing would need such a law, decree or regulation to be in force.

MDG.short: A draft decree on electronic signature and interoperability was validated at a workshop in September 2025; nothing is in force.
MDG.summary: In September 2025 Madagascar's ministry of digital development held a workshop to validate a draft decree on electronic signature and interoperability. The draft would set up a framework, a digital governance unit and a national interoperability committee. No change has been found in the last twelve months, and no adoption by the government is recorded. The report does not say the decree would oblige public bodies to exchange data or connect to a common platform. No law, decree or regulation on sharing has been found in force. Establishing would need such a decree to be in force.

MLI.short: Nothing found names a law or decree on public bodies sharing data for Mali, or a draft, so no stage is set.
MLI.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data, or a draft of one. Nothing found says there is none.

MOZ.short: A 2017 decree obliges public bodies to share data and use one exchange platform; a revised regulation was still in consultation in June 2026.
MOZ.summary: Mozambique's Decree 67/2017 of 1 December 2017 approves the regulation of the e-government interoperability framework. It obliges public bodies to share the data they hold, and to use the single platform. In the last twelve months, the regulator described a review in December 2025. TGO.short: A 2026 framework makes the state digital agency a platform provider, but no source shows government staff running a system, so no stage is set.

No source found from 2023 or later says government staff run a named system. Preparing would need a source from 2023 or later saying government's own staff run, maintain or built one of its systems.

TUN.short: A government technology body runs systems for the rest of government by 2026; no in-house build is known since 2023.
TUN.summary: The Centre National de l'Informatique manages the RNIA network and the government Intranet, and its backup centre keeps national applications running. It is a public establishment. In 2016 its National Backup Centre, with its own technical staff, was the State's recovery site. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found says a system built by government staff, not by a contractor or vendor, went live since October 2023. Operating would need a system built by government staff, not a contractor, to go live within the last three years.

TZA.short: Government staff run, maintain or built three or more of its systems by 2026, no contractor named.

In July 2025 the Vice President launched the Bank of Tanzania's core banking system, built by the bank's own experts.

In July 2026 the Prime Minister launched a census of urban owners to build a digitised, geo-referenced land register, starting in six towns. No source found since October 2023 says the digital land register covers the whole country. Operating would need the digital land register in service nationally or in all land offices.

BEN.short: A digital land register was in service for part of the country in 2026; no source found reports national coverage.
BEN.summary: On 6 November 2026 the project chief of the land agency ANDF put its national cadastre at 643,993 parcels in 12 communes, 3 of them fully covered. In the last twelve months, Parakou had 196,474 parcels registered by September 2026. In July 2026 ANDF said E-TERRE takes certain land procedures online. In November 2026 the government launched TERRA BENIN, which aims to register 1.5 million parcels, starting in 14 communes. No source found since October 2023 says the digital land register covers the whole country. Operating would need the digital land register in service nationally or in all land offices.

In the last twelve months, in September 2026, SYC@D managed the cadastre, state domain and land, with FasoSign signing provisional cession orders. No source found since October 2023 says the digital land register covers the whole country. Operating would need the digital land register in service nationally or in all land offices.

CMR.short: Digital land registration was under way in 2026; none in service is on record.

No source found since October 2023 says a digital land register is in service. No source found since October 2023 says a digital land register is in service. Mindelo was declared cadastred on 19 March 2025. On 11 January 2026 the national domain directorate generalised Amlak, one system with a central database for cadastre, land conservation and state domains. The National Land Authority lists a National Registry system, LAIS, with a spatial database. In the last twelve months, in October 2026, the Scorecard said LAIS is linked to IFMIS, the Rwanda Revenue Authority and Irembo, putting 12 land services online.
