BDI.summary: In June 2025 INSBU's Accord de Licence Ouverte granted a free, worldwide, non-exclusive licence to use, copy, modify and distribute the platform's data. Derivative products are allowed, commercially or not, with attribution. In November 2023 INSBU's acting director-general said all national statistics are published on a data portal anyone can consult. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found since October 2023 names two or more public bodies publishing data. Operating would need two or more public bodies publishing data under an open licence, named or counted by a source from the past three years.

BEN.short: Government data was published for download on a government site in 2026; no open licence is on record.
BEN.summary: In July 2025 a workshop prepared the migration of INStaD's Open Data portal of the national statistical system to its SDMX 2.0 version. In 2025 ASIN ran the national portal data.gouv.bj. In the last twelve months, in July 2026 the budget directorate's open-data API served budget classification data for 2008-2024. No source found since October 2023 states an open licence for the data. Establishing would need the data published under an open licence, or terms that let anyone reuse it.

BFA.short: More than five national agencies published open-licensed data on one portal in 2026.
BFA.summary: In June 2026 CITADEL, at the Université Joseph Ki-Zerbo, listed 147 datasets on its national data portal, with twelve more in validation. INSD, the statistics institute, licenses its data free of charge to anyone, worldwide. The licence covers data on its website and open data portal, and allows copying, changes and commercial use with attribution. In the last twelve months, CITADEL said its portal holds more than 145 datasets from more than 5 national agencies and official portals. That count of June 2026 meets the Mature test of four or more public bodies publishing. The portal has no public API.

BWA.short: Government data was published for download on the Statistics Botswana microdata portal in 2026; no open licence is on record.
BWA.summary: In August 2026 Statistics Botswana's own microdata portal showed the office moving toward publishing datasets for reuse. No dataset count was given, and the office was still exploring licensing, Creative Commons rather than non-commercial clauses. In the last twelve months, this August 2026 report is the one source found, and no earlier position has been found to compare it with. No source found since October 2023 names two or more public bodies publishing data. Establishing would need the data published under an open licence, or terms that let anyone reuse it.

CAF.short: The statistics institute, regional central bank and finance ministry published data in 2025, with an open licence held; no source found reports four or more publishers.
CAF.summary: In May 2025 the country launched its National Summary Data Page, a portal of key macroeconomic and financial data. The IMF says three public bodies publish on it: ICASEES, the regional central bank BEAC and the finance ministry. ICASEES's education data page offers yearbook and key-indicator files for download, each under CC BY 4.0. In the last twelve months, more than fifty indicators on ICASEES's platforms were updated in 2026. No source found since November 2024 names or counts a fourth body. Mature would need four or more public bodies publishing under an open licence.

CIV.short: Government data was published for download on the portail Open Data de la Côte d'Ivoire in 2025; no open licence is on record.
CIV.summary: The 2024-2026 national open government action plan lists an open data portal among the government's initiatives since joining the OGP. Under commitment 6 it calls the portal running and to be enriched. By June 2020, after training, the petroleum and renewable energy ministry had published around 50 new datasets on the data.gov.ci portal. In the last twelve months, in October 2026 the official open data portal of the Government Information and Communication Centre listed 211 datasets across five sectors. No source found since October 2023 states an open licence for the data. Establishing would need the data published under an open licence, or terms that let anyone reuse it.

CMR.short: Government data was published for download on the Open SDG in 2025; no open licence is on record.
CMR.summary: The INS launched its Open SDG platform on 17 September 2025, set up in 2024 with UNECA support. In November 2025 an INS officer presented its Portail Open Data, Open SDG and ANADOC platforms. In the last twelve months, on 22 April 2026 the National Institute of Statistics unveiled platforms giving direct access to macroeconomic series and, through a national data archive, to survey microdata. No licence was stated. The INS is the one publisher on record. No source found since October 2023 names two or more public bodies publishing data. Establishing would need the data published under an open licence, or terms that let anyone reuse it.

COD.short: Government data was published for download on the Banque Centrale du Congo website in 2026; no open licence is on record.
COD.summary: The National Institute of Statistics (INS) launched data.gouv.cd on 23 February 2026 as the national open data platform. ITIE-RDC publishes extractive revenue, production, mining-rights and contract datasets in CSV, Excel and JSON as at November 2026, with a public API. The Ministry of Mines publishes validated mining statistics files for 2017 to 2025, each stated to be open access. No licence is named for these. In the last twelve months, the Banque Centrale du Congo opened a new site in August 2026 showing exchange rates, inflation and other indicators, with no download stated. No one source found since October 2023 names two or more of these bodies publishing data. Establishing would need the data published under an open licence, or terms that let anyone reuse it.

COG.short: The forest ministry published open-licensed datasets in 2024 and the statistics institute offered downloads in 2026; four or more publishing bodies have not been found.
COG.summary: The SYNA-MNV forest monitoring programme of the Ministry of Forest Economy publishes five datasets for download, the newest from 2024. The programme publishes them under an open licence, asking only that reusers credit the source. In the last twelve months, on 5 June 2026 the director general of the Institut national de la statistique said anyone can download data from its Open Data Portal. That makes two public bodies offering data for download, and only the forest programme states an open licence. No source found since November 2024 names or counts four or more public bodies publishing data. Mature would need four or more public bodies publishing under an open licence.

COM.short: Government data was published for download on the Archive nationale de microdonnees in 2026; no open licence is on record.
COM.summary: INSEED, the national statistics institute, runs a national microdata archive (NADA) whose catalogue held 15 datasets on 23 August 2026. They include the 2025 agricultural census and the 2024 household survey; no open licence is stated. On 29 August 2024 the UN country team and national partners presented the Open Data Comores portal in Moroni, giving free access to development data. In the last twelve months, the household survey's cleaned data files and public anonymised version were dated April 2026. No source found since October 2023 names two or more public bodies publishing data. Establishing would need the data published under an open licence, or terms that let anyone reuse it.

CPV.short: Government data was published for download on a transparency portal and a fisheries system in 2026; no open licence is on record.
CPV.summary: The government launched the Portal da Transparência on 21 January 2026. The minister said it shows in real time how public money is raised, planned and spent. The OGP review says the finance ministry publishes budget execution and spending data on its website. In the last twelve months, the fisheries directorate has published fisheries data on its Fisheries Information System since January 2026, FiTI reports. The directorate, the Maritime and Port Institute and the National Institute of Statistics update it. No source found since October 2023 states an open licence for the data. Establishing would need the data published under an open licence, or terms that let anyone reuse it.

DJI.short: Government data was published for download on the Page Nationale Recapitulative de Donnees (PNRD) in 2025; no open licence is on record.
DJI.summary: On 12 June 2025 Djibouti launched its National Summary Data Page under the IMF e-GDDS at the Central Bank. Central Bank, INSTAD and Budget Ministry staff built it with the IMF and AfDB. It is publicly accessible worldwide and hosted on the Djibouti Open Data Platform. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found since October 2023 states an open licence for the data. Establishing would need the data published under an open licence, or terms that let anyone reuse it.

DZA.short: No government data published for download since 2023 is on record, so no stage is set.
DZA.summary: No stage is set. No government data published for download has been found since October 2023, and no change has been found in the last twelve months. A dashboard with nothing to download, or a portal only planned, does not count. Preparing would need a public body publishing data online for anyone to download, on a portal or its own site, in the past three years.

EGY.short: Nothing found says whether a public body publishes data for anyone to download, so no stage is set.
EGY.summary: Not found. Nothing found names government data published for download, or says there is none.

ERI.short: Nothing found says whether a public body publishes data for anyone to download, so no stage is set.
ERI.summary: Not found. Nothing found names government data published for download, or says there is none.

ETH.short: Two public bodies published agricultural data for download on one ministry hub in 2026; no open licence is on record.
ETH.summary: In June 2026 the Ministry of Agriculture's National Agri Data Hub listed 1,910 datasets in RDF and JSON-LD. No data licence is stated. The hub listed datasets from two public bodies, the Ministry of Agriculture and the Ethiopian Institute of Agricultural Research. The Ethiopian Statistics Service says in 2026 that it runs STATBANK, microdata repositories and web portals. In the last twelve months, the hub's June 2026 listing is the source found that names more than one public body publishing. No source found since October 2023 states an open licence for the data. Establishing would need the data published under an open licence, or terms that let anyone reuse it.

GAB.short: The statistics office offered data files for download on its website in 2025; no open licence for them has been found.
GAB.summary: In February 2025 the download page of the Direction Générale de la Statistique offered files for anyone to download. They include monthly consumer price indices, foreign trade bulletins, population projections and census results. The newest files date from April 2022, and the page gives no terms of reuse. In the last twelve months, Gabon hosted a CEMAC and African Development Bank workshop on regional statistics platforms in September 2026. No source found since November 2023 states an open licence for the data. Establishing would need the data published under an open licence, or terms that let anyone reuse it.

GHA.short: Government data was published for download on the Ghana Open Data Initiative portal (data.gov.gh) in 2026; no open licence is on record.
GHA.summary: The Bank of Ghana launched a beta database portal on 5 February 2024 for extracting macroeconomic data. It held 255 monthly and 86 quarterly series across five sectors, with no licence stated. The World Bank said in December 2024 that 315 datasets had been uploaded to the Ghana Open Data portal since 2020. It added that the count had not grown for three years and the portal was down. In the last twelve months, the National Information Technology Agency's Ghana Open Data Initiative catalogue was described in August 2026. No source found since October 2023 states an open licence for the data. Establishing would need the data published under an open licence, or terms that let anyone reuse it.

GIN.short: Government data was published for download on the Open Data Platform (ODP) 2.0 in 2026; no open licence is on record.
GIN.summary: In 2017 the ITIE-Guinee steering committee's policy said five bodies publish revenue data on their own sites. They are the Ministry of Mines, CPDM, SOGUIPAMI, the Chambre des Mines and the central bank (BCRG). In the last twelve months, from 20 to 25 July 2026 the INS held a workshop, with African Development Bank support, on migrating to its Open Data Platform (ODP) 2.0. The platform is the system through which the INS disseminates official statistics, and participants recommended feeding it regularly. No source found since October 2023 states an open licence for the data. Establishing would need the data published under an open licence, or terms that let anyone reuse it.

GMB.short: Government data was published for download on the GBoS downloads (gbosdata.org/downloads) in 2026; no open licence is on record.
GMB.summary: In October 2026 the Gambia Bureau of Statistics offered GDP, CPI, PPI, trade and survey reports with microdata for download at gbosdata.org/downloads. On 2 July 2026 its microdata catalogue held three survey studies: MICS 2000, DHS 2019-2020 and the Labour Force Survey 2018. The latest entries are dated June and July 2025. In the last twelve months, the bureau's catalogue of July 2026 is the latest dated source found. No source found since October 2023 states an open licence for the data or names two or more public bodies publishing it. Establishing would need the data published under an open licence, or terms that let anyone reuse it.

GNB.short: The statistics office and partners launched a data page on the national open data portal in 2024; no open licence for the data is known.
GNB.summary: The National Institute of Statistics says the page, hosted on the national Open Data Portal, was launched on 14 June 2024. It is the National Summary Data Page, and it gives public access to key economic information. In July 2024 the IMF said the page's data comes from the statistics institute, the finance ministry and the BCEAO. In April 2015 the National Assembly's open data page published 4 open datasets in JSON via APIs. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found since October 2023 states an open licence for the data. Establishing would need the data published under an open licence, or terms that let anyone reuse it.

GNQ.short: Nothing found says whether a public body publishes data for anyone to download, so no stage is set.
GNQ.summary: Not found. Nothing found names government data published for download, or says there is none.

KEN.short: A national open data portal gave free access to government data in 2025; no open licence for it has been found.
KEN.summary: In 2025 the civic technology group Pollicy said the Kenya Open Data Initiative portal gives free access to government data in machine-readable formats. The portal it names is kenya.opendataforafrica.org. President Kibaki launched the first national portal, opendata.go.ke, on 8 July 2011. The Open Government Partnership's record of Kenya's commitments says that portal later went offline. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found since November 2023 states an open licence for the data. Establishing would need the data published under an open licence, or terms that let anyone reuse it.

LBR.short: The statistics office put its data under an open licence in 2026 and two bodies publish; no source found says whether four or more do.
LBR.summary: LISGIS, the statistics office, adopted CC BY 4.0 as its licence standard from 8 June 2026. Its notice grants anyone a free, worldwide licence to use and redistribute its data, including on its open data portal. Commercial use is allowed with attribution. In the last twelve months, the EITI said in July 2026 that LEITI's online data portal had made extractive data much more open. It names two public sources of company production data: the LEITI Data Warehouse and the Ministry of Mines and Energy's online cadastre. No source found since November 2024 names four or more public bodies publishing data on a portal. Mature would need four or more public bodies publishing under an open licence.

LBY.short: Nine government bodies published on the national open data platform in 2026, under terms that let anyone reuse the data.
LBY.summary: The General Information Authority launched the Open Government Data Platform on 27 November 2025, with datasets, APIs and indicators. Its terms let anyone use the datasets lawfully and republish them, crediting the platform and the dataset. The authority reported 91 datasets on the platform in February 2026, with nine government bodies taking part across eight sectors. In the last twelve months, the platform held 166 datasets by November 2026, the authority told the Libyan Permanent Economic Forum in Tripoli. In September 2026 the communications authority listed its 2025 ICT workforce figures there as a downloadable spreadsheet.

LSO.short: Government data was published for download on the bos.gov.ls/publications.htm in 2025; no open licence is on record.
LSO.summary: In April 2025 the Bureau of Statistics Lesotho said all reports listed on its publications page can be downloaded. Excel tables are given for national accounts, CPI and GDP. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found since October 2023 states an open licence for the data or names two or more public bodies publishing it. Establishing would need the data published under an open licence, or terms that let anyone reuse it.

MAR.short: Government data was published for download on the data.gov.ma national open data portal in 2026; no open licence is on record.
MAR.summary: The Agence de Développement du Digital manages the national open data portal, data.gov.ma, as its documentation page said in August 2026. In December 2024 the agency said connected APIs now publish the planning commission's employment, price and national accounts figures on the portal. The Open Government Partnership's review counted over 500 datasets and over 70,000 downloads by the end of 2023. It says 37 institutions were updating datasets by then. In the last twelve months, in December 2025 the national open data steering committee discussed a 2026 action plan. No source found since November 2023 states an open licence for the data. Establishing would need the data published under an open licence, or terms that let anyone reuse it.

MDG.short: The National Assembly published open-licensed data in 2026 and the finance ministry launched a portal in 2025; four or more publishers have not been found.
MDG.summary: In August 2026 the Assemblée nationale de Madagascar published five parliamentary datasets as JSON and CSV on its open data page and a read-only REST API. The data is under Licence Ouverte v2.0 (compatible CC-BY), free to reuse including commercially with attribution. In February 2025 the Ministry of Economy and Finance launched PortES, a socio-economic data portal with six components. In the last twelve months, the Assembly's August 2026 publication is the development found, and only the Assembly states an open licence. No source found since November 2024 names or counts four or more public bodies publishing data. Mature would need four or more public bodies publishing under an open licence.

MLI.short: Government data was published under an open licence on the INSTAT open data licence agreement in 2026; several publishing bodies are not on record.
MLI.summary: INSTAT's open data licence grants a free, worldwide, non-exclusive licence to use, copy, modify and distribute its datasets, tables, indicators and dashboards. Derived products and commercial use are allowed with attribution. In August 2026 INSTAT's data catalogue listed 107 studies, including the 2022 census (RGPH5) and agricultural surveys. In the last twelve months, in November 2026 FAO said INSTAT and CPS/SDR had published the 2023-24 agricultural survey results. No source found since October 2023 names two or more public bodies publishing data under the licence. Operating would need two or more public bodies publishing under an open licence.

MOZ.short: Government data was published under an open licence on a government site in 2026; several publishing bodies are not on record.
MOZ.summary: The Fundo de Estradas, a Mozambican public fund, runs the IPDP portal for data on road, bridge and other public infrastructure projects, and was validated as an OC4IDS publisher in 2026. The portal puts its data under a Creative Commons licence with attribution. In the last twelve months, in August 2026, the fund published public infrastructure project data on that portal. No source found since October 2023 names two or more public bodies publishing data. Operating would need two or more public bodies publishing under an open licence.

MRT.short: Government data was published for download on the Data Warehouse (Mauritania EITI) in 2024; no open licence is on record.
MRT.summary: In November 2024 the EITI Board said Mauritania EITI makes extractive revenue, production and export data available on its Data Warehouse portal. The data sets download in CSV. Mauritania EITI is a government-backed multi-stakeholder body set up by Decree 2018-135. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found since October 2023 states an open licence for the data or names two or more public bodies publishing it. Establishing would need the data published under an open licence, or terms that let anyone reuse it.

MUS.short: Government data was published for download on the BOMStats in 2026; no open licence is on record.
MUS.summary: On 22 October 2025 Statistics Mauritius and UNDP launched the MauStats data platform, a hub built to SDMX standards. The National Open Data Portal, set up under the May 2017 National Open Data Policy, releases government datasets as open data in CSV and XML. In the last twelve months, on 3 September 2026 the Bank of Mauritius launched BOMStats, its statistical data platform. It offers an API and SDMX-format data sharing. No source found since October 2023 states an open licence for the data. Establishing would need the data published under an open licence, or terms that let anyone reuse it.

MWI.short: Government data was published for download on the Malawi Open Data Portal in 2025; no open licence is on record.
MWI.summary: On 3 September 2025 the OGP Malawi Secretariat announced the launch of Malawi's new Open Data Portal. It gives citizens budget, development project and public service delivery data through dashboards and downloadable datasets. It is part of the Third OGP National Action Plan. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found since October 2023 states an open licence for the data or names two or more public bodies publishing it. Establishing would need the data published under an open licence, or terms that let anyone reuse it.

NAM.short: Government data was published for download on the NSA Central Data Catalog (NADA microdata archive) in 2026; no open licence is on record.
NAM.summary: In August 2026 the Namibia Statistics Agency's microdata catalogue listed 16 studies. Most were marked open access. They include the 2023 census public-use microdata sample, last modified on 21 July 2026. In the last twelve months, on 18 November 2026, the agency launched a public online portal for the Sustainable Development Goals. No source found since October 2023 states an open licence for the data or names two or more public bodies publishing it. Establishing would need the data published under an open licence, or terms that let anyone reuse it.

NER.short: Government data was published under an open licence on the INS Niger open data licence (stat-niger.org) in 2024; several publishing bodies are not on record.
NER.summary: Under a licence dated 30 October 2024, Niger's Institut National de la Statistique lets anyone use, modify and distribute its data. The worldwide, free, non-exclusive licence covers commercial and non-commercial use, with attribution. In May 2025 the World Bank said the national Open Data Portal, with some of its data, is accessible on the statistics office's website. On 18 September 2025 the national nutrition information platform PNIN launched its renovated portal, with a download space. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found since October 2023 names two or more public bodies publishing data. Operating would need two or more public bodies publishing under an open licence.

NGA.short: Anambra State's website offered open data in 2026; no open licence is known.
NGA.summary: In October 2026 Anambra State Government launched a redesigned website whose Open Government section gives access to budgets, audit reports, procurement plans, contract awards and open data. No dataset count or licence is given. The 2018 national open data policy names Data.gov.ng as the national catalogue of open data, and requires agencies to link their datasets to it. In the last twelve months, the October 2026 launch is the one development found. Anambra is the one publisher on record, at the level of one state. No open licence for the data has been found since November 2023. Establishing would need the data published under an open licence, or terms that let anyone reuse it.

RWA.short: Procurement data was published for download from 2024; its licence bars commercial reuse, so no open licence is known.
RWA.summary: In November 2024 the Rwanda Public Procurement Authority launched an open contracting portal with procurement data back to 2016. The data download in spreadsheet formats or by API. In the last twelve months, in October 2026 the authority published its Umucyo data on tenders, awards and contracts, December 2013 to April 2026, updated daily. The licence is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, which bars commercial reuse. No source found states an open licence that lets anyone reuse the data. Establishing would need the data published under an open licence, or terms that let anyone reuse it.

SDN.short: The ports corporation published annual port statistics for download in 2026; no open licence is on record.
SDN.summary: The Sea Ports Corporation lists annual port statistics for 2007 to 2025 as downloadable files on its website. The latest was posted on 2 April 2026. The files for 2019 to 2021 went up together in April 2023, and those for 2022 and 2023 in October 2024. Most files are in Arabic, and no licence is stated. The corporation is the one public body found publishing data for download. In the last twelve months, the April 2026 posting is the newest development found. No source found since October 2023 states an open licence for the data. Establishing would need the data published under an open licence, or terms that let anyone reuse it.

SEN.short: The statistics agency put its data under an open licence by 2026 and two bodies publish geodata; no source found says whether four or more do.
SEN.summary: ANSD, the statistics agency, licenses its open data to anyone, free and worldwide. Users may copy, change, publish and distribute it, commercially or not, citing the source. The Géoportail carries data from at least two public bodies. They are the Centre de suivi écologique, with 2023 bushfire areas, and ANSD, with 2023 school locations. In the last twelve months, in June 2026 ANSD trained about thirty regional staff to publish datasets on its Open Data Platform 2.0. No source found since November 2024 names four or more public bodies publishing data on a portal. Mature would need four or more public bodies publishing under an open licence.

SLE.short: Government data was published for download on the Open Data Sierra Leone data portal in 2024; no open licence is on record.
SLE.summary: In February 2024 Statistics Sierra Leone said its publications, metadata and microdata are released free of charge on its website. They include an Open Data Sierra Leone data portal, with unrestricted datasets available online to all. In November 2019 the third OGP National Action Plan described the government Open Data Portal as being revamped, hosted at the Ministry of Information and Communications. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found since October 2023 states an open licence for the data or names two or more public bodies publishing it. Establishing would need the data published under an open licence, or terms that let anyone reuse it.

SOM.short: Government data was published under an open licence on the SNBS Open Data Portal in 2024; several publishing bodies are not on record.
SOM.summary: In July 2024 the Somali National Bureau of Statistics (SNBS) published data free of charge on its Open Data Portal, in human- and machine-readable formats. All data and datasets there are under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International licence (CC-BY 4.0). In March 2025 the Federal Ministry of Finance and Puntland's Ministry of Finance publicly released income and expenditure reports. In the last twelve months, in November 2026 the federal finance ministry's transparency portal offered budget, fiscal, debt, procurement and audit publications as downloadable files. No source found since October 2023 names two or more public bodies publishing data under an open licence. Operating would need two or more public bodies publishing under an open licence.

SSD.short: Government data was published under an open licence on the NBS Open Data Portal in 2026; several publishing bodies are not on record.
SSD.summary: In August 2026 the National Bureau of Statistics described an operational Open Data Portal with publicly accessible datasets, CSV and Excel downloads and API access. Its Public Data tier is freely available to access, use and share without restrictions for any purpose. In the last twelve months, on 21 April 2026 the bureau and UNICEF released the results of the 2025 Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey. No source found since October 2023 names two or more public bodies publishing data. Operating would need two or more public bodies publishing under an open licence.

STP.short: Nothing found says whether a public body publishes data for anyone to download, so no stage is set.
STP.summary: Not found. Nothing found names government data published for download, or says there is none.

SWZ.short: Nothing found says whether a public body publishes data for anyone to download, so no stage is set.
SWZ.summary: Not found. Nothing found names government data published for download, or says there is none.

SYC.short: Government data was published for download on a government site in 2026; no open licence is on record.
SYC.summary: In June 2026 the Ministry of Fisheries, Agriculture and Blue Economy said its Fisheries Information Management System (FIMS) was running. It gives the public fisheries statistics, licensing and export data, which the ministry calls open data. In the last twelve months, that June 2026 statement is the one development found. No source found since October 2023 states an open licence for the data or names two or more public bodies publishing it. Establishing would need the data published under an open licence, or terms that let anyone reuse it.

TCD.short: The customs directorate published 2025 trade statistics for download; no open licence is on record.
TCD.summary: The customs directorate's public data page lists two 2025 trade statistics documents for download. One covers exports and one imports through Douala and Kribi, both by the Chad Shippers' Council, and no licence is stated. The directorate is the one public body found publishing data for download. Nothing newer than these 2025 documents has been found in the last twelve months. No source found since October 2023 states an open licence for the data or names two or more public bodies publishing it. Establishing would need the data published under an open licence, or terms that let anyone reuse it.

TGO.short: Data from 23 ministries was on the national geoportal in 2025, and the open data portal put its data under an open licence by 2026.
TGO.summary: The Open Data portal and the Geoportail were launched in December 2024, run by the Agence Togo Digital. The portal's terms of use say its data is open-licensed unless marked otherwise, and name no particular licence. The Geoportail centralises data from 23 ministries and over 550 administrative units, a January 2025 report says. In May 2025 the digital ministry launched a government geoportal with an open version for the public. In the last twelve months, in April 2026 INSEED trained about thirty staff to move datasets to its new open data platform.

TUN.short: A national open data portal was running in 2025; no open licence for its data has been found.
TUN.summary: In March 2025 the government's Open Government Partnership office called the national portal data.gov.tn a major advance. It said the portal is linked to several sector portals. The same notice cites government decree 2021-03 and circular 4 of 2024 as the legal basis for open data. It gives no terms of reuse for the portal's data. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found since November 2023 states an open licence for the data or names two or more public bodies publishing it. Establishing would need the data published under an open licence, or terms that let anyone reuse it.

TZA.short: The procurement authority published open-licensed data in 2026, and two statistics offices ran a data portal; four or more publishing bodies have not been found.
TZA.summary: The Public Procurement Regulatory Authority publishes its open contracting data under a CC BY-SA 4.0 licence, as listed in February 2026. In August 2026 the National Bureau of Statistics and the Office of the Chief Government Statistician ran the Tanzania Integrated Statistical Portal, which lets users explore administrative, demographic and survey data. In the last twelve months, the February 2026 licence listing and the August 2026 portal are the developments found. Three public bodies publish data online, and only the procurement authority states an open licence. No source found since November 2024 names or counts four or more public bodies publishing data. Mature would need four or more public bodies publishing under an open licence.

UGA.short: The procurement authority published open-licensed data in 2026 and the statistics bureau offered downloads; four or more publishing bodies have not been found.
UGA.summary: The procurement authority PPDA publishes open contracting data from July 2015 to October 2026, updated monthly. The data carry the Open Data Commons Attribution Licence, which lets anyone share and adapt the data with credit. In July 2026 a working group chaired by the Uganda Bureau of Statistics reported all 155 SDG indicators it reports, of 201, on the National SDG Open Data Portal. In the last twelve months, these two publications are the developments found, and only the procurement authority states an open licence. No source found since November 2024 names or counts four or more public bodies publishing data. Mature would need four or more public bodies publishing under an open licence.

ZAF.short: Four public bodies, among them National Treasury under an open licence, published data in 2025 and 2026; no count of publishing bodies has been found.
ZAF.summary: National Treasury's transparency portal offers monthly eTender procurement data from May 2021 in CSV, JSON and Excel under CC BY 4.0, as at November 2026. The Open Contracting Partnership lists the same Treasury data under the Open Data Commons PDDL, 35,309 tenders and 9,551 awards to September 2026. The South African National Biodiversity Institute publishes its 2025 national species checklist under CC BY 4.0. The environment department offers free geospatial data for download. In the last twelve months, the mayor of the City of Tshwane said in October 2026 that it runs an open data portal. No source found counts the public bodies publishing data.

ZMB.short: Fifty-eight dataset layers were published on the national geoportal in 2026; no open licence for the data is known.
ZMB.summary: In June 2026 an article on the Zambia National Spatial Data Infrastructure (ZNSDI) policy said 58 dataset layers have been published through the country's existing geoportal platform. They include the road network and the power utility networks. In the last twelve months, a new national geoportal run by the SMART Zambia e-Government Division launched alongside the ZNSDI Policy. The geoportal integrates datasets from custodians such as the Zambia Electricity Supply Corporation and the Road Development Agency. No source found since October 2023 states an open licence for the data. Establishing would need the data published under an open licence, or terms that let anyone reuse it.

ZWE.short: Government data was published for download on the ZIMSTAT Open Data Portal (ODP 2.0) in 2025; no open licence is on record.
ZWE.summary: On 9 July 2025 ZIMSTAT, the national statistics agency, launched the OpenSDG portal. In July 2025 the OpenSDG Data Portal offered downloadable datasets. In October 2025 ZIMSTAT's Open Data Portal (ODP 2.0) had a public frontend at zw.dbr.afdb.org showing published datasets and dashboards. In the last twelve months, in June 2026 ZIMSTAT's open data portal disseminated key indicators including GDP, inflation and trade statistics. No source found since October 2023 states an open licence for the data or names two or more public bodies publishing it. Establishing would need the data published under an open licence, or terms that let anyone reuse it.

AGO.short: In 2026 journalists, the opposition and the bar criticised Angola's false-information law, and in October a court jailed a news editor for defamation.
AGO.summary: The Law Against False Information on the Internet was published on 4 August 2026 with prison terms of up to 10 years. In the last twelve months, on 2 October 2026, a Luanda court sentenced Reporter Angola editor Daniel Frederico in absentia to 14 months in prison for slander and defamation. At the closing arguments in November 2024, the prosecutor's side asked for three years in prison. No law repealing a speech offence has been found. Establishing would need twelve months with no arrest, charge, jailing, suspension or closure for speech.

BDI.short: A journalist was jailed over messages in 2024-2025 and a media coalition suspended in 2025; criticism of policy and internet cuts are unknown.
BDI.summary: No stage is set. On 14 September 2026 the National Communications Council suspended a Yaga Burundi programme for six months after it aired an interview with a politician critical of the authorities. In the last twelve months, on 14 January 2026, journalist Sandra Muhoza received a four-year prison sentence over information shared in a private press group. On 13 April 2026 the Ngozi appeal court convicted her of 'racial aversion' with six months already served. Nothing found says a paper, broadcaster, party or group inside the country criticised a government policy in public. Preparing would need a source showing such criticism, with no internet cut in the past twelve months.

BEN.short: In November 2026 a media union and Amnesty Bénin criticised the digital code in public; journalists were jailed over posts in 2025 and 2026.
BEN.summary: On 3 November 2026 the media professionals' union UPMB and Amnesty International Bénin called for a review of articles 550 and following of the Code du numérique. In the last twelve months, journalist Pascal Mitowade was sentenced to five years in prison on 24 March 2026 over Facebook posts about the December 2025 coup attempt. Journalist Angela Kpeidja was detained on 16 December 2025 over two Facebook posts. CPJ says she was sentenced to 12 months in prison. Nothing found says the internet was cut or a platform blocked. Establishing would need twelve months with no arrest, charge, jailing, suspension or closure for speech.

BFA.short: In 2026 a student union criticised the government and was suspended, and TV5 Monde was suspended; no source says whether anyone was jailed for speech.
BFA.summary: On 5 May 2026 the Higher Council for Communication indefinitely suspended TV5 Monde broadcasts. In the last twelve months, on 26 May 2026, the Minister of Territorial Administration suspended UGEB for three months after its statement criticising the military authorities' security record. The Ouagadougou prosecutor opened an investigation into its authors. The online platforms of RFI, France 24, Jeune Afrique and Le Monde, among others, remained inaccessible in Burkina Faso in 2024. Nothing found says whether anyone was arrested or jailed for speech. Establishing would need twelve months with no arrest, charge, jailing, suspension or closure for speech.

BWA.short: In February 2026 a civil society chairperson called for fuller consultation on a court process; no source reports any cut, block or punishment for speech.
BWA.summary: On 9 February 2026 the chairperson of the civil society body BOCONGO told the minister that the Constitutional Court process needs meaningful, inclusive participation. In July 2022 Tshepo Sethibe, director of Moeladilotlhoko News Boiler, was charged with publishing “alarming information” on Facebook over posts on the police handling of a disappearance. The state withdrew the charge in October 2024. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Nothing found says whether anyone in Botswana was punished for speech in that time, and no cut or block has been found. Establishing would need twelve months with no arrest, charge, jailing, suspension or closure for speech.

CAF.short: Two counts list a 2025 internet shutdown without a month, and nothing found shows policy criticised in public, so no stage is set.
CAF.summary: No stage is set. Access Now lists the Central African Republic among 15 African countries with an internet shutdown in 2025, and ISS Africa lists it among six in Central Africa that year. Neither gives a month or an order, so no cut is shown inside the last twelve months. A decree set up a government spokesperson's unit to counter rumours, a communications monitoring unit. Nothing found says government policy is criticised in public inside the country, or that anyone was punished for what they said. Absent would need a dated cut or block inside the past twelve months.

CIV.short: In 2025 Côte d'Ivoire's opposition denounced an activist's arrest and courts jailed people for social-media speech; no source found says whether any internet cut occurred.
CIV.summary: On 3 September 2025 the opposition party PPA-CI publicly denounced the arrest of one of its activists as a violation of freedom of expression. The activist, Mamadou Zigui, was arrested on 2 September 2025 over a social-media video. RFI also reports that on 30 June 2025 the Abidjan court sentenced activist Gala Kolebi to 18 months for spreading false news. The prosecutor says a nurse received 36 months and a 5 million fine on 18 July 2025. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Nothing found says the internet was cut. Establishing would need twelve months with no arrest, charge, jailing, suspension or closure for speech.

CMR.short: In October 2025 Cameroon restricted internet access during its presidential election; no source found says who ordered the cuts and when they ended.
CMR.summary: OONI's measurements suggest Cameroon blocked TikTok, Facebook, Instagram and Telegram from 31 October to 5 November 2025, during post-election protests. Access Now's #KeepItOn report counts four internet shutdowns in Cameroon in 2025. In the last twelve months, on 8 and 9 June 2026, Civic Watch Cameroon's head and others met at a workshop in Yaounde on the 2010 cybercrime law. They said it limits free expression. Nothing found names who ordered the 2025 blocks, and no source says the government is barred from such cuts. Preparing would need public criticism of a government policy from inside the country, and no cut in the past twelve months.

COD.short: A rights group criticised government policy in public in 2026, but a journalist was jailed over a post in September 2026.
COD.summary: In October 2026 Fidèle Mbilizi Mutimanwa of the indigenous peoples' league LINAPYCO criticised the state for leaving the Commission's 2022 Batwa decision and law 22/030 largely unapplied. In the last twelve months, the Committee to Protect Journalists says, journalist Tresor Muntu was detained on 15 September 2026 and charged with defamation and publishing false news. OLPA says the main mobile networks in Fizi have been cut since July 2026. No source names who ordered the cuts in Fizi or at Goma. Establishing would need twelve months with no arrest, charge, jailing, suspension or closure for speech.

COG.short: The internet was shut down nationwide on the March 2026 election day, and a rights defender was jailed in May after a passport campaign.
COG.summary: On 15 March 2026, the day of the presidential election, NetBlocks recorded a nation-scale shutdown of the internet in Congo. ISS Africa calls it an ad hoc shutdown during the polls. It says the government's reasons do not appear to meet the UN's tests of legality and necessity. In the last twelve months, police arrested the human rights defender Ghislain Ondele Kanga at his home on 30 May 2026. FIDH says he was charged with false dissemination and with declaring an unauthorised demonstration. Nothing found names the authority that ordered the March 2026 shutdown, or says when it ended. Preparing would need public criticism of a government policy from inside the country, and no cut in the past twelve months.

COM.short: Police arrested a journalist over a Facebook post in November 2025; no source found reports a year without arrests or closures.
COM.summary: Mayotte Hebdo says police arrested Al-Watwan correspondent Abdou Moustoifa on 17 November 2025 over a Facebook post about migrants held in a Moroni police station. In the last twelve months, in December 2025, the Comorian press mobilised against a ministry and CNPA proposal to amend article 169 of the Information Code on source protection. The draft would have let a judge compel journalists to reveal sources, and MPs rejected it on 26 December 2025. Article 361 of the penal code makes defamation a criminal offence. Nothing found says the internet was cut or a service blocked. Establishing would need twelve months with no arrest, charge, jailing, suspension or closure for speech.

CPV.short: Rights groups criticised prosecutions of journalists in August 2025; no internet cut is known, and no source found says whether anyone was punished since.
CPV.summary: On 10 November 2026 the opposition party UCID questioned the government's digital transition. Its deputy Zilda Oliveira feared a higher tax burden on small firms. In August 2025 the RECADDH human-rights network denounced prosecutions and intimidation of journalists and called for the cases to be dropped. It named two journalists accused of qualified disobedience over reports on a death, Herminio Silves and Daniel Almeida. Nothing found says whether anyone was punished for speech in the last twelve months, and no cut or block has been found. Establishing would need twelve months with no arrest, charge, jailing, suspension or closure for speech.

DJI.short: In 2024 to 2026 Djibouti's state media stayed uncritical, opposition sites were blocked and journalists were arrested; no source says whether anyone criticises policy publicly.
DJI.summary: The US State Department's 2024 human rights report says the government owned the only radio and television stations. It says the newspaper La Nation held a monopoly on authorized print media. It adds that official media generally did not criticise government policy. In the last twelve months, exiled journalist Zineb Haddaji told CIVICUS Lens in July 2026 that opposition and exiled media websites are blocked in Djibouti. The opposition party RADDE says police arrested a journalist and a cameraman of its citizens' rights programme on 20 November 2025. Nothing found says a newspaper, broadcaster, party or group inside Djibouti criticised government policy in public in the last three years. Preparing would need public criticism of a government policy from inside the country, and no cut in the past twelve months.

DZA.short: Journalists were held and convicted over their work in 2025 and 2026, but nothing found shows policy criticised in public, so no stage is set.
DZA.summary: No stage is set. Amnesty International says seven journalists and media workers were detained, prosecuted or convicted from November 2025 over their work or opinions. On 7 July 2026 the Algiers appeal court upheld journalist Saad Bouakba's conviction over statements on historical events. In the last twelve months, from 7 June 2026, Algeria confined its exam shutdown measures to the inside of exam centres. On 15 June 2025, the first day of the baccalaureate, Facebook and TikTok were blocked in Algeria. Nothing found says a paper, broadcaster, party or group inside the country criticised a government policy in public. Preparing would need a dated source showing such criticism, and no cut in the past twelve months.

EGY.short: In February 2026 Egypt was still blocking independent news sites, at least 630 websites; no source says whether the journalists arrested since 2025 were charged.
EGY.summary: In February 2026 Access Now and other groups said the authorities were still blocking independent media sites, at least 630 websites in all. In November 2026 CPJ said the site of the outlet Zawia3 is blocked inside Egypt. In the last twelve months, on 27 October 2026, a Cairo court fined Mada Masr editor Lina Attalah EGP 3 million and ordered the news website closed. Human Rights Watch says security forces arrested the six journalists of the Matsda2sh newsroom on 28 and 29 September 2026. On 10 November 2026 the UN human rights office said they remained in detention. No bar on cuts or blocks has been found. Preparing would need public criticism of a government policy from inside the country, and no cut in the past twelve months.

ERI.short: In 2026 UNESCO states that the state runs all media and private outlets ended after a 2001 ban; no source found reports cuts and punishments.
ERI.summary: UNESCO states, in a document dated January 2026, that the Ministry of Information runs all television, radio and newspapers in Eritrea. It states that privately owned outlets effectively ceased to exist after a government ban in 2001. It presents that position as continuing. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No outlet independent of the state has been found carrying public criticism. Nothing found says whether anyone in Eritrea has been cut off, arrested or charged for speech. Preparing would need public criticism of a government policy from inside the country, and no cut in the past twelve months.

ETH.short: In November 2026 the regulator suspended The Reporter after its editorial criticised the authorities; who ordered the 2026 regional outages is not stated.
ETH.summary: On 2 November 2026 the Ethiopian Media Authority suspended the registration of The Reporter's publisher indefinitely. It said the paper's reports undermine national interests. On 31 October 2026 The Reporter had published an editorial, 'Press Freedom Is Not A Luxury!', criticising the authorities for treating independent reporting as a threat to national security. In the last twelve months, Amnesty International says, Addis Standard's managing editor, Million Beyene, was abducted by intelligence agents on 15 April 2026 and held for two weeks. In October 2026 Access Now reported new internet shutdowns in Tigray. No source names who ordered the 2026 outages in Tigray and Amhara. Establishing would need twelve months with no arrest, charge, jailing, suspension or closure for speech.

GAB.short: The regulator suspended social media in Gabon from February to October 2026; no source found says whether anyone was punished for speech.
GAB.summary: The HAC lifted the suspension, ordered on 17 February 2026, on 24 October 2026, citing cooperation with TikTok, Meta and YouTube. The regulator had suspended social media in Gabon by decision no. 0002/HAC/2026, until further notice. On 10 August 2026 the HAC suspended the news site Info241 until further notice. Activist Bob Mengome was arrested on 19 January 2026 and charged with defamation over a voice message criticising the president. In the last twelve months, nine civil-society organisations met in Libreville on 11 July 2026 and called the suspension unconstitutional and disproportionate. No bar on such cuts has been found. Preparing would need public criticism of a government policy from inside the country, and no cut in the past twelve months.

GHA.short: In September 2026 a nursing officer was arrested and charged over alleged false-news videos; no source says whether anyone else was punished or access cut.
GHA.summary: On 13 September 2026 senior nursing officer Salomey Awiti Bafoh was arrested and charged with abetment of publishing false news. She pleaded not guilty and was remanded without bail. On 13 April 2026 police arrested opposition figures Kwame Baffoe and Abubakar Yakubu over online publications. MFWA counted 14 arrests under the false-news laws in the 16 months from 7 January 2025. On 7 November 2026 Minority Leader Alexander Afenyo-Markin called for repeal of Section 208 of the Criminal Offences Act, the false-news offence. No cut or block has been found in the last twelve months. Establishing would need twelve months with no arrest, charge, jailing, suspension or closure for speech.

GIN.short: In September 2026 the regulator barred France 24, and social media have been restricted since 28 July; no source found says who ordered the restrictions.
GIN.summary: On 17 September 2026 the HAC ordered the telecoms regulator ARPT to block all France 24 digital access points. The same day it revoked the national broadcasting authorisation of France 24 and withdrew its correspondents accreditations. In the last twelve months, Facebook, YouTube and TikTok were blocked from 28 July 2026, according to the bloggers association ABLOGUI. On 4 August 2026 the Union pour la defense des consommateurs denounced the social media restrictions as a state decision harming the right to information. No source says who ordered the July 2026 restrictions, or when they ended. Preparing would need public criticism of a government policy from inside the country, and no cut in the past twelve months.

GMB.short: The Gambia Press Union criticised new media laws in 2025 and 2026; no source shows twelve months without anyone punished for speech.
GMB.summary: On 24 March 2025 the National Assembly passed the Criminal Offence and Procedure Bill 2025. It dropped the offences of criminal defamation and sedition. In the last twelve months, on 14 May 2026, the Gambia Press Union called the Cybercrime Bill 2023, the Communications Bill 2025 and the Criminal Offences Act 2025 threats to media freedom. It said that the Supreme Court had struck down criminal defamation and false publication online, with no date for the ruling. In October 2024 the High Court charged The Voice's editor and a reporter with false publication. Nothing found says the last twelve months passed with no one punished for speech. Establishing would need twelve months with no arrest, charge, jailing, suspension or closure for speech.

GNB.short: On 26 November 2025, the day the military took power, social media access was restricted; no end date is known.
GNB.summary: On 26 November 2025 citizens reported widespread restrictions on Facebook, YouTube, TikTok and Instagram. The Media Foundation for West Africa says the military imposed them. The source gives no end date. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found reports public criticism of government policy, or a person punished for speech. No source found names a bar on such cuts. Preparing would need public criticism of a government policy from inside the country, and no cut in the past twelve months.

GNQ.short: The government has kept Annobón island without internet since July 2024; no public criticism of policy from inside the country is known.
GNQ.summary: Access Now says the island of Annobón has had no internet or phone service since July 2024. It puts the blackout down to the government. Its report of 20 October 2026 lists Annobón among places under indefinite blackouts. In the last twelve months, AFP reported on 16 September 2026 that the author of a viral video accusing the vice-president of corruption was arrested by the authorities. Ley 7/2024 on social networks and cybercrime is in full force, the government said on 1 July 2026. Nothing found says a paper, party or group inside the country criticised a government policy in public. Preparing would need public criticism of a government policy from inside the country, and no cut in the past twelve months.

KEN.short: A journalist was charged over a WhatsApp message in February 2026; courts struck down false-publication offences in March; no source found reports a bar on cuts.
KEN.summary: In March 2026 the Court of Appeal struck down two sections of the Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act on false publication. The sections carried fines up to KSh 5 million, and the National Assembly has appealed to the Supreme Court. In the last twelve months, on 25 February 2026, journalist Peter Mwita was charged under the Act over a WhatsApp message. Access Now counts three internet shutdowns in Kenya in 2025. OONI recorded a same-day block of Telegram Web on 25 June 2025. No law or court ruling barring cuts has been found. Establishing would need twelve months with no arrest, charge, jailing, suspension or closure for speech.

LBR.short: In September 2026 police arrested a man under the Cybercrime Act over posts about the Vice President; no source found reports the court outcome.
LBR.summary: In September 2026 police arrested Jerry Nyanti Wratto in Monrovia, charged him and sent him to court under the Cybercrime Act over Facebook and TikTok posts about the Vice President. The Vice President asked for his release, and no court outcome is given. On 24 September 2026 the Cybercrime Act's provisions on false information and offensive communication were called vague and a weapon to silence critics. The critics were the Press Union of Liberia and civil society groups. In October 2026 the Press Union called for the withdrawal of a confidentiality agreement for civil servants. No cut or block of internet access has been found. Establishing would need twelve months with no arrest, charge, jailing, suspension or closure for speech.

LBY.short: An activist was arrested over online posts in August 2026 and a draft cybercrime law was criticised in 2025; no source found reports cuts.
LBY.summary: On 14 August 2026 the Committee for Justice documented the arrest of Benghazi activist Aziz Al-Orfi by the Internal Security Agency. The arrest was over his Facebook and TikTok posts on public affairs. He says he was held five days on accusations of incitement. On 3 May 2026 the UN mission said journalists and critics are still arrested and prosecuted, including under cybercrime law. In 2025 a representative of Internet Society Libya said Article 39 on defamation in the draft cybercrime law could be used to suppress activists and journalists. Nothing found gives a cut or block of internet access, or a bar on one, in the last twelve months. Establishing would need twelve months with no arrest, charge, jailing, suspension or closure for speech.

LSO.short: Courts struck down criminal defamation, reported in 2026 without a date, but no recent public criticism of policy is known, so no stage is set.
LSO.summary: No stage is set. The Southern Africa Litigation Centre said in October 2026 that courts in Lesotho struck down criminal defamation. It gave no date for the ruling. Nothing found says the internet was cut or a site blocked in the last twelve months. No bar on cutting the internet has been found. No source from the last three years says anyone in the country criticised a government policy in public. Preparing would need a dated source showing such public criticism, and no cut in the past twelve months.

MAR.short: Nationwide protests criticised policy from September 2025 and a man was jailed in October 2025 for posts; no source says whether the internet was cut.
MAR.summary: Human Rights Watch says the youth movement GenZ212 called nationwide protests from 27 September 2025. The movement criticised public spending on mega-sporting events and demanded more for health care and education. On 4 October 2025 the Agadir Court of First Instance sentenced a man to four years in prison and a 50,000 dirham fine for 'inciting minor offenses and crimes via social media'. In December 2025 opposition members proposed deleting part of Article 51 bis of Organic Law 53.25 as a threat to free expression. The government rejected the amendment. Nothing found says the internet was cut in the last twelve months. Establishing would need twelve months with no arrest, charge, jailing, suspension or closure for speech.

MDG.short: In 2026 a news site questioned the cybercrime bill, and the Presidency said people were being prosecuted for insulting senior officials online.
MDG.summary: On 8 January 2026 the Presidency said people and pages were being prosecuted for insulting senior officials online. Amnesty International says at least nine Gen Z leaders were arrested in April 2026. It says they were held for being in a WhatsApp group or messaging an opposition figure. On 3 September 2026 Madagascar-Tribune questioned the government's cybercrime bill n°042/2026. It said the bill's digital police powers raise issues of freedom of expression. In January 2025 journalist Fernand Cello was charged with false news over a Facebook post. No cut of internet access, and no bar on one, has been found in the last twelve months. Establishing would need twelve months with no arrest, charge, jailing, suspension or closure for speech.

MLI.short: Mali banned the online circulation of Jeune Afrique in January 2026 and blocked its website, while journalists were jailed for criticism.
MLI.summary: In January 2026 the government banned the distribution, sale and online circulation of the magazine Jeune Afrique. Readers report its website blocked in Mali since late January 2026. In the last twelve months the cybercrime tribunal sentenced the journalist Abdrahamane Keita to two years in prison on 14 September 2026. On 17 August 2026 the Bamako appeal court sentenced radio commentator Ras Bath and activist Rose Vie Chère to ten years, three suspended. Editor Chahana Takiou, arrested on 8 June 2026, was sentenced on 3 August to 12 months, six suspended. Nothing found says whether the block on Jeune Afrique's website has been lifted. Preparing would need public criticism of a government policy from inside the country, and no cut in the past twelve months.

MOZ.short: In March 2026 civil society and opposition criticised telecommunications regulations as allowing internet shutdowns; no source found says whether anyone was punished for speech.
MOZ.summary: In March 2026 civil society bodies and opposition parties said the new telecommunications regulations allowed internet shutdowns on national security grounds. The journalist Tomas Vieira Mario condemned the minister's defence on Facebook. On 29 July 2026 the Constitutional Council issued Acórdão 6/CC/2026. After the October 2024 election, OONI measurements show internet providers blocked Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp from 29 October to 14 November 2024. No cut is on record from the last twelve months. No arrest, charge or sentence for speech has been found. Establishing would need twelve months with no arrest, charge, jailing, suspension or closure for speech.

MRT.short: Two MPs were arrested in 2026 and a news site closed in 2025; policy criticism and internet cuts not known, so no stage is set.
MRT.summary: No stage is set. In the last twelve months, on 4 May 2026, a court sentenced two opposition MPs to four years in prison for social media videos denouncing 'apartheid'. They were Mariem Cheikh Dieng and Ghamou Achour. Traders told Le360 that mobile internet was cut during the exam period of 23 June to 10 July 2025. After the June 2024 election the authorities cut mobile internet for 22 days from 2 July 2024. Nothing found from the last three years says a paper, broadcaster, party or group inside the country criticised a government policy in public. Preparing would need a dated source showing such criticism, and no cut in the past twelve months.

MUS.short: Social media was suspended for a day in November 2024 amid public outcry; whether anyone was punished for speech in the last year is unknown.
MUS.summary: On 1 November 2024 the Information and Communications Authority directed internet service providers to suspend access to Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and X. The ban was lifted on 2 November after 24 hours. Civil society groups and businesses opposed the November 2024 social media suspension. Human Rights Watch reports swift and widespread outcry from business, civil society and opposition politicians inside Mauritius. In the last twelve months, in August 2026, the ministry reminded the public of the sanctions for unwanted content online. Nothing found says no one was punished for what they said or published. Establishing would need twelve months with no arrest, charge, jailing, suspension or closure for speech.

MWI.short: Civil-society groups criticised policy before parliament in 2026; a contributor was arrested over posts in December 2025, though criminal defamation was struck down.
MWI.summary: In July 2025 the High Court, sitting as a Constitutional Court, declared criminal defamation under section 200 of the Penal Code unconstitutional, MISA Malawi reports. In the last twelve months, on 5 December 2025, police arrested Maravi Post contributor Jones Gadama over two documents posted online. The documents alleged misconduct by an employee of the state broadcaster MBC. He was placed on fortnightly police bail. On 9 March 2026 civil society groups told parliamentary committees the 2026/27 education budget falls short of a UNESCO benchmark. No cut or block has been found. Establishing would need twelve months with no arrest, charge, jailing, suspension or closure for speech.

NAM.short: In May 2026 a media foundation criticised the government for not bringing the access-to-information law into force; whether anyone was punished is not found.
NAM.summary: On 5 May 2026 the director of the NMT Media Foundation criticised in The Namibian the government's failure to bring the Access to Information Act into force. The director wrote as rapporteur of the 2026 African Media Barometer for Namibia. In April 2026 The Namibian ran a column by Dianne Hubbard listing flaws in the cybercrime bill. In December 2022 the Institute for Public Policy Research called the draft Data Protection Bill 'not fit for purpose'. No cut or block of the internet has been found. No arrest, charge or closure for speech has been found. Establishing would need twelve months with no arrest, charge, jailing, suspension or closure for speech.

NER.short: In 2026 Niger suspended nine foreign outlets and charged journalists and a lawyer for their words; Transparency International's chapter criticised the cybercrime ordinance in 2025.
NER.summary: In the last twelve months, on 8 May 2026, the National Communication Observatory suspended nine outlets from reaching audiences in Niger, CPJ reports. On 21 September 2026 the lawyer Abrourahamane Lirwana was charged and detained over comments about the army, Human Rights Watch says. Journalist Ibro Chaibou was freed on 28 August 2026 after nearly ten months in detention. On 10 November 2025 ANLC, Transparency International's Niger chapter, said the 2011 access to information ordinance still had no implementing decree. No law or court ruling barring such cuts has been found. Preparing would need public criticism of a government policy from inside the country, and no cut in the past twelve months.

NGA.short: In 2026 the State Services department prosecuted Omoyele Sowore for criticising the president, then paused the case; other recent arrests are not dated.
NGA.summary: In the last twelve months, on 10 November 2026, a court remanded journalist Daniel Ojukwu on cybercrime and criminal defamation charges over published investigations. The Department of State Services is prosecuting Omoyele Sowore under the Cybercrimes Act for calling President Tinubu a criminal. On 30 August 2026 its Director-General said the prosecution would be suspended until after the 2027 election. In August 2026 SERAP and the Nigerian Guild of Editors called for Section 24 of the Cybercrimes Act to be suspended. Media Rights Agenda recorded 38 arrests and detentions of journalists and citizens in 2025. No source names who ordered the Zamfara North disconnection of 2025. Establishing would need twelve months with no arrest, charge, jailing, suspension or closure for speech.

RWA.short: ARTICLE 19 said in November 2025 that independent news sites remained blocked in Rwanda; no public criticism of policy inside the country has been found.
RWA.summary: On 27 November 2025 ARTICLE 19 said independent online news sites, including The Rwandan and Le Prophete, remained blocked. It did not say who ordered the block. ARTICLE 19 said in November 2025 that journalists and online commentators continued to face arrests and prosecutions. An ARM project brief says 26 online radio stations and websites of exiled critics were made inaccessible in 2019, after the Senate accused them of genocide denial. No law or court ruling barring such blocks has been found. No criticism of a government policy from inside the country has been found. Preparing would need public criticism of a government policy from inside the country, and no cut in the past twelve months.

SDN.short: In August 2026 a court in El Obeid jailed a pharmacist for six years over a private call opposing the war; no repeal is known.
SDN.summary: In the last twelve months, in August 2026, a criminal court in El Obeid sentenced pharmacist Ahmed Suleiman Ahmed al-Waqi to six years in prison. His offence was a private phone conversation opposing the war. On 21 July 2026 the cybercrime prosecutor in Red Sea State charged at least 15 journalists and two outlets over reporting on alleged corruption. MTN Sudan suspended internet service in the afternoons of 13 to 15 April 2026, on government directives. The Sudanese Journalists Syndicate condemned the detention of journalist Gurashi Awad on 14 August 2026. Nothing found says a cut was barred or a penalty for speech repealed. Preparing would need public criticism of a government policy from inside the country, and no cut in the past twelve months.

SEN.short: Press bodies and commentators criticised policy in 2026, and a columnist was charged with false news in October 2026 for criticising the police.
SEN.summary: In the last twelve months, on 16 October 2026, Sen TV columnist Mamadou Cissé was charged with disseminating false news over YouTube comments criticising the police handling of an influencer's arrest. On 5 August 2026 a Dakar court sentenced three commentators for offending the head of state over a video criticising President Faye. In February 2026 columnist Abdou Nguer was charged with spreading false information and remanded in custody. On 31 March 2026 the journalists' union SYNPICS and the publishers' council CDEPS called the regulator law a threat to press freedom. No bar on cutting the internet has been found. Establishing would need twelve months with no arrest, charge, jailing, suspension or closure for speech.

SLE.short: In 2025 the journalists' association objected to the regulator withdrawing two broadcasters' frequencies; whether anyone was punished since is not found.
SLE.summary: In July 2025 the regulator NaTCA withdrew broadcast frequencies from Truth Media and G8 Media Group. The Sierra Leone Association of Journalists raised concerns with the information minister, warning that such actions could undermine press freedom. In June 2025 police arrested Citizens Radio reporter Hassan Kamara after a post on the football association election. The TV personality Hawa Hunt was arrested on 22 December 2024 and held for over a month. The Public Order (Amendment) Act, 2020 repealed the part of the 1965 Act on defamatory and seditious libel. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Establishing would need twelve months with no arrest, charge, jailing, suspension or closure for speech.

SOM.short: Police shut Risaala Media and arrested five journalists in March 2025; Amnesty reports arrests in 2026; no source found says who was punished since.
SOM.summary: In the last twelve months, on 25 June 2026, police arrested journalist Abdukadir Abukar Ali after he published a video questioning the fairness of a trial. On 30 June 2026 intelligence officers detained Mascuud Warsame, founder of the outlet Xogbile. In August 2026 the National Union of Somali Journalists criticised the draft Penal Code adopted by the Council of Ministers in December 2025. On 18 March 2025 armed police took the Risaala Media station in Mogadishu off air and arrested five journalists. In 2026 the government closed 82,000 social media pages it called extremist-linked, Hiiraan reported on 4 September 2026. No cut of a connection has been found since March 2025. Establishing would need twelve months with no arrest, charge, jailing, suspension or closure for speech.

SSD.short: A media body criticised the January 2025 social media block publicly; no source says whether anyone was punished for speech in the last twelve months.
SSD.summary: President Kiir signed the Cybercrime and Computer Misuse Act 2026 on 18 February 2026. In the last twelve months, on 20 November 2026, the South Sudan Human Rights Defenders Network asked for three sections of the new Act to be amended. It said they could be used against journalists. On 22 January 2025 the National Communication Authority directed all internet service providers to block all social media accounts for 30 to 90 days. On 28 January 2025 AMDISS, a South Sudanese media body, criticised the block on Facebook and TikTok. No punishment for speech is on record. Nothing found says when the block ended. Establishing would need twelve months with no arrest, charge, jailing, suspension or closure for speech.

STP.short: Nothing found says whether policy is criticised in public, the internet was cut, or anyone was punished for speech, so no stage is set.
STP.summary: Not found. Nothing found says government policy is criticised in public inside the country. Nothing found says the internet was cut, or that anyone was punished for what they said.

SWZ.short: In April 2026 an outlet published an investigation holding the ICT ministry to account; a 2009 speech charge still stands untried.
SWZ.summary: An opinion piece in Independent News Eswatini says that the Swazi Bridge outlet published an investigation on 12 April 2026. The investigation held the ICT ministry to account for how its memorandum of understanding with Google Cloud EMEA was communicated. In a blog dated 27 February 2026 MISA engaged the Eswatini government on expression and media freedom. The Southern Africa Litigation Centre says that Mphandlana Shongwe was charged under the Suppression of Terrorism Act in 2009 for shouting political slogans at a meeting. The charge still stands untried. No cut or block has been found. Nothing found says no one was punished in the last twelve months. Establishing would need twelve months with no arrest, charge, jailing, suspension or closure for speech.

SYC.short: Nothing found says whether policy is criticised in public, the internet was cut, or anyone was punished for speech, so no stage is set.
SYC.summary: Not found. Nothing found says government policy is criticised in public inside the country. Nothing found says the internet was cut, or that anyone was punished for what they said.

TCD.short: Internet access in Lac province has been cut since October 2024 and was still limited in September 2026; no source found says who ordered it.
TCD.summary: Internet access in Lac province has been cut since 28 October 2024. A citizen's open letter to the president, reported on 10 September 2026, says connectivity in Lac has been heavily limited for nearly two years. In the last twelve months, as reported on 4 August 2026, the regulator HAMA suspended the examination of applications to create online newspapers. On 5 August 2026 the online media association AMET said the suspension must respect press freedom and citizens' right to pluralistic information. No source names who ordered the cut or gives an end date. Preparing would need public criticism of a government policy from inside the country, and no cut in the past twelve months.

TGO.short: Access Now reports 2025 protest throttling in Togo, but not where, who ordered it or when it ended, so no stage is set.
TGO.summary: No stage is set. Access Now lists Togo among states with a 2025 internet shutdown, described as protest throttling. CIPESA says Togo had a three-day internet shutdown during the 2017 protests, which the ECOWAS Court later found violated freedom of expression. In October 2025 the prosecutor cited the penal code, cybersecurity and cybercrime law, data protection law and press code. No source found dates a cut inside the last twelve months. No source dated in the last three years says a newspaper, broadcaster, party or group inside the country criticised a government policy in public. Absent would need a cut or block dated inside the past twelve months.

TUN.short: Messaging apps were disrupted across Tunisia during the June 2026 exams, and journalists were jailed for speech; no source found says whether any law bars cuts.
TUN.summary: On 15 July 2026 the Sfax Court of Appeal sentenced journalist Haythem El Mekki to one year in prison over a post about a Sfax hospital. Journalists Borhen Bsaies and Mourad Zeghidi got one year, cut to eight months, under Decree-Law 54. On 25 May 2026 Sonia Dahmani was convicted again under Decree-Law 54 and sentenced to two years. In the last twelve months, Access Now, citing OONI data, says mobile internet disruptions hit messaging apps across Tunisia during the Baccalaureate from 3 June 2026. No law or ruling barring cuts has been found. Preparing would need public criticism of a government policy from inside the country, and no cut in the past twelve months.

TZA.short: The internet was slowed around an opposition leader's sentencing in November 2026, after the October 2025 election cut; no source found reports a bar on cuts.
