TZA.summary: In the last twelve months, the EastAfrican says, connections were slowed around the 6 November 2026 sentencing of Chadema leader Tundu Lissu. Access Now reports a five-day nationwide internet blackout during the 29 October 2025 election. The Legal & Human Rights Centre filed a case at the East African Court of Justice on 8 December 2025 alleging a nationwide internet shutdown. The Tanzania Communications Regulatory Authority suspended the online content licence of JamiiForums for 90 days from 6 September 2025. Nothing on public criticism of policy has been found. Nothing found says who ordered the October 2025 blackout. Preparing would need public criticism of a government policy from inside the country, and no cut in the past twelve months.

UGA.short: The government cut the internet for four days in January 2026, and Facebook stayed blocked in March; no source found reports a bar on cuts.
UGA.summary: The Uganda Communications Commission ordered operators to suspend public internet access from 18:00 on 13 January 2026, two days before the presidential election. The blackout lasted four days. On 27 March 2026 the ICT minister of state said the Facebook suspension, in place since January 2021, would stay until Meta meets the government's conditions. In the last twelve months, in late June 2026, soldiers seized critic Timothy Kalyegira and activist Miria Matembe. On 17 August 2026 editor Remmy Asiteza was charged with publishing fake news. The Uganda Law Society condemned the shutdown as illegal and unconstitutional. Preparing would need public criticism of a government policy from inside the country, and no cut in the past twelve months.

ZAF.short: Parliament repealed criminal defamation in 2024, but nothing found shows policy criticised in public in the last three years, so no stage is set.
ZAF.summary: No stage is set. On 3 April 2024 the President signed the Judicial Matters Amendment Act, repealing the crime of defamation. In 2026 the Electoral Commission gazetted a code of conduct on election disinformation. Nothing found shows the internet cut, or anyone punished for speech, in the last twelve months. Nothing found says a newspaper, broadcaster, party or group inside the country criticised a government policy in public in the last three years. Preparing would need a dated source that shows such criticism.

ZMB.short: A vlogger got nine months in September 2026 over a post about a presidential aide; whether any year passes without such cases is unknown.
ZMB.summary: On 15 September 2026 a Lusaka court sentenced vlogger Joseph Chishimba to nine months over a screenshot about a presidential aide. Journalist MacPherson Mukuka was detained from 17 July 2026 over an audio recording of a campaign committee. Police in Mansa arrested Kennedy Mwansa for insulting the president on TikTok. On 8 August 2026 the Net Rights Coalition said arrests of journalists under the Cyber Crimes Act signal a chilling climate. No cut or block is on record from the last twelve months. Access Now says the authorities reportedly blocked WhatsApp, Facebook, Twitter and Instagram in the August 2021 elections. Establishing would need twelve months with no arrest, charge, jailing, suspension or closure for speech.

ZWE.short: Journalists were reportedly arrested on cyberbullying charges in 2026 and the data protection law was criticised; no source found says whether any outlet was closed.
ZWE.summary: On 15 October 2026 the Media Alliance of Zimbabwe held a dialogue criticising the Cyber and Data Protection Act as a tool to silence journalists. Its coordinator said four journalists were reportedly arrested in 2026 on cyberbullying charges. Amnesty International says a Bulawayo24 journalist has been in custody since 18 February 2026, charged with cyberbullying after a story alleging corruption. On 23 June 2026 MISA Zimbabwe published an analysis criticising the National AI Strategy 2026-2030. Nothing found says whether an outlet was suspended or closed, or access cut, in the last twelve months. Establishing would need twelve months with no arrest, charge, jailing, suspension or closure for speech.

AGO.short: Angola's 2020 payment system law is in force and since 2022 lets non-bank companies be authorised; no rule to connect providers is known.
AGO.summary: Angola's payments law is Lei n.º 40/20 of 16 December 2020, the Lei do Sistema de Pagamentos de Angola. Under it, Aviso n.º 2/22 of February 2022 lets non-bank financial institutions provide payment services as authorised payment service companies. In the last twelve months, Aviso n.º 1/26 of January 2026 set the rules for acquirers that are not banks, and only authorised companies may now act as non-bank acquirers. No rule has been found that requires providers to connect to each other or to a switch. Mature would need such a rule.

BDI.short: Burundi's 2018 payment system law is in force, and a 2024 regulation licenses non-bank payment institutions; no rule to connect providers is known.
BDI.summary: Burundi's Loi n°1/07 of 11 May 2018 on the national payment system is in force, and the central bank's oversight framework of November 2025 cites it as the current law. Under it the bank made Règlement n°002/2024, which revises a 2017 regulation and under which it licenses payment institutions. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No rule has been found that requires providers to connect to each other or to a switch. Mature would need such a rule.

BEN.short: Benin is under the regional central bank's 2024 payment rules, which license non-banks; since November 2026 transfers between providers must use its platform.
BEN.summary: Benin is bound by the BCEAO's Instruction n°001-01-2024 on payment services, applied since January 2024. It requires every company offering payment services in the union to hold a licence or stop. Four companies held payment institution licences in Benin at 31 August 2026. In the last twelve months, the BCEAO told banks, e-money institutions and payment institutions to connect to its instant payment platform, PI-SPI. On 25 June 2026 it moved the deadline to 30 September. Since 2 November 2026 a BCEAO notice requires interoperable e-money transfers to go through PI-SPI.

BFA.short: Burkina Faso is under the regional central bank's 2024 payment rules, which license non-banks; in 2026 it ordered all providers to connect.
BFA.summary: Burkina Faso is bound by the BCEAO's instruction of 23 January 2024 on payment services, under which payment institutions are licensed. Two payment institutions are licensed in Burkina Faso. INTOUCH Burkina has held a licence since 9 May 2025 and KERRY Payments Burkina since 2 September 2025. In the last twelve months, in April 2026, the BCEAO told every bank, e-money issuer and payment institution to connect to its instant payment platform, PI-SPI, by 30 June. On 25 June it moved the deadline to 30 September 2026. L'Oeil du Sahel reports a BCEAO communique of 2 October 2026 requiring interoperable e-money transfers to pass through PI-SPI from 2 November 2026.

BWA.short: Botswana's electronic payment regulations, amended in April 2026, license payment companies that are not banks; no rule requiring providers to connect is known.
BWA.summary: Botswana's Electronic Payment Services (Amendment) Regulations, 2026, made by the Minister of Finance as Statutory Instrument No. 46 of 2026, took effect on 2 April 2026. In the last twelve months, they began to require anyone operating an electronic payment service, e-money issuance included, to hold a Bank of Botswana licence and be a company incorporated in Botswana. They do not apply to banks licensed under the Banking Act. No rule has been found that requires providers to connect to each other or to a switch. Mature would need such a rule.

CAF.short: The Central African Republic is under the 2018 regional payment services regulation, which licenses non-banks; none was licensed there by 2023.
CAF.summary: The Central African Republic is bound by CEMAC regulation n°04/18 of 21 December 2018 on payment services. The regional central bank's strategy of February 2025 says the regulation created payment establishments, licensed to provide payment services without being tied to a bank. The strategy lists six licensed across the region by July 2023, and none was in the Central African Republic. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No rule has been found that requires providers to connect to each other or to a switch. Mature would need such a rule.

CIV.short: Côte d'Ivoire is under the regional central bank's 2024 payment rules, with ten non-bank payment institutions licensed; in 2026 all providers were ordered to connect.
CIV.summary: Côte d'Ivoire is bound by the BCEAO's Instruction n°001-01-2024 on payment services, applied since January 2024. Ten payment institutions were licensed in Côte d'Ivoire at 31 August 2026, the newest on 27 April 2026. In the last twelve months, in April 2026 the BCEAO told every bank and e-money and payment institution to connect to PI-SPI by 30 June. On 25 June it moved the deadline to 30 September 2026. On 4 November 2026 a National Assembly committee adopted a 258-article banking bill. The bill brings fintech and e-money operations into national law.

CMR.short: Cameroon licenses payment institutions that are not banks under regional rules, the newest in July 2026; no rule requiring providers to connect is known.
CMR.summary: Cameroon's regulatory framework lets payment institutions, banks and microfinance institutions offer payment services, with a licence granted by order of the finance minister on a decision of COBAC, the regional banking commission. In the last twelve months, Konoom Cameroun was licensed as a payment institution by arrêté n°681/MINFI of 21 July 2026. Orange Money Cameroun and Mobile Money Corporation were already licensed. No rule has been found that requires providers to connect to each other or to a switch. Mature would need such a rule.

COD.short: DR Congo's 2018 payments law is in force, the central bank approves non-bank e-money issuers, and all providers must join the national switch.
COD.summary: Loi n° 18-019 of 9 July 2018 on payment systems is the Democratic Republic of the Congo's payments law. The central bank's map of the payment system lists the providers it has approved, five non-bank financial companies among them at end-2023. Instruction No. 58 of September 2024 obliges every regulated entity to join the National E-Payment Switch within six months, under sanction. In the last twelve months, the central bank licensed Wave as an e-money institution in November 2026.

COG.short: Congo licenses non-bank payment institutions under the 2018 regional payment services regulation, one since 2022; no rule to connect providers has been found.
COG.summary: Congo's payment institutions are governed by CEMAC/UMAC/COBAC Regulation No. 04/18 of 21 December 2018 on payment services. The finance ministry approved Mobile Money Congo SA as a payment institution by an order of 27 May 2022. In the last twelve months, COBAC's 2025 annual report named Mobile Money Congo SA and Mobile Commerce Congo SA as the payment institutions operating in Congo, neither a bank. Their revenues rose 28.1% to FCFA 20.6 billion in 2025. No rule has been found that requires providers to connect to each other or to a switch. Mature would need such a rule.

COM.short: The Comoros has had e-money rules since 2017 and two licensed e-money firms by 2025; no rule requiring providers to connect is known.
COM.summary: The Central Bank of the Comoros issued Regulation n°01/2017/BCC/DSBR in 2017, setting the conditions for carrying on e-money activity. No later amendment is reported. In the last twelve months, in December 2025, the central bank listed Telco Money SA and Hury Money SA among the e-money institutions legally established in the Comoros, beside its licensed banks. No rule has been found that requires providers to connect to each other or to a switch. Mature would need such a rule.

CPV.short: Cabo Verde's 2018 decree-laws on payments are in force and let the central bank authorise non-bank institutions; no rule to connect providers is known.
CPV.summary: Cabo Verde legislated on payments in three decree-laws published on 28 November 2018. Decreto-legislativo n.º 7/2018 sets the regime for the payment system, and Decreto-legislativo n.º 8/2018 regulates payment services and e-money. Under Decreto-legislativo n.º 9/2018, the Banco de Cabo Verde authorises payment institutions and e-money institutions, which are distinct from banks. No licensed institution has been found. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No rule has been found that requires providers to connect to each other or to a switch. Mature would need such a rule.

DJI.short: Djibouti's 2016 payment law is in force and the central bank has licensed two non-bank e-money issuers; no rule requiring providers to connect is known.
DJI.summary: Djibouti's Loi n° 118/AN/15/7ème L, which created the National Payment System, was promulgated in 2016 and applies to every payment service and system. The central bank's register of licensed institutions lists two e-money issuers beside the banks, D-Money (licensed 2020) and WAAFI (licensed 2022). No amendment to the law has been found, and no change in the last twelve months. No rule has been found that requires providers to connect to each other or to a switch. Mature would need such a rule.

DZA.short: Algeria's 2023 banking law and 2025 regulation license payment providers that are not banks; the first mobile operator subsidiary was authorised in September 2026.
DZA.summary: Algeria's Loi n° 23-09 of 21 June 2023 on money and banking lists payment service providers apart from banks. Under it the Bank of Algeria made Regulation no. 25-02 of 14 April 2025, which lets a company be licensed as one by the Governor after authorisation by the Monetary and Banking Council. In the last twelve months, on 23 September 2026 the Council authorised Djezzy Payment Services, a subsidiary of a mobile operator, to set itself up as a provider. It has twelve months to apply for the licence. No rule has been found that requires providers to connect to each other or to a switch. Mature would need such a rule.

EGY.short: Egypt's central bank licenses payment companies that are not banks under 2025 rules; no source found says whether providers must connect to each other.
EGY.summary: The Central Bank of Egypt issued Rules for Licensing and Registration of Payment System Operators and Payment Service Providers in June 2025. The rules of 19 June 2025 set licensing conditions, minimum capital and financial guarantees for payment institutions, and existing ones had twelve months to apply for a licence. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No rule has been found that requires providers to connect to each other or to a switch. Mature would need such a rule.

ERI.short: Nothing found names a payments law or e-money rules for Eritrea, or says there are none, so no stage is set.
ERI.summary: Not found. Nothing found names a payments law, e-money rules or a draft of either, or says there is none.

ETH.short: Ethiopia licenses non-bank payment firms under 2020 central bank directives, and a May 2025 directive makes mobile wallets interoperable.
ETH.summary: The National Bank of Ethiopia introduced two sets of rules in 2020: the Payment Instrument Issuers directives and the Payment Systems Operators directive. Companies that are not banks, among them Chapa, Arifpay, Santimpay and Kacha, were licensed under the operators directive. Directive ONPS/10/2025 entered into force on 12 May 2025. It requires issuers to make their wallets interoperate through the national switch or another licensed switch. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No act of parliament on payments is named.

GAB.short: Gabon is under the 2018 regional payment regulation, with non-bank payment institutions operating; a national digital payments ordinance was before parliament in 2026.
GAB.summary: Gabon is bound by CEMAC regulation n°04/18 of 21 December 2018 on payment services, which a BEAC instruction of 5 May 2026 supplements. In the last twelve months, the Council of Ministers adopted a draft ordinance on digital payments on 29 January 2026, and on 22 May the digital economy minister defended the bill ratifying it before the National Assembly's finance committee. COBAC's 2025 report names Airtel Money Gabon and Clikpay Gabon as payment institutions. No rule has been found that requires providers to connect to each other. Mature would need such a rule.

GHA.short: Ghana's 2019 payments act licenses e-money issuers that are not banks, and mobile money interoperability was mandated in 2018.
GHA.summary: Ghana's Payment Systems and Services Act, 2019 (Act 987) has applied since February 2020. It requires payment service providers and e-money issuers to hold a Bank of Ghana licence. Ghana mandated mobile money interoperability in 2018, and the rule that did so is not named. In the last twelve months, in March 2026 the Bank listed 63 approved non-bank entities. On 14 July 2026 it revoked a licence under section 13. It was the dedicated e-money issuer licence of Zeepay Ghana, withdrawn over inadequate cash backing of its e-money.

GIN.short: Central bank decisions from 2015 license non-bank e-money companies; as of 2026 no rule is known requiring providers to connect to a switch.
GIN.summary: The central bank's licensing committee issued Decision D/2015/003/CAM on 31 March 2015, which governs e-money and the firms that issue it. It classes them as financial establishments, not banks, and requires each to hold a central bank licence. In the last twelve months, in October 2026 the central bank was preparing a bill on payment systems and instruments, with no text published. No rule has been found that requires providers to connect to each other or to a switch. Mature would need such a rule.

GMB.short: The Gambia's 2011 mobile money regulation authorises providers that are not banks, beside a 2013 payments act; no rule to connect providers is known.
GMB.summary: The Gambia's central bank made the Mobile Money Regulation, 2011, which took effect on 15 October 2011. It provides for retail transfers by persons not licensed as banks and has the central bank authorise such providers as limited liability companies. The Electronic Payments System Act 2013 defines the establishment and operation of the electronic payments system. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No rule has been found that requires providers to connect to each other or to a switch. Mature would need such a rule.

GNB.short: Guinea-Bissau is under the regional central bank's 2024 payment rules, with two non-banks licensed; in 2026 all providers were ordered to connect.
GNB.summary: Guinea-Bissau is bound by the BCEAO's Instruction n°001-01-2024 on payment services, under which payment institutions are licensed. The banking commission's register lists one payment institution and one e-money institution in Guinea-Bissau. They are INTOUCH Guinée-Bissau and Finances Mobiles Bissau. In the last twelve months, the BCEAO required every bank, e-money issuer and payment institution to connect to its instant payment platform, PI-SPI, by 30 June 2026. On 25 June it moved the deadline to 30 September. Five institutions in Guinea-Bissau were authorised on the platform at 31 July 2026.

GNQ.short: Equatorial Guinea is under the 2018 regional payment services regulation, which licenses non-banks; none was licensed there by 2023.
GNQ.summary: Equatorial Guinea is bound by CEMAC regulation n°04/18 of 21 December 2018 on payment services. The regional central bank's strategy of February 2025 says the regulation created payment establishments, licensed to provide payment services without being tied to a bank. The strategy lists six licensed across the region by July 2023, and none was in Equatorial Guinea. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No rule has been found that requires providers to connect to each other or to a switch. Mature would need such a rule.

KEN.short: Kenya's 2011 payment system act and 2014 regulations authorise mobile money operators; a replacement bill was published for comment in September 2026.
KEN.summary: Kenya's National Payment System Act 2011 is the legal framework for payment systems and providers, with the National Payment System Regulations 2014 under it. Mobile phone money transfer operators are authorised as payment service providers under them. In the last twelve months, in September 2026 the National Treasury and the Central Bank of Kenya published a draft National Payment System Bill, 2026 to repeal and replace the Act, with comments due by 9 October. No rule has been found that requires providers to connect to each other or to a switch. Mature would need such a rule.

LBR.short: Liberia's central bank mobile money regulations were in force in 2024; no source found says whether they license companies that are not banks.
LBR.summary: The Central Bank of Liberia's Mobile Money Regulations are the framework governing e-money and mobile money operators, and the bank is the regulator. In June 2024 it fined Lonestar Cell MTN Mobile Money Inc. for persistent breaches of its mobile money regulations. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source has been found that says the regulations license companies that are not banks, or names one licensed under them. Operating would need a source that says companies that are not banks can be licensed under the rules in force, or names one licensed.

LBY.short: Libya's 2022 electronic transactions law covers e-money, and the central bank licenses electronic payment companies; no rule to connect providers is known.
LBY.summary: Libya's Law No. 6 of 2022 on Electronic Transactions defines e-money. The Central Bank's circular 18 of 2025 is addressed to the electronic payment companies it has licensed, which are not banks. In the last twelve months, in April 2026 the Central Bank agreed that the IMF will help its teams draft an updated licensing regulation for electronic payment companies. No rule has been found that requires providers to connect to each other or to a switch. Mature would need such a rule.

LSO.short: Lesotho's 2014 payment systems act is in force; a bill to replace it and license all payment providers reached second reading in May 2026.
LSO.summary: Lesotho's Payment Systems Act, 2014 was published in the Government Gazette on 12 September 2014 and came into operation that day. In the last twelve months, on 5 May 2026 the Minister of Finance moved the Payment System Bill, 2025 for second reading in the National Assembly. The bill would repeal the Act and license all payment service providers. It had first been presented on 2 May 2025. No source has been found that says companies that are not banks can be licensed under the Act in force. Operating would need a source that says so, or names one licensed.

MAR.short: Morocco's 2014 banking law licenses payment institutions that are not banks, and they were active in 2026; no rule requiring providers to connect is known.
MAR.summary: Morocco's Law 103-12 on credit institutions, enacted on 24 December 2014, defines payment institutions as entities separate from credit institutions, which need Bank Al-Maghrib's approval before operating. In the last twelve months, in July 2026 Bank Al-Maghrib and the Competition Council said that newly licensed payment institutions and older ones were taking up card acquiring. Switch Al Maghrib says newly licensed payment institutions joined its mobile payment hub. No rule has been found that requires providers to connect to each other or to a switch. Mature would need such a rule.

MDG.short: Madagascar's 2017 e-money law licenses non-bank e-money institutions, and since 2024 banks and e-money institutions must join the central bank's instant payment system.
MDG.summary: Madagascar's Loi n°2016-056 on electronic money and electronic money institutions was promulgated on 2 February 2017. It requires any legal entity running e-money operations to be approved by the CSBF as an e-money institution. Such an institution is separate from credit institutions. In October 2024 the central bank made connection to its instant payment system compulsory for banks and e-money institutions, with a deadline of 31 January 2025. In the last twelve months, in June 2026 the central bank governor announced audits of the e-money institutions.

MLI.short: Mali is under the regional central bank's 2024 payment rules, which license non-banks; in 2026 it ordered all providers to connect.
MLI.summary: Mali is bound by the BCEAO's Instruction n°001-01-2024 on payment services, under which payment institutions are licensed. Two payment institutions are licensed in Mali: INTOUCH Mali, since 9 May 2025, and CAURIDOR, since 3 September 2025. In April 2026 the BCEAO told every bank, e-money issuer and payment institution to connect to PI-SPI by 30 June. In the last twelve months, on 25 June it set 30 September 2026 as the new deadline. L'Oeil du Sahel reports a BCEAO communique of 2 October 2026 requiring interoperable e-money transfers to pass through PI-SPI from 2 November 2026.

MOZ.short: Mozambique passed a new payment system law in July 2026, licenses mobile operators' e-money institutions and requires them to join the instant payment system.
MOZ.summary: Mozambique's Lei n.º 15/2026 of 2 July approves the National Payments System Law and revokes Lei n.º 2/2008. Parliament approved it in April and the president promulgated it in June. In the last twelve months, that law replaced the 2008 law. Three electronic money institutions authorised by the central bank, M-Pesa, e-Mola and M-Kesh, belong to the three mobile operators. Article 8 of the regulation annexed to Aviso n.º 1/GBM/2026 makes participation in the instant payment system compulsory for them and for credit institutions above a set size.

MRT.short: Mauritania's 2021 electronic payments law and 2022 instruction license payment institutions that are not banks; no rule requiring providers to connect is known.
MRT.summary: Mauritania's Loi n°2021-014 of 5 July 2021 on electronic payment services regulates payment service providers and e-money issuers, and bars anyone except banks from running a payment institution or issuing e-money without the central bank's licence. The central bank issued Instruction no. 03/GR/2022 of 31 March 2022 regulating payment institutions. In the last twelve months, in November 2026 Le Quotidien reported that Mattel Money, a mobile operator's subsidiary, is licensed by the central bank as an e-money institution. No rule has been found that requires providers to connect to each other. Mature would need such a rule.

MUS.short: Mauritius's 2018 payment systems act licenses non-bank payment providers, with new rules for aggregators in 2026; no rule to connect providers is known.
MUS.summary: Mauritius's National Payment Systems Act 2018 was assented to on 29 November 2018 and makes the Bank of Mauritius the regulator of payment service providers. In the last twelve months, the Act was last amended in April 2026, and the Bank's Guideline for Payment Aggregators took effect on 31 August 2026. It requires non-bank companies acting as payment aggregators to hold a licence. The Bank's list of licensees names Emtel MFS Co Ltd, Cellplus Mobile Communications Limited and EZ Dash Limited. No rule has been found that requires providers to connect to each other. Mature would need such a rule.

MWI.short: A non-bank fintech was licensed under Malawi's payments law in 2026; no source found says whether providers must connect to a switch.
MWI.summary: On 30 September 2026 the Reserve Bank of Malawi issued a payment service provider licence to PayChangu Limited under the Payment Systems Act, 2016. The company is a local fintech and not a bank. In the last twelve months, on 6 August 2026 Parliament passed an amendment to the Act removing its provisions on cheques. The Finance Minister said detailed regulations would follow. No source has been found that says a rule requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a switch. Mature would need such a rule.

NAM.short: Namibia's 2023 payment system act licenses non-bank providers, and a 2025 directive requires e-money issuers to interoperate through the instant payment switch.
NAM.summary: Namibia's Payment System Management Act 14 of 2023 was promulgated on 28 July 2023 and commenced on 8 August 2023. PSD-1 on licensing took effect on 6 January 2026. It sets a licensing process for payment services by non-bank financial institutions. Directive PSDIR-11 of 16 June 2025 requires every provider issuing payment instruments to make e-money interoperable through the instant payment switch by 26 February 2026. In the last twelve months, PSD-10 on fees and charges took effect on 24 December 2025. PSD-12 on operational and cybersecurity standards took effect on 3 July 2026.

NER.short: Niger is under the regional central bank's rules, with one non-bank e-money issuer licensed in 2025; in 2026 all providers were ordered to connect.
NER.summary: The banking commission of the West African monetary union counted one licensed e-money issuer in Niger at 31 December 2025. It is not a bank. Niger follows the BCEAO's rules. In April 2026 the BCEAO told every bank, e-money issuer and payment institution in the eight states to connect to PI-SPI by 30 June 2026. In the last twelve months, on 25 June it set 30 September 2026 as the new deadline. L'Oeil du Sahel reports a BCEAO communique of 2 October 2026 requiring interoperable e-money transfers to pass through PI-SPI from 2 November 2026.

NGA.short: Nigeria's central bank licenses mobile money operators and payment service banks under its frameworks; no rule binding them to a switch is known.
NGA.summary: OPay's October 2026 US filing names the central bank's licensing frameworks for payment service banks, mobile money operators and payment service providers, which it says opened payments to non-bank players. In the last twelve months those frameworks were cited and not changed: operators told a March 2026 hearing that the central bank licenses them, mobile money operators and digital banks among them. Payments already clear through NIBSS Instant Payment, but joining it is not shown to be required. No rule has been found that binds providers and banks to a switch. Mature would need such a rule.

RWA.short: Rwanda's central bank directive of January 2026 requires banks and e-money issuers to route all transfers through one national platform from July 2026.
RWA.summary: The National Bank of Rwanda issued Directive No. 45/2026 on 9 January 2026. It required domestic retail payments between banks and electronic money issuers to move to the eKash platform, the national instant payment rail. In the last twelve months, from 14 July 2026 every transfer between bank accounts and electronic money issuers is routed through eKash. This includes account to wallet and wallet to wallet. The Rwanda Bankers' Association states that the directive took effect on that date. The law under which those issuers are licensed is not named.

SDN.short: Sudan's 2020 central bank regulation licenses non-bank mobile payment companies; a 2026 circular asks them to connect to a switch not yet available.
SDN.summary: Sudan's central bank approved its Regulation on Licensing and Organising Mobile Payment Financial Institutions 2020 on 28 December 2020. It has the central bank license companies that are not banks to run mobile payment and open e-money wallet accounts. In the last twelve months, Circular 7/2026 of 31 March 2026 set binding minimum rules for financial services over USSD. It asks providers to connect to a national switch once one is available, and sets no date. No rule has been found that requires providers to connect to each other or to a switch. Mature would need such a rule.

SEN.short: Senegal is under the regional central bank's 2024 payment rules, with eleven non-bank payment institutions licensed; in 2026 all providers were ordered to connect.
SEN.summary: Senegal is bound by the BCEAO's instruction of 23 January 2024 on payment services, the rule under which payment institutions are licensed. Eleven payment institutions were licensed in Senegal at 31 August 2026, Flutterwave Sénégal and Julaya Sénégal among them. In the last twelve months, by a communiqué of 25 June 2026 the BCEAO set 30 September 2026 as the deadline. It applies to banks, e-money institutions and payment institutions connecting to PI-SPI, its instant payment platform. From 2 November 2026 the BCEAO required interoperable e-money transfers to go through PI-SPI.

SLE.short: Sierra Leone's 2022 payment systems act licenses non-bank providers, and since April 2025 banks and mobile money operators must route payments through the national switch.
SLE.summary: Sierra Leone's National Payment Systems Act, 2022 was assented to on 2 June 2022 and commenced on 23 June 2022, repealing the Payment Systems Act 2009. Section 6 bars anyone from providing payment services without a Bank of Sierra Leone licence, so the licence is one for companies that are not banks. Directives issued in December 2024 require all commercial banks and mobile money operators to route payments through the national switch. No change has been found in the last twelve months. In April 2025 the bank moved the deadline for joining from 31 March to 30 June 2025.

SOM.short: Somalia's 2020 mobile money regulations license mobile money providers; no rule making providers connect to each other is known.
SOM.summary: The Central Bank of Somalia made the Mobile Money Regulations, Amended 2020 under its 2012 Act. They set out the licensing and supervision of mobile money service providers. A National Payment System Bill would let the central bank license payment systems and digital money platforms, and the House of the People passed it on 8 November 2025. In the last twelve months, the Upper House passed its third reading on 11 January 2026, and in October 2026 the House of the People approved a separate Digital Transactions Bill. Signing of the first bill is not reported. No rule has been found that requires providers to connect to each other. Mature would need such a rule.

SSD.short: South Sudan's amended e-money rules took effect in 2026, licensing non-bank issuers and requiring every payment platform to connect through a licensed switch.
SSD.summary: South Sudan's Electronic Money Regulation 2017 Amendment 2025 took effect, as reported, on 1 September 2026. It was issued under the Bank of South Sudan Act 2011 Amendment 2023. Under it non-bank e-money issuers are licensed. Every digital payment platform must connect to the National Payment System through a licensed switch. In the last twelve months, the Bank of South Sudan opened a five-day workshop on 10 August 2026 to validate the broader National Payment System Bill, 2025, which is still a draft. At its close the governor called for faster progress.

STP.short: São Tomé and Príncipe's 2018 payment system law lets the central bank license non-bank providers; no rule requiring providers to connect is known.
STP.summary: São Tomé and Príncipe's Lei n.º 17/2018 was published on 7 September 2018 and sets the legal regime for the National Payment System. It lets the central bank authorise and license payment service providers, e-money issuance included, while banks need no new authorisation. The central bank's organic law, Lei n.º 03/2025, makes it responsible for regulating payment systems. No licensed provider has been found. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No rule has been found that requires providers to connect to each other or to a switch. Mature would need such a rule.

SWZ.short: Eswatini's 2023 payment system act licenses mobile money providers, and since December 2024 all providers must join the national payment switch.
SWZ.summary: Eswatini's National Payments System Act, 2023 regulates payment systems and payment service providers. The central bank said in November 2025 that licensing runs under it now. Fast payments launched on the Eswatini Payment Switch on 11 December 2024. The Governor said participation is mandated for all payment service providers offering local payments. No change has been found in the last twelve months. A central bank directive binds all licensed payment service providers from 31 March 2025. It gives them until 31 March 2027 to move low-value transfers within the Common Monetary Area to the TCIB scheme.

SYC.short: Seychelles' 2014 payment system act and 2022 e-money regulations license issuers that are not banks; no rule requiring providers to connect is known.
SYC.summary: Seychelles' National Payment System Act, 2014 commenced on 18 August 2014. Under it the Central Bank made the Electronic Money Regulations, 2022, which commenced on 12 December 2022 and set capital and liquidity rules for issuers other than banks. In the last twelve months, on 15 December 2025 it amended its licensing and authorisation regulations, setting the conditions on which it may license any company incorporated under the Companies Act as a payment service provider. No rule has been found that requires providers to connect to each other or to a switch. Mature would need such a rule.

TCD.short: Chad is under the 2018 regional payment services regulation, with three non-banks licensed by 2026; no rule requiring providers to connect is known.
TCD.summary: Chad is bound by the CEMAC regulation of 21 December 2018 on payment services, the framework under which its payment establishments are licensed. In the last twelve months, in July 2026 COBAC confirmed Moov Money Tchad, a telecom subsidiary, as a payment establishment. It is the third company that is not a bank so licensed in Chad, after Airtel Money in 2023 and Konoom in 2025. In February 2026 the finance ministry signed conventions with four such operators on mobile money for state payments. No rule has been found that requires providers to connect to each other. Mature would need such a rule.

TGO.short: Togo follows regional central bank rules; an e-money institution was licensed in 2025, and since November 2026 transfers between providers must use the regional platform.
TGO.summary: A BCEAO communique of 2 October 2026 sets binding terms for e-money transfers between persons through PI-SPI from 2 November. Togo follows the BCEAO's rules. Tmoney was licensed as an e-money institution in September 2025. In the last twelve months, on 25 June 2026 the BCEAO moved the deadline to 30 September for banks, e-money issuers and payment institutions to connect to PI-SPI. A BCEAO instruction of 8 October 2026 raises the e-money balance cap to CFAF 4 million per issuer, from CFAF 2 million since 2015. Since 2 November 2026 e-money transfers between individuals across providers must go through PI-SPI.

TUN.short: Tunisia's 2016 banking law licenses non-bank payment establishments, with new central bank rules in September 2026; no rule to connect providers is known.
TUN.summary: Tunisia's Law n° 2016-48 of 11 July 2016 on banks and financial institutions has payment services run by a specialised payment establishment, which is not a bank. In the last twelve months, in March 2026 OFT Tunisie, a subsidiary of Ooredoo, received definitive authorisation as one. On 25 September 2026 the central bank issued Circular n° 2026-10 on payment establishments, replacing a 2018 circular, which lets them open client payment accounts and issue electronic payment instruments. No rule has been found that requires providers to connect to each other or to a switch. Mature would need such a rule.

TZA.short: Tanzania's 2015 National Payment Systems Act is in force and covers electronic money; no source found says whether non-banks are licensed under it.
TZA.summary: Tanzania's National Payment Systems Act, 2015 was assented to on 25 April 2015 and gazetted on 22 May 2015. It puts payment systems, payment instruments and electronic money under Bank of Tanzania licensing. No change has been found in the last twelve months, and no regulation made under the Act is named. No source has been found that says companies other than banks are licensed under it, or names one licensed. Operating would need a source that says so, or names one licensed.

UGA.short: Uganda's 2020 National Payment Systems Act is in force, and the central bank licenses two mobile money operators; no rule to connect providers is known.
UGA.summary: Uganda's law is the National Payment Systems Act, 2020. Bank of Uganda officials told a parliamentary committee on 14 September 2026 that the wallet providers the bank licenses and supervises are MTN and Airtel, mobile money operators that are not banks. In the last twelve months, NALA, a Tanzanian firm, announced payment service provider and payment system operator licences from the Bank of Uganda in December 2025, and Payaza a payment system operator licence in February 2026. No rule has been found that requires providers to connect to each other. Mature would need such a rule.

ZAF.short: South Africa's 1998 payment system act is in force and non-banks are designated under it; no rule requiring providers to connect is known.
ZAF.summary: South Africa's National Payment System Act of 1998 gives the Reserve Bank responsibility for clearing and settlement. The Reserve Bank has designated non-banks as clearing system participants under it, among them Yoco Technologies in 2021 and Payfast in 2024. In the last twelve months it published a draft framework in May 2026 that would let approved non-banks issue e-money. On 1 September 2026 the governor said a National Payment System Bill would soon go out for comment. No rule has been found that requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a switch. Mature would need such a rule.

ZMB.short: Zambia's 2007 National Payment Systems Act is in force; no source found says whether it licenses companies that are not banks.
ZMB.summary: Zambia's National Payment Systems Act was enacted by parliament on 12 April 2007 and empowers the Bank of Zambia to regulate payment mechanisms. Under it and the Bank of Zambia Act 2022 the bank issued directives on e-money charges, binding from 2 August 2024, which bind e-money institutions, banks and financial institutions. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source has been found that says companies other than banks can be licensed under the Act, or names one licensed. Operating would need a source that says so, or names one licensed.

ZWE.short: Zimbabwe's 2001 National Payment Systems Act is in force; no source found says whether it licenses companies that are not banks.
ZWE.summary: Zimbabwe's National Payment Systems Act (Chapter 24:23), Act 21 of 2001, commenced on 16 November 2001 and provides for the recognition, operation, regulation and supervision of payment and clearing systems. The text held is consolidated to 31 December 2016. No change has been found in the last twelve months, and no regulation made under the Act or later amendment is named. No source has been found that says companies other than banks can be licensed under it, or names one licensed. Operating would need a source that says so, or names one licensed.

AGO.short: The central bank put the population with a bank account at 31.54% in 2024; no survey since 2023 has been found.
AGO.summary: The central bank reported that 31.54% of the population held at least one bank account in 2024, up 0.76 points on 2023. In December 2025 the Minister of State for Economic Coordination put the share of the population with a bank account at 31%. No change has been found in the last twelve months. The central bank does not say its figure comes from a survey, and no survey since 2023 has been found. Establishing would need a survey from the past three years that puts adults with an account at 53% or more.

BDI.short: Nothing found names a survey share of adults with an account or says there is none, so no stage is set.
BDI.summary: Not found. Nothing found gives a survey share of adults with an account.

BEN.short: Nothing found names a survey share of adults with an account or says there is none, so no stage is set.
BEN.summary: Not found. Nothing found gives a survey share of adults with an account.

BFA.short: The national financial inclusion agency put use of financial services at 81.8% at the end of 2025; the share paying digitally has not been found.
BFA.summary: In November 2026 the director of the national financial inclusion agency put the overall rate of use of financial services at 81.8% at the end of 2025. In the last twelve months the rate rose from 79.7% at the end of 2024, which C’Finance reported. The agency does not say the rate comes from a survey. No survey found gives the share of adults who made or received a digital payment. Mature would need a survey from the past three years that puts adults who made or received a digital payment at 79% or more.

BWA.short: FinScope found 75% of Batswana used mobile money in 2024; whether four in five adults hold an account was not found.
BWA.summary: FinScope's 2024 survey found that 75% of Batswana use mobile money, TechCabal reported in September 2026. A mobile money account counts as an account. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No survey found gives the share of adults holding either a bank or a mobile money account, or the share who made or received a digital payment. Operating would need a survey from the past three years that puts adults with an account at 79% or more.

CAF.short: Nothing found names a survey share of adults with an account or says there is none, so no stage is set.
CAF.summary: Not found. Nothing found gives a survey share of adults with an account.

CIV.short: Global Findex put adults with an account at 58% in 2024; no survey found puts the share at four in five.
CIV.summary: World Bank Global Findex puts Côte d'Ivoire's financial inclusion rate at 58% in 2024, up from 41% in 2017. The regulator ARTCI's 2024 survey found 50.3% of people aged five and over with a personal mobile money account. That base includes children, so it is not a share of adults. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No survey found since 2023 puts adults with an account at 79% or more. Operating would need a survey from the past three years that puts adults with an account at 79% or more.

CMR.short: Global Findex put adults with an account at 61% in 2024; no survey found puts the share at four in five.
CMR.summary: The World Bank's Global Findex puts account ownership among Cameroonian adults at 60.87% in 2024. The figure counts accounts at a financial institution or a mobile money provider. No later survey of Cameroonian adults has been found, and no change has been found in the last twelve months. No survey found gives the share of adults who made or received a digital payment. Operating would need a survey from the past three years that puts adults with an account at 79% or more.

COD.short: Global Findex put formal account ownership at nearly 39% in 2022; nothing found since 2023 updates it, so no stage is set.
COD.summary: No stage is set. The newest figure found, Global Findex for 2022, puts formal account ownership at nearly 39%. It is older than three years, so it does not count against the test. No survey since 2023 gives a share of adults with an account. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Establishing would need a survey from the past three years that puts adults with an account at 53% or more.

COG.short: Nothing found names a survey share of adults with an account or says there is none, so no stage is set.
COG.summary: Not found. Nothing found gives a survey share of adults with an account.

COM.short: Nothing found names a survey share of adults with an account or says there is none, so no stage is set.
COM.summary: Not found. Nothing found gives a survey share of adults with an account.

CPV.short: The central bank put residents holding a current or payment account at 85.6% in 2025; the share paying digitally has not been found.
CPV.summary: The Banco de Cabo Verde’s 2025 payment system report put the banking rate at 85.6%. The rate is the share of the resident population holding a current or payment account. In the last twelve months the rate rose from 81.5% in 2024, Expresso das Ilhas reported in September 2026. The report does not say the figure comes from a survey. No survey found gives the share of adults who made or received a digital payment. Mature would need a survey from the past three years that puts adults who made or received a digital payment at 79% or more.

DJI.short: Nothing found since 2023 names a survey share of adults with an account, so no stage is set.
DJI.summary: No stage is set. The only figure found is the central bank governor's 36% of the population with bank account access, given in November 2024. It is not attributed to a survey and is not limited to adults. No survey share of adults with an account has been found. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Establishing would need a survey from the past three years that puts adults with an account at 53% or more.

DZA.short: Global Findex put Algerian adults with an account at 35% in 2024; no survey has been found that puts it above half.
DZA.summary: A presentation of Global Findex data put Algerian adults with an account at 35.3% in 2024, Maghreb Emergent reported in April 2026. La Voix de l’Algérie gave the Findex rate as 35%. The same report puts adults who made or received a digital payment at 13%. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No survey has been found that puts adults with an account at half or more. Establishing would need a survey from the past three years that puts adults with an account at 53% or more.

EGY.short: Global Findex put Egyptian adults with a formal account at 43% in 2024; the central bank's higher 79% counts accounts, not survey respondents.
EGY.summary: Global Findex 2025 puts Egyptian adults with a formal account at 43%, Al Borsa News reported in July 2025. The survey year is 2024. In the last twelve months the Central Bank of Egypt put its financial inclusion rate at 79% at the end of June 2026, up from 77.6% at the end of 2025. The bank’s rate counts people with accounts and is not a survey. No survey has been found that puts adults with an account at half or more. Establishing would need a survey from the past three years that puts adults with an account at 53% or more.

ERI.short: Nothing found names a survey share of adults with an account or says there is none, so no stage is set.
ERI.summary: Not found. Nothing found gives a survey share of adults with an account.

ETH.short: Global Findex put adults with an account at 49% in 2024; no survey found puts the share above half.
ETH.summary: A 2025 paper citing Global Findex puts account ownership among Ethiopian adults at 49% in 2024. The same paper gives 22% for 2014 and 35% for 2017. The National Bank of Ethiopia put adults with a bank account at about 45% in 2020. No change has been found in the last twelve months, and no survey found since 2024 gives a higher share. Establishing would need a survey from the past three years that puts adults with an account at 53% or more.

GAB.short: The GSMA put adults with a mobile money account at 62% in 2026; no source found says whether four in five hold an account.
GAB.summary: The GSMA's October 2026 report on Gabon says 62% of adults hold a mobile money account. It does not name the survey behind the figure. An earlier report put about 54% of adults unbanked in the World Bank's Global Findex 2025, which leaves about 46% with a bank account. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No survey puts account holding at four in five adults. Operating would need a survey from the past three years that puts adults with an account at 79% or more.

GHA.short: Global Findex 2025 put adults with a financial account above 80%; the share paying digitally was not found.
GHA.summary: In November 2026 the Governor of the Bank of Ghana said that recent global surveys put about 81% of Ghanaian adults as owning a financial account. In November 2026 Citi Newsroom reported that the Deputy Minister of Finance cited Global Findex 2025 at above 80%. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No survey found gives the share of Ghanaian adults who made or received a digital payment. Mature would need a survey from the past three years that puts adults who made or received a digital payment at 79% or more.

GIN.short: The central bank put the account access rate at nearly 36% in 2024; no survey share of adults has been found.
GIN.summary: In July 2026 the central bank put the account access rate at nearly 36% in 2024, up from 4% in 2011. Its first deputy governor gave the figure at a meeting of central banks in Luanda. The central bank does not say the figure comes from a survey. No change has been found in the last twelve months, and no survey share of adults with an account has been found. Establishing would need a survey from the past three years that puts adults with an account at 53% or more.

GMB.short: In 2025 a national survey counted 82% of adults formally served, but no survey gives adults with an account, so no stage is set.
GMB.summary: No stage is set. In 2025 FinScope found 82% of adults with access to formal financial services. That is an inclusion share and not a share of adults with an account. No survey found since October 2023 gives the share of adults with an account. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Operating would need a survey from the past three years that puts adults with an account at 79% or more.

GNB.short: The regional central bank put access to financial services at 79.5% at the end of 2025; the share paying digitally has not been found.
GNB.summary: In September 2026 the national director of the regional central bank, the BCEAO, put the overall access rate to financial services at 79.5% at the end of 2025. The rate was 20.5% in 2018. She said the rise came mainly from electronic money. The bank does not say the rate comes from a survey. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No survey found gives the share of adults who made or received a digital payment. Mature would need a survey from the past three years that puts adults who made or received a digital payment at 79% or more.

GNQ.short: Nothing found names a survey share of adults with an account or says there is none, so no stage is set.
GNQ.summary: Not found. Nothing found gives a survey share of adults with an account.

KEN.short: A 2024 central bank survey found 84.8% of adults with a formal account; the share paying digitally was not found.
KEN.summary: The Central Bank of Kenya's 2024 FinAccess Household Survey puts formal financial access at 84.8% of adults. It was 83.7% in 2021. Formal access means an active account in the adult's own name with a bank, a mobile money provider or a SACCO. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No survey found gives the share of Kenyan adults who made or received a digital payment. Mature would need a survey from the past three years that puts adults who made or received a digital payment at 79% or more.

LBR.short: Global Findex put account ownership at 52% in 2024, the finance minister said; no survey found puts it above half.
LBR.summary: Finance Minister Augustine Ngafuan, citing the World Bank's Global Findex, said Liberia reached 52% account ownership by 2024. The New Dawn reported the statement in July 2026. Findex is a survey of adults. No later survey of Liberian adults has been found, and no change has been found in the last twelve months. Establishing would need a survey from the past three years that puts adults with an account at 53% or more.

LBY.short: Nothing found names a survey share of adults with an account or says there is none, so no stage is set.
LBY.summary: Not found. Nothing found gives a survey share of adults with an account.

LSO.short: Nothing found names a survey share of adults with an account or says there is none, so no stage is set.
LSO.summary: Not found. Nothing found gives a survey share of adults with an account.

MAR.short: The Findex survey put adults with an account at 44% in 2024; the central bank's higher 58% is a count, not a survey.
MAR.summary: Bank Al-Maghrib's 2024 financial-inclusion report cites the Global Findex 2024 survey: 44% of Moroccan adults hold a bank or payment account. The same report puts its own bank account holding rate at 58% at the end of 2024, up from 53% in 2021. That rate counts residents with an active bank account, and is not a survey. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Establishing would need a survey from the past three years that puts adults with an account at 53% or more.

MDG.short: Global Findex 2025 put adults with a formal account at 24%; no survey found puts the share at a quarter or more.
MDG.summary: AfricaNenda's 2025 consumer deck for Madagascar cites Global Findex 2025: 24% of adults own a formal account. The deck was published in November 2025, and it puts adults who used digital payments in the past year at 22%. In the last twelve months it was cited and not changed. No other survey of Malagasy adults since 2023 has been found. Preparing would need a survey from the past three years that puts adults with an account at 26% or more.

MLI.short: Nothing found names a survey share of adults with an account or says there is none, so no stage is set.
MLI.summary: Not found. Nothing found gives a survey share of adults with an account.

MOZ.short: Global Findex put adults with a mobile money account at 46% in 2024; the share holding any account was not found.
MOZ.summary: A Banco de Moçambique report cites Global Findex 2025: 46% of adults hold an electronic money account and 25% a traditional bank account. The survey was face to face, from 15 October to 16 December 2024. It left out Cabo Delgado and some other districts, about 11% of the population. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No share of adults holding either a bank or an electronic money account has been found. Establishing would need a survey from the past three years that puts adults with an account at 53% or more.

MRT.short: Nothing found names a survey share of adults with an account or says there is none, so no stage is set.
MRT.summary: Not found. Nothing found gives a survey share of adults with an account.

MUS.short: A 2021 report put adults with a bank account at 90%; nothing found since 2023 updates it, so no stage is set.
MUS.summary: No stage is set. The newest figure found is a 2021 COMESA report of 90% of adults with a bank account. It is older than three years. No survey since 2023 gives a share of adults with an account. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Mature would need a survey from the past three years that puts adults who made or received a digital payment at 79% or more.

MWI.short: Global Findex put adults with an account at 50% in 2024; a 2023 FinScope survey found 69% using mobile money.
MWI.summary: The Bankers Association of Malawi's chief executive said in July 2025 that Global Findex 2025 puts adults with a financial account at 50% in 2024. FinScope's 2023 survey of 3,000 adults found 69% currently using mobile money and 13% banked. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No survey found puts adults with an account at 53% or more. Establishing would need a survey from the past three years that puts adults with an account at 53% or more.

NAM.short: A 2025 national survey found 75.6% of adults with a bank account; no survey found puts account holding at four in five.
NAM.summary: The Namibia Statistics Agency's 2025 Financial Inclusion Survey found 75.6% of adults aged 15 and over with a bank account. It puts adults with a smart card account at 18.3%. World Bank economist Leora Klapper said in October 2025 that Global Findex 2025 puts Namibian adults with a financial account at 73%. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No survey found gives the share of adults holding a bank or smart card account together. Operating would need a survey from the past three years that puts adults with an account at 79% or more.

NER.short: Nothing found names a survey share of adults with an account or says there is none, so no stage is set.
NER.summary: Not found. Nothing found gives a survey share of adults with an account.

NGA.short: A 2026 government household survey put adults holding financial accounts at 86.5%; the share paying digitally was not found.
NGA.summary: NITDA's Nigeria Tech Outlook Report 2026, launched on 11 November 2026, says 86.5% of adults hold financial accounts. It names neither bank nor mobile money accounts. In the last twelve months EFInA's survey, released on 16 September 2026, put formal financial inclusion at 73% of adults, up from 64% for 2023. EFInA, reading the 2025 Global Findex, says 54% of Nigerian adults make digital payments. Mature would need a survey from the past three years that puts adults who made or received a digital payment at 79% or more.

RWA.short: In 2024 a national survey found 77% of adults with a registered mobile money account; no survey found puts account holding at four in five.
RWA.summary: In June 2024 the Ministry of Finance launched FinScope 2024. It found 77% of adults holding a registered mobile money account, up from 60% in 2020, and 22% banked. In the last twelve months the survey was cited and not changed: KT Press reported FinScope at 73% of adults using services such as mobile money in December 2025. No survey found since October 2023 puts adults with an account at 79% or more. Operating would need a survey from the past three years that puts adults with an account at 79% or more.

SDN.short: A 2021 FinScope survey found 15% of adults banked; nothing found since 2023 updates it, so no stage is set.
SDN.summary: No stage is set. A FinScope survey of 2021 found 15% of adults banked. It is the newest survey found and is older than three years. No survey since 2023 gives a share of adults with an account. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Preparing would need a survey from the past three years that puts adults with an account at 26% or more.

SEN.short: The central bank put adults with an account at 83.3% in 2023; the share paying digitally was not found.
SEN.summary: The BCEAO's national director said in July 2024 that Senegal's financial inclusion rate reached 83.3% in 2023, up from 61.9% in 2016. The rate is the share of adults with a bank, postal, treasury, microfinance or e-money account. The BCEAO does not say the rate comes from a survey. No change has been found in the last twelve months, and no survey of Senegalese adults since 2023 has been found. Mature would need a survey from the past three years that puts adults who made or received a digital payment at 79% or more.

SLE.short: About 29% of adults held a bank or mobile money account by 2025; no source found says whether more do now.
SLE.summary: The WTO's 2025 trade policy review summary says only about 29% of adults in Sierra Leone have an account. The account may be with a formal financial institution or a mobile money provider. The figure names no survey and no year. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Nothing found puts adults with an account at over half, or gives the share paying digitally. Establishing would need a survey from the past three years that puts adults with an account at 53% or more.

SOM.short: A 2026 national survey put mobile money reach at 87% of adults; the share paying digitally has not been found.
SOM.summary: An opinion piece on the Somalia Financial Access Survey 2026 puts mobile money reach at 87% of adults. The Central Bank of Somalia launched the survey in July 2026. The Somali Microfinance Association reported that it found 90% of adults financially included, largely through mobile money. In the last twelve months the bank ran the country's first nationally representative survey of financial access. No survey found gives the share of adults who made or received a digital payment. Mature would need a survey from the past three years that puts adults who made or received a digital payment at 79% or more.

SSD.short: Under 6% of adults held an account in 2021, a UNDP report says; nothing found since 2023 updates it, so no stage is set.
SSD.summary: No stage is set. A UNDP report says under 6% of adults held an account in 2021. That is the newest figure found, and it is older than three years. No survey since 2023 gives a share of adults with an account. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Preparing would need a survey from the past three years that puts adults with an account at 26% or more.

STP.short: A 2025 central bank survey put adults with a bank account at 38%; the share with mobile money was not found.
STP.summary: The central bank's second demand-side survey on financial inclusion and literacy, run in early 2025, found 38% of adults with a bank account. The Alliance for Financial Inclusion published the report in February 2026. The survey counts bank accounts alone, without mobile money. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No survey share of adults with a mobile money account, or with any account, has been found. Establishing would need a survey from the past three years that puts adults with an account at 53% or more.

SWZ.short: Global Findex 2025 put adults with an account at 63%; no survey found puts the share at four in five.
SWZ.summary: The Times of Eswatini reported in August 2025 that Global Findex 2025 puts 63% of adults with an account at a financial institution or a mobile money provider. Findex is a World Bank survey of adults. No later survey of adults in Eswatini has been found, and no change has been found in the last twelve months. Operating would need a survey from the past three years that puts adults with an account at 79% or more.

SYC.short: Nothing found names a survey share of adults with an account or says there is none, so no stage is set.
SYC.summary: Not found. Nothing found gives a survey share of adults with an account.

TCD.short: Nothing found names a survey share of adults with an account or says there is none, so no stage is set.
TCD.summary: Not found. Nothing found gives a survey share of adults with an account.

TGO.short: A 2022 Afrobarometer survey found 78% of adults with a mobile money account; nothing found since 2023 updates it, so no stage is set.
TGO.summary: No stage is set. An Afrobarometer survey of March 2022 found 78% of adults with a mobile money account. It is the newest survey found and is older than three years. No survey since 2023 gives a share of adults with an account. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Operating would need a survey from the past three years that puts adults with an account at 79% or more.

TUN.short: Global Findex put Tunisian adults with an account at 37.8% in 2024; no survey has been found that puts it above half.
TUN.summary: Global Findex puts Tunisian adults with an account at a financial institution or mobile money service at 37.8% in 2024, Challenges reported in November 2026. Findex 2021 put it at 37%, unchanged from 2017. In the last twelve months the number of bank accounts fell 1.8% to 10.5 million in 2025. No survey has been found that puts adults with an account at half or more. Establishing would need a survey from the past three years that puts adults with an account at 53% or more.

TZA.short: FinScope put mobile money adoption at 72% in 2023; no survey found puts account holding at four in five.
TZA.summary: The Citizen reported in September 2026 that the FinScope Tanzania 2023 survey put mobile money adoption at 72%, up from 60% in 2017. A mobile money account counts as an account. No newer survey of Tanzanian adults has been found, and no change has been found in the last twelve months. No survey found gives the share of adults holding a bank or mobile money account. Operating would need a survey from the past three years that puts adults with an account at 79% or more.

UGA.short: Global Findex put Ugandan adults with an account at 73% in 2024; no survey has been found that puts it at four in five.
UGA.summary: FSD Uganda, quoting Global Findex 2025, says 73% of Ugandan adults have a financial account. The survey year is 2024. FinScope Uganda 2023 found 64% registered for mobile money. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No survey has been found that puts account holding at 79% or more. Operating would need a survey from the past three years that puts adults with an account at 79% or more.

ZAF.short: FinScope surveys of 2024 and 2025 put adults with a bank account at 89%; the share paying digitally was not found.
ZAF.summary: The payments group ASAPP, citing FinMark Trust's FinScope surveys of 2024 and 2025, says 89% of South African adults have a bank account. Marketing Spread published the statement in September 2026. The figure counts bank accounts alone, without mobile money. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No survey found gives the share of South African adults who made or received a digital payment. Mature would need a survey from the past three years that puts adults who made or received a digital payment at 79% or more.

ZMB.short: FinScope found 76.2% using mobile money in 2025; whether its 80.1% inclusion rate means four in five hold an account was not found.
ZMB.summary: ITWeb reported in July 2026 that Bank of Zambia figures from the 2025 FinScope survey put mobile money usage at 76.2%. The same figures put financial inclusion at 80.1%, up from 69.4% in 2020. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No survey found gives the share of adults holding a bank or mobile money account. Operating would need a survey from the past three years that puts adults with an account at 79% or more.

ZWE.short: A 2022 FinScope survey found 70% of adults with an account; nothing found since 2023 updates it, so no stage is set.
ZWE.summary: No stage is set. A FinScope Zimbabwe survey of 2022 found 70% of adults with an account. It is the newest survey found and is older than three years. No survey since 2023 gives a share of adults with an account. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Operating would need a survey from the past three years that puts adults with an account at 79% or more.

AGO.short: Only surveillance, identification and personnel systems are held, to 2026; nothing found says whether stations record on paper or digitally, so no stage is set.
AGO.summary: Not found. No source found states whether stations record reports or cases on paper or digitally. Nor has a system or a count of stations been found.

BDI.short: Only traffic, statistics and staff systems are held, the latest from 2026; no source found says how stations record reports, so no stage is set.
BDI.summary: Not found. Nothing found states whether stations record reports or cases on paper or digitally. Nor has a system or a count of stations been found.

BEN.short: Only fingerprint, criminal-file and public online services are held, to 2026; no source found says how stations record reports, so no stage is set.
BEN.summary: Not found. Nothing found states whether stations record reports or cases on paper or digitally. Nor has a system or a count of stations been found.

BFA.short: A computerised occurrence book for police and gendarmerie stations was over 80% built in December 2023; no source found says whether any station uses it.
BFA.summary: In late December 2023 the security ministry's director of information systems told a delegation that its computerised main courante platform was not yet operational. The digital transition ministry put it at more than 80 per cent built. The platform is to replace the physical registers in which main courantes are kept at police commissariats and gendarmerie brigades. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Nothing dated on or before 30 September 2026 says it went live in any commissariat or brigade, and no station count has been found. Establishing would need reports or cases entered digitally, past any pilot, in some stations outside the capital.

BWA.short: Only cameras, traffic enforcement and tablets for statistics are held, to 2026; no source found says how stations record reports, so no stage is set.
BWA.summary: Not found. Nothing found states whether stations record reports or cases on paper or digitally. Nor has a system or a count of stations been found.

CAF.short: Only one specialised unit's case system (2026) and donated equipment are held; no source found says how stations record reports, so no stage is set.
CAF.summary: Not found. Nothing found states whether police stations or gendarmerie brigades record reports or cases on paper or digitally. Nor has a system or a count of stations been found.

CIV.short: Only cameras, fingerprint files and online court documents are held, to 2026; no source found says how stations record reports, so no stage is set.
CIV.summary: Not found. Nothing found states whether police stations or gendarmerie brigades record reports or cases on paper or digitally. Nor has a system or a count of stations been found.

CMR.short: A digital system for investigation and case information was barely used in 2020; no source found since says it runs, so no stage is set.
CMR.summary: No stage is set. In June 2020 GIZ said the police had a digitised system for investigations, criminal proceedings, arrest warrants, fines and sanctions. It also said the system was barely used. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Nothing has been found since 2020. No source found says which units use the system or whether any is outside the capital. Nor does any say how many stations enter records in it. Preparing would need a system for stations to record reports or cases being prepared or piloted.

COD.short: Police documents were typed or handwritten on paper in 2023; no source found says whether any station has had a digital system since.
COD.summary: On 15 March 2023 a human rights programme officer told Canada's Immigration and Refugee Board that a police statement must by law be written out and signed by the officer who drafts it, on pain of nullity. In March 2023 the Executive Secretary of Héritiers de la justice told the board that police documents are typed, and the record of the parties' hearings is handwritten in most cases. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found reports a digital system for stations. Neither account says in terms that none exists. Preparing would need a system for stations to record reports or cases being prepared or piloted.

COG.short: A 2014 survey of two towns found police stations working by hand; nothing found reports the rest of the country, so no stage is set.
COG.summary: No stage is set. The one statement that stations work by hand is a survey of commissariats in Pointe-Noire and Nkayi from January 2014. Nothing has been found on Brazzaville, the rest of the country or the gendarmerie beyond one brigade, and nothing dated since. In the last twelve months, the criminal-record extract in the first wave of state services to go online was planned in July 2026. Nothing has been found on who would own a station system. Preparing would need a system for stations to record reports or cases being prepared or piloted.

COM.short: Only a criminal-record directorate (2026) and a driving-licence programme are held; no source found says how stations record reports, so no stage is set.
COM.summary: Not found. Nothing found states whether stations record reports or cases on paper or digitally. Nor has a system or a count of stations been found.

CPV.short: Complaints ran digitally from national police stations to the courts by March 2026; no source found says how many stations use the system.
CPV.summary: On 27 December 2024 two ministries issued an order making use of the electronic criminal process obligatory in the Polícia Nacional. The Attorney General says the system entered service in the Praia and São Vicente police districts on 30 January 2025. In the last twelve months, on 16 March 2026 NOSi formally handed the subsystem over to the Ministry of Justice. No count or share of stations using it has been found. Operating would need more than half of stations entering reports or cases digitally, with a published share or count.

DJI.short: Only body cameras (2026), a gendarmerie intranet and a fingerprint file are held; nothing found says how stations record reports, so no stage is set.
DJI.summary: Not found. Nothing found states whether police stations or gendarmerie brigades record reports or cases on paper or digitally. Nor has a system or a count of stations been found.

DZA.short: Only public online services, traffic-fine payment and criminal registers are held, to 2026; nothing found says how stations record reports, so no stage is set.
DZA.summary: Not found. Nothing found states whether police stations or gendarmerie brigades record reports or cases on paper or digitally. Nor has a system or a count of stations been found.

EGY.short: A rights group said in 2021 that stations often lack the means to type reports; nothing found reports digital recording, so no stage is set.
EGY.summary: No stage is set. The one statement on stations dates from January 2021 and says they often lack the technology to write reports on a computer. It names no system, no place and no count of stations, and it does not say that stations record on paper only. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Nothing has been found on who would own a station system. Absent would need a dated source stating that police stations record reports and cases on paper only.

ERI.short: A 2017 state report names a police computerized data system; no source found says how stations record reports, so no stage is set.
ERI.summary: Not found. No source found states whether stations record reports or cases on paper or digitally. Nor has a system or a count of stations been found.

ETH.short: A criminal records system covering crime report to sentence was still being built in January 2026; no station is known to use it.
ETH.summary: Ethiopia's Ministry of Justice says the Ethiopian Artificial Intelligence Institute is developing it, its Criminal Records Information Management System, CRIMS. In August 2023 the ministry was training federal investigating police and prosecutors, about 100 in all, to launch it widely. In the last twelve months, in January 2026 the ministry said the system is under development and not yet in use. No station or place has been found, and no launch since 2023. Establishing would need reports or cases entered digitally, past any pilot, in some stations outside the capital.

GAB.short: A vendor presented a case-file system design in January 2026; no source found says whether any force uses it, so no stage is set.
GAB.summary: No stage is set. The only records system found is a vendor's design, presented at a Libreville seminar on 10 January 2026. No adoption by the police, the gendarmerie or a ministry is stated, and no station is shown using it.
