In the last twelve months, the gendarmerie's Identity Secu mobile application was deployed at the PK9 brigade in Libreville on 8 May 2026, as an application for the public. No dated statement says how stations record today, and no plan, finance or count of stations has been found. Preparing would need a system for stations to record reports or cases being prepared or piloted.

GHA.short: Case dockets were held digitally in 55 police stations across seven regions in 2022; no source found reports the total of stations, and anything since.
GHA.summary: Ghana's Government launched the Case Tracking System, as it calls it, in 2018 with USAID support, as a common platform for the police, the Attorney General's office and the Prisons Service. The Legal Resources Centre reported in 2022 that 55 police stations and 3 prisons services were using the system, in seven regions. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Nothing on the system since 2022 has been found. No total of stations has been found to set beside the 55. Operating would need more than half of stations entering reports or cases digitally, with a published share or count.

GIN.short: Ten police and gendarmerie units in Greater Conakry were equipped in 2021; no source found says whether any enters records, so no stage is set.
GIN.summary: No stage is set. An account dated 31 March 2021 says ten police and gendarmerie units of Greater Conakry were equipped. It gives no total of units, does not state that any entered records, and gives the digitising of procès-verbaux as an intention. A decree of 13 May 2019 created the police data centre and its information system, and names no station. No change has been found in the last twelve months, and no dated statement says how stations record today. Preparing would need a system for stations to record reports or cases being prepared or piloted: staff trained, equipment delivered, an agreement signed or pilot stations using it.

GMB.short: The police chief said in March 2026 that documentation is on paper; no source found says what became of a 2021 pilot.
GMB.summary: At a media briefing reported on 24 March 2026 the Inspector General of Police described the force's documentation as paper-based. He said the force needs to move from paper-based documentation to a digitalised mode. UNDP's terms of reference of 22 April 2021 had described a mobile app for crime reporting by police officers as in its pilot phase. In the last twelve months, the briefing is the only source found on how the force records. Nothing says what became of the app or how many stations took part. Preparing would need a system for stations to record reports or cases being prepared or piloted.

GNB.short: A 2024 student project states that police stations have no system for recording occurrences; no source found says how stations record.
GNB.summary: In August 2024 the author of an undergraduate project at IFBA stated that Guinea-Bissau does not have a system for recording criminal occurrences in police stations. The author cited no source. In the last twelve months, on 12 September 2025 INTERPOL described the West African Police Information System as strengthening information exchange and coordination among the region's law enforcement agencies. No station is named as entering its cases at the criminal-information centre in Bissau. Nothing has been found on how stations record, or on a plan. Preparing would need a system for stations to record reports or cases being prepared or piloted.

GNQ.short: A project to interconnect police stations is in the 2026 budget law; no source found says how stations record reports, so no stage is set.
GNQ.summary: Not found. No source found states whether stations record reports or cases on paper or digitally. Nor has a system or a count of stations been found.

KEN.short: Five Eldoret stations had a digital occurrence book in March 2026, but in May the police chief said the service had none yet.
KEN.summary: The National Police Service's annual report for 2022 says its Digital Occurrence Book was launched at Kasarani Sub-County, Nairobi, on 21 November 2019. The Star reported that 76 police stations in and around Nairobi had digital Occurrence Books by 30 June 2023. In the last twelve months, in March 2026 the Uasin Gishu police commander said the digital Occurrence Book had been rolled out at five Eldoret stations. In May 2026 the Inspector General told MPs the service did not yet have digital Occurrence Books. No source reconciles the two. Establishing would need reports or cases entered digitally, past any pilot, in some stations outside the capital.

LBR.short: Six officers in the capital's county began entering crime reports on tablets in a 2021 pilot; nothing found says whether any station outside it does.
LBR.summary: UNDP reports that the crime statistics system went live at police headquarters on 25 January 2021, with training for 15 personnel. Six officers were chosen to pioneer it in Montserrado County, the seat of the capital, that month. UNDP also reported that a case management system was up and running at the police in June 2022. In the last twelve months, FrontPageAfrica reported in 2026 that Nyehn Town Police Station, the only police facility serving Todee District, has no computers. No fact shows either system in use at a station outside Montserrado County. Establishing would need reports or cases entered digitally, past any pilot, in some stations outside the capital.

LBY.short: Tripoli's police stations got a digital system for investigation reports in December 2025; no source found reports use outside the capital.
LBY.summary: On 3 May 2025 Tripoli's security director told the heads of investigation of the police stations to attend to the running of the digital system. In the last twelve months, the directorate inaugurated its digital transformation system, including the police-station investigation-reports system, on 31 December 2025. The Libyan News Agency reports that it serves the police stations and traffic sections of the Tripoli Security Directorate. No station outside that directorate is shown using a records system. No count of stations, plan or finance has been found. Establishing would need reports or cases entered digitally in some stations outside the capital.

LSO.short: An inspection begun in 2023 found posts without stationery keeping registers by hand; nothing found says what other stations do, so no stage is set.
LSO.summary: No stage is set. The Ombudsman's inspection, begun in July 2023, found posts without stationery keeping registers by hand. The Inspector of Police's report for 2024/25 describes a makeshift paper incident book at a station. Neither says that stations record on paper only. In the last twelve months, 20 desktop computers were handed to the police service in June 2026, and the communications authority put a Wi-Fi project for thirteen police stations out for proposals in July 2026. No records system for stations has been found. Preparing would need a system for stations to record reports or cases being prepared or piloted.

MAR.short: Police stations record complaints and cases in connected national systems, cases in 16 of 22 commands in 2025; nothing found reports the share of stations.
MAR.summary: Morocco's national police, the DGSN, built GESTARR with its own technical staff. Complaints lodged at arrondissements were managed in it in October 2019. In 2024 the DGSN added a system for crime and misdemeanour cases at the arrondissements, each case followed through investigation to submission to the judicial authorities. In the last twelve months, its review of 2025 says Qadaya's rollout continued during the year. It reached 16 of the 22 police commands. The DGSN counts commands, not stations, so no share of stations has been found. Operating would need more than half of stations entering reports or cases digitally, with a published share or count.

MDG.short: The police opened an online platform for reporting violence and disappearances in 2026; nothing found says how stations record reports, so no stage is set.
MDG.summary: Not found. No source found states whether stations record reports or cases on paper or digitally. Nor has a system or a count of stations been found.

MLI.short: An online criminal-record service opened in 2026; no source found says how stations record reports, so no stage is set.
MLI.summary: Not found. No source found states whether stations record reports or cases on paper or digitally. Nor has a system or a count of stations been found.

MOZ.short: Police kept almost no digital records in 2007 and stations used no computers; no source found says whether any station records digitally now.
MOZ.summary: UNDP's evaluators visited stations and commands in September 2007 and verified the almost complete absence of digital records of autos, case files or any other procedure across the force. They found that the use of information technology was non-existent at district and police station level. On 23 August 2024 Club of Mozambique reported a public security management information system for the Ministry of the Interior. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No fact says that stations enter reports or cases in that system. Preparing would need a system for stations to record reports or cases being prepared or piloted.

MRT.short: A police information system launched in June 2025 runs in Nouakchott's commissariats, 34 centres linked; no source found reports use by stations outside the capital.
MRT.summary: The central office for collecting police information supervises the police information system, which the General Directorate of National Security calls WAPIS. The system was launched on 19 June 2025. At the launch the director of the central office gave the centres linked as 27 of the National Police and 7 of the National Gendarmerie. The report puts the rollout across Nouakchott's commissariats at 90 per cent complete. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source shows the system in use at a station outside Nouakchott, and no total of stations has been found. Establishing would need reports or cases entered digitally, past any pilot, in some stations outside the capital.

MUS.short: All police stations had computers linked to the headquarters complaint and case system in 2025; nothing found says how many stations enter records in it.
MUS.summary: The Prime Minister told the National Assembly on 17 June 2025 that the Crime Occurrence Tracking System manages and tracks complaints and declarations from initial reporting to final case disposal. He said all police stations are equipped with personal computers for the system, and that the police had begun to replace it with a new case management system. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No count has been found of police stations. Nor has a share entering records in the system. Operating would need more than half of stations entering reports or cases digitally, with a published share or count.

MWI.short: Officers were trained in July 2026 for a crime management system's introduction, after a 2022 pilot in six districts; nothing found reports stations using it.
MWI.summary: In 2022 a combined crime and gender-based violence record system was piloted in six districts: Mzimba, Nkhata Bay, Ntchisi, Dowa, Nsanje and Machinga. In the last twelve months, on 29 July 2026 the police and UNDP opened a three-day training on the system in Lilongwe. In July 2026 the Crime Management System was being introduced across stations and formations. No source names or counts a station using it, or says whether the 2022 system stayed in use. Establishing would need reports or cases entered digitally, past any pilot, in some stations outside the capital.

NAM.short: In 2026 the police said their case docket system reaches nearly all stations; no source found says how many enter cases there.
NAM.summary: In October 2026 the Acting Inspector-General said the Force Case Docket Management System is accessible at all Class A and Class B police stations and about 90% of Class C stations. In the last twelve months, the force said it had begun an overhaul of the E-Policing System. No timetable or funding was given. A 2022 study of stations in the Omusati region found that officers there record by hand. No count of stations has been found. Operating would need more than half of stations entering reports or cases digitally, with a published share or count.

NER.short: In 2019 a team of eight in Niamey entered cases into the police database; nothing found says whether any station outside the capital records digitally.
NER.summary: EUCAP Sahel Niger reported on 23 May 2019 that the Direction de la Police Technique et Scientifique in Niamey works the database, called SIPAO. Cases are entered by a team of 8 under the director in Niamey, and more than 8,000 had been entered by then. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Nothing since May 2019 says the system reached stations outside Niamey or still runs, and no count of stations has been found. Establishing would need reports or cases entered digitally, past any pilot, in some stations outside the capital.

NGA.short: Gombe opened the first digital police station, with case files managed digitally, in 2026; no station elsewhere is shown recording digitally.
NGA.summary: In June 2021 the Ministry of Police Affairs said statements and reports at stations were written by hand. On 25 September 2025 the Inspector-General opened nationwide training on the new Criminal Database Systems. In the last twelve months, in June 2026, Gombe State became the first to receive a digital police station, where case files can be managed digitally on a cloud-based system. No station outside Gombe is shown recording cases digitally. No count of stations using the Criminal Database Systems has been found. Establishing would need reports or cases entered digitally in some stations outside the capital.

RWA.short: The investigation bureau processes criminal case files in the justice ministry's electronic system, by its 2024 history; no source found says whether stations enter them.
RWA.summary: The Rwanda Investigation Bureau's history of 2017 to 2023, published in October 2024, says the Ministry of Justice manages the Integrated Electronic Case Management System. The bureau has incorporated the system to process criminal investigation files. Case handling is digitalised from investigation to final judgment through the system. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Nothing has been found on whether the bureau's stations and posts enter the case file themselves, or on how many do. Establishing would need reports or cases entered digitally, past any pilot, in some stations outside the capital.

SDN.short: Police stations took reports on paper in 2022, before the war; no source found says how they record now.
SDN.summary: A thesis abstract from Sudan University of Science and Technology, dated 2022, proposes converting the reports taken in Sudanese police stations to an electronic system. No source found says how stations have recorded reports since 2022, or how many stations use a system. Preparing would need a system for stations to record reports or cases being prepared or piloted.

It also said stationery would be kept mainly for operational work. No source found shows the planned survey of case management done, or any other step to prepare the system. Preparing would need a system for stations to record reports or cases being prepared or piloted.

A United Nations Development Programme assessment of December 2025 describes the bureau as the national standards body and a correspondent member of the international standards organisation. It says public information shows no specific programme on standards for artificial intelligence or data governance. Neither source names a national standard on information technology or data. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Establishing would need a national standard on information technology or data, issued or adopted as a national standard.

None of the three sources names a national standard on information technology or data. The ordinance names no certification against one. Decree 8/2022 of 14 March 2022 charges it with implementing Mozambican technical standards and certifying management systems, products, services and people. The decree also creates a national council for standardisation and quality promotion under the industry minister, and gives the office its secretariat and that of an accreditation cell. It names no national standard on information technology or data, no body accredited to certify and no certification against such a standard. No change has been found in the last twelve months. MUS.short: Mauritius's standards bureau certifies against the national information security standard; six public bodies held its certificates at the end of 2025.

The bureau certifies organisations itself. Its register at 31 December 2025 lists ten certificates, all marked as accredited, six of them held by public bodies. In the last twelve months the count has risen: by 30 June 2026 the register listed 11 certified organisations. The Passport and Immigration Office's certificate in that register is dated 30 October 2025.

The bureau lists the e-Government Authority as certified to ISO 27001:2022 from 30 January 2026. No source says that standard is a Tanzania Standard. It is listed among revised information technology standards. No source found says the bureau or an accredited certifier offers certification against a national standard on information technology or data. It names no standard on information technology or data. In September 2026 the bureau signed a technical cooperation agreement with the Rwanda Standards Board. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Establishing would need a named national standard on information technology or data, issued or adopted as a national standard.

ZWE.summary: The Standards Association of Zimbabwe lists ZWS ISO/IEC 27001:2022, on information security management systems, as a Zimbabwe standard. Its list of standards published in the first quarter of 2026 adds national standards on artificial intelligence, cloud security and digital evidence. In the last twelve months its scheme for certifying organisations against the information security standard was accredited in February 2026. Its quality, environmental and occupational health schemes were accredited earlier. The page names no organisation certified against it. Mature would need a dated source naming a public body certified in the past three years, by the standards body or an accredited certifier.

AGO.short: Refugees or displaced people were registered and documented in 2026; their access to digital services is not on record.
AGO.summary: UNHCR counted 8,921 registered Kasai refugees in 2,101 households in April 2026. They came to Angola in 2017, and UNHCR says every registered refugee family receives identity documents. The same report says the government has suspended registration of new arrivals since October 2017. In late 2024 UNHCR and the migration service held their first joint registration missions in the southern provinces, registering 7,200 refugees. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found since October 2023 says refugees may use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID. Operating would need a source showing that they may register SIM cards, open mobile money or bank accounts, or enrol in the national digital ID.

BDI.short: 54,343 Congolese refugees were biometrically registered in 2026; no source found says refugees may use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID.
BDI.summary: ONPRA and UNHCR completed level-2 biometric registration of 54,343 Congolese refugees at the Busuma site in July 2026. In the last twelve months, in late July 2026, ONPRA also began registering and updating the records of about 4,000 refugees at the Cishemere transit centre. For two years to September 2025 the Merankabandi programme paid selected refugees 73,600 BIF every two months through their mobile phones. No source found since October 2023 says refugees may use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID. Operating would need a source showing refugees may use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID.

BEN.short: About 30,400 refugees and asylum-seekers were registered and 2,337 given protection documents by 2026; no source found reports their access to digital services.
BEN.summary: UNHCR says about 30,400 refugees and asylum-seekers were individually registered by 30 June 2026. In the last twelve months, in January 2026, UNHCR, the refugee commission SP-CNRA and the identification agency ANIP set a roadmap for enrolling refugees biometrically in the national register. On 30 October 2026 ANIP said it planned to enrol about 30,000 refugees in November 2026. In August 2026 Decryptage counted 16,463 recognised refugees without valid ID cards. No source found says refugees may use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID. Operating would need a source showing that they may register SIM cards, open mobile money or bank accounts, or enrol in the national digital ID.

BFA.short: Refugees or displaced people could use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID in 2023; how many do is not counted.
BFA.summary: ANOTEL applies decree 2023-1721 of 15 December 2023. It says the refugee identity card and the CONAREF attestation are the only documents accepted for refugees to buy a SIM card. The territorial administration ministry issued more than 121,000 civil-status documents to displaced people in 2025. In the last twelve months, when enrolment for the unique identifier began on 11 November 2026, the minister said mobile teams would go to displaced people. No source found since October 2023 counts refugees or displaced people with a SIM, an account or a digital ID. Mature would need a published number or share of them with a SIM, an account or a digital ID.

BWA.short: Refugees or displaced people were registered and documented in 2026; their access to digital services is not on record.
BWA.summary: In September 2024 Parliament passed a bill to issue the national identity card, the Omang, to every person granted refugee status. The Patriot says the bill gives refugees an Omang so they can register SIM cards. In the last twelve months, at the World Refugee Day event at Dukwi in June 2026, Minister Pius Mokgware handed citizenship documents to 64 refugees. No source found says refugees have been issued the Omang under the 2024 bill. Operating would need a source showing refugees may use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID.

CAF.short: 37,389 Sudanese refugees had been registered by 2026; no source found says refugees may use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID.
CAF.summary: UNHCR says 37,389 Sudanese refugees had been registered in the Central African Republic by June 2026. Registration began in April 2023, with the National Commission for Refugees. In October and November 2024 UNHCR and the commission registered 1,189 Sudanese refugees biometrically in Rafai. In the last twelve months, UNHCR's report for April to June 2026 says 737 were registered individually, and 1,958 new arrivals in Manou. No source found since October 2023 says refugees may use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID. Operating would need a source showing that they may register SIM cards, open mobile money or bank accounts, or enrol in the national digital ID.

CIV.short: Refugees or displaced people were registered and documented in 2026; their access to digital services is not on record.
CIV.summary: In 2024 29,233 refugees were registered individually with DAARA, the government counterpart. A July 2025 interministerial order recognised as refugees over 69,000 Burkinabe and about 1,500 Malians registered since May 2021, the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights says. In the last twelve months, from April to June 2026, UNHCR and the government registered 3,619 new arrivals in 684 households in the north. Registered new arrivals receive refugee attestations or other proof of identity. No source found since October 2023 says refugees may use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID. Operating would need a source showing that they may register SIM cards, open mobile money or bank accounts, or enrol in the national digital ID.

CMR.short: 25,000 refugees had been given legal identification by 2025; no source found says whether refugees may use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID.
CMR.summary: UNHCR says a biometric identification programme had given 25,000 refugees legal identification by March 2025. In April 2024 IOM and the civil registration office BUNEC handed displaced and vulnerable people 507 rebuilt birth certificates in Bertoua and 683 legal identity documents in Yaoundé. A December 2024 law lets displaced people have civil-status records issued or rebuilt. No change has been found in the last twelve months. In October 2024 UNHCR and partners agreed to install digital kiosks with internet and Mobile Money services at Minawao refugee camp. No source found says refugees may use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID. Operating would need a source showing that they may, by law or in practice.

COD.short: 391,764 refugees and asylum-seekers were registered and held protection documents in 2025; no source found reports their access to digital services.
COD.summary: UNHCR and the refugee commission CNR say 391,764 refugees and asylum-seekers were registered in proGres at 31 May 2025, each holding at least one protection document. On 20 November 2024 ONIP and the CNR signed a protocol to identify refugees systematically. In November 2025 the interior minister told the Senate how ONIP will identify the population, by strata, starting with Kinshasa. No later change to the count or the protocol has been found in the last twelve months. No source found says refugees or displaced people may use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID. Operating would need a source showing refugees may use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID.

COG.short: Refugees or displaced people were registered and documented in 2026; their access to digital services is not on record.
COG.summary: On 6 February 2026 the foreign affairs and social affairs ministers handed biometric passports to ten refugees in Brazzaville. The passports are refugee travel documents, and the news agency ACI reported the handover. In the last twelve months this is the one event found. ACI says the handover will continue progressively, under a government partnership with UNHCR. No source found since October 2023 says refugees may use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID. Operating would need a source showing that they may register SIM cards, open mobile money or bank accounts, or enrol in the national digital ID.

COM.short: UNHCR listed 24 registered asylum-seekers and refugees in 2025; no source found says refugees may use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID.
COM.summary: UNHCR's southern Africa office publishes a monthly statistical report from its joint registration exercise. On 30 November 2025 it listed 24 people in Comoros: 17 asylum-seekers and 7 refugees. The report counts people registered in each country of asylum and gives no other figure for Comoros. In the last twelve months it is the only count found. No source found since October 2023 says refugees may use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID. Operating would need a source showing that they may register SIM cards, open mobile money or bank accounts, or enrol in the national digital ID.

CPV.short: Nothing found names registration of refugees and displaced people or says there is none, so no stage is set.
CPV.summary: Not found. Nothing found says whether refugees or displaced people are registered or can use digital services.

DJI.short: Refugees were registered and issued documents in 2025, and 158 refugee teachers opened bank accounts in 2024; no source found reports a wider count.
DJI.summary: In March 2024 the education ministry helped 158 refugee teachers in Ali Addeh and Holl-Holl open accounts at East Africa Bank. UNHCR says registration of new arrivals and status determination were suspended in February 2024. On 28 January 2025 UNHCR and the refugee office ONARS registered 18 people in Djibouti-ville and delivered 122 attestations. By early March 2025 they had registered 29 more new arrivals and issued 199 certificates and 14 identity cards. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found counts refugees with a SIM, an account or a digital ID across the country.

DZA.short: UNHCR finalised 4,056 new registrations of refugees and asylum-seekers to March 2024; no source found says they may use SIM cards or digital ID.
DZA.summary: UNHCR finalised 4,056 new and 15,301 continuous registrations of refugees and asylum-seekers up to March 2024, the RDPP North Africa programme reports. Algeria has no national asylum system. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found since October 2023 says refugees or displaced people may use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID, or counts those who do. Operating would need a source showing that they may register SIM cards, open mobile money or bank accounts, or enrol in the national digital ID, by law or in practice.

EGY.short: 691,000 Sudanese refugees held UNHCR documents in 2025; no source found says whether refugees may use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID.
EGY.summary: UNHCR Egypt says 1,100,600 refugees and asylum-seekers were registered with it as of 30 April 2026. In April 2025 691,000 Sudanese registered with UNHCR held its yellow card, a temporary substitute for residency, Radio Dabanga reports. In the last twelve months, UN experts put registered refugees and asylum-seekers at 1,098,311 in December 2025. No source found since October 2023 says refugees may use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID, or counts those who do. Operating would need a source showing refugees may use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID.

ERI.short: A 2026 source says Eritrea has no legal framework for refugees and withdrew their status; no source found reports any registration.
ERI.summary: In 2026 UNHCR's rights mapping platform said Eritrea has no national legal framework for refugees or asylum seekers. The Elite Camp closed in 2012, and the government then withdrew refugee status from refugees living in towns. Their legal status remains unclear. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found since October 2023 says registration of refugees is planned or under way. Preparing would need a source showing that the government or UNHCR planned, began or resumed registering or documenting refugees, or piloted a digital service for them.

ETH.short: The number of refugees or displaced people using digital services was published in 2026.
ETH.summary: The World Bank reports 191,335 refugees had received a Fayda ID by 23 March 2026. In the last twelve months that count rose from 120,765 at 30 September 2025. Issue began in March 2024, and 9,669 refugees held Fayda-numbered ID cards by August 2024. UNHCR said in 2024 that the refugee digital IDs let refugees open bank accounts and get mobile connectivity. Under the Makatet inclusion framework launched in June 2026, the ID programme is issuing Fayda to refugees.

GAB.short: Nothing found names registration of refugees and displaced people or says there is none, so no stage is set.
GAB.summary: Not found. Nothing found says whether refugees or displaced people are registered or can use digital services.

GHA.short: 9,625 Burkinabe refugees were registered in 2025 and refugees may register SIMs with their ID in 2026; how many do is not counted.
GHA.summary: The 2026 SIM registration rules list refugees among those who must register, using the Refugee Non Citizen ID. By 6 February 2025 the Ghana Refugee Board and UNHCR had biometrically registered 9,625 displaced Burkinabes. In the last twelve months, in March 2026, registration of refugees for the Ghana Card spread to the Western and Volta regions. It began in Greater Accra in 2023. In August 2026 the foreign ministry gave the refugee board passport equipment to register refugees and produce their IDs. No source found since October 2023 counts refugees or displaced people with a SIM, an account or a digital ID. Mature would need a published number or share of them with a SIM, an account or a digital ID.

GIN.short: Registration or a digital service for refugees or displaced people was under way in 2026; documents issued are not on record.
GIN.summary: In October 2024 Guinea told UNHCR it counted 2,322 refugees, and that new asylum seekers go through status determination. The executive secretary of the CNISR commission says it registers asylum seekers with UNHCR. Guinea's 2018 asylum law provides biometric refugee ID cards and travel documents, but no implementing decree has been published, UNHCR says. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found since October 2023 says how many refugees were issued documents. Establishing would need refugees registered and issued identity documents, with a number stated.

GMB.short: Nothing found since 2023 names registration of refugees and displaced people, so no stage is set.
GMB.summary: No stage is set. Nothing found since October 2023 says whether refugees or displaced people in the Gambia are registered or can use digital services. An earlier source says The Gambia joined regional initiatives on digital identity for displaced people, and nothing since October 2023 says it plans or runs their registration. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Preparing would need a source showing that the government or UNHCR planned, began or resumed registering or documenting refugees or internally displaced people, or piloted a digital service for them.

GNB.short: Nothing found since 2023 names registration of refugees and displaced people, so no stage is set.
GNB.summary: No stage is set. Nothing found since October 2023 says whether refugees or displaced people in Guinea-Bissau are registered or can use digital services. Every earlier source found dates from 2017 or 2018, outside the three-year range. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Absent would need a source from the past three years saying that refugees or internally displaced people are not registered, hold no documents, are barred from SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID, or that their registration is suspended.

GNQ.short: A 2026 source says refugees or displaced people are not registered or are barred from digital services.
GNQ.summary: In 2026 UNHCR's rights mapping platform said Equatorial Guinea has no domestic framework for refugee status determination. Asylum seekers therefore have no formal procedure to apply for refugee status, and refugees have no established rights or entitlements. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found since October 2023 says registration of refugees is planned or under way. None says refugees may use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID. Preparing would need a source showing that registration of refugees was planned, begun or resumed.

KEN.short: Over 650,000 refugees held identity cards in 2024 and may register SIMs since 2025; no source found says how many hold a SIM.
KEN.summary: On 30 May 2025 the government issued Legal Notice No. 90, GSMA reports. It recognises refugee identity cards for SIM card registration for the first time. In February 2024 the Commissioner of Refugee Affairs put registered refugees and asylum-seekers at over 650,000. The 2026 Economic Survey says registration of new arrivals in Dadaab resumed in May 2023, the first since 2016. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No count of refugees with a SIM, an account or a digital ID has been found since October 2023. Mature would need a published number or share of them with a registered SIM, an account or a national digital ID.

LBR.short: Registration or a digital service for refugees or displaced people was under way in 2026; documents issued are not on record.
LBR.summary: In February 2025 Executive Order No. 144 speeds up residence and documents for registered former Ivorian refugees, free of charge. In the last twelve months, on 25 February 2026, the refugee commission, the immigration service and the National Identification Registry signed an agreement on refugee identity. The registry is to capture refugees' biometrics. In June 2026 the commission, now RAMCO, said the agreement would improve legal documentation. No source found says refugees were issued the new cards, with a number stated. Establishing would need refugees registered and issued identity documents, with a number stated.

LBY.short: Refugees or displaced people were registered and documented in 2025; their access to digital services is not on record.
LBY.summary: In the last twelve months UNHCR's report for 2025 says it had registered 108,455 refugees and asylum-seekers individually in Libya by the end of 2025, 40,699 of them new that year. A year earlier the total was 79,019, registered at UNHCR's Tripoli centre. Each refugee registered receives an asylum-seeker or refugee certificate. But Libyan authorities do not recognise UNHCR's documents, and most Sudanese refugees in the east are undocumented. No source found since October 2023 says refugees may use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID. Operating would need a source showing that they may, by law or in practice.

LSO.short: A 2026 source says refugees or displaced people are not registered or are barred from digital services.
LSO.summary: The Lesotho Times reports a government freeze on refugee identity cards and travel documents. It began in July 2025, after corruption allegations against refugee and passport officials. In 2026 the freeze was in its second year, and hundreds of refugees were left without valid documents. In March 2024 the National Assembly committee allowed SIM rules that let asylum seekers register SIM cards on their asylum-seeker certificate. In the last twelve months no source found says the freeze has ended. Preparing would need a source showing that the government or UNHCR planned, began or resumed registering or documenting refugees, or piloted a digital service for them.

MAR.short: UNHCR had registered 18,900 refugees and asylum-seekers by 2024; no source found says refugees may use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID.
MAR.summary: By the end of 2024 UNHCR had registered 18,900 people from 64 countries in Morocco, including 4,679 new registrations in 2024, mostly of Sudanese people. UNHCR says Morocco's refugee bureau, which regularises refugees UNHCR has registered, sat twice a week in 2024. It reviewed about 20 people a week and admitted undocumented refugees and unaccompanied children. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found since October 2023 says refugees may use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID. Operating would need a source showing that they may register SIM cards, open mobile money or bank accounts, or enrol in the national digital ID.

MDG.short: A 2025 source says refugees or displaced people are not registered or are barred from digital services.
MDG.summary: UNHCR's rights mapping platform says Madagascar has no operational asylum system. The Office for Refugees and Stateless Persons has never worked in practice, and refugees and asylum seekers receive no formal protection or legal status. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found since October 2023 says registration of refugees is planned or under way. None says refugees may use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID. Preparing would need a source showing that registration of refugees was planned, begun or resumed.

MLI.short: Refugees or displaced people were registered and documented in 2026; their access to digital services is not on record.
MLI.summary: Early in 2025 biometric registration was suspended indefinitely after US funding stopped, leaving 64,315 asylum-seekers without formal status. In the last quarter of 2025 CNCR registered 13,628 refugees biometrically, while 10,345 remained unregistered. In the last twelve months, from April to June 2026, CNCR and UNHCR registered and enrolled 4,950 people biometrically and distributed 17,806 refugee ID cards. No source found since October 2023 says refugees may use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID. Operating would need a source showing refugees may use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID.

MOZ.short: Refugees or displaced people were registered and documented in 2025; their access to digital services is not on record.
MOZ.summary: In the nine months to October 2024 the provincial identification service took about 12,478 ID card applications from displaced families in Cabo Delgado. It produced 5,516 cards and delivered 4,764. The National Director of Registries and Notaries says more than 145,000 displaced people have been registered since the attacks in the north began. In the last twelve months, in March 2026, Japan and UNHCR agreed a USD 6.9 million grant for 2026 to 2028. It will bring mobile civil documentation to about 100,000 displaced and returnee people in Cabo Delgado. No source found since October 2023 says displaced people may use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID. Operating would need a source showing that they may.

MRT.short: The number of refugees or displaced people using digital services was published in 2023.
MRT.summary: UNHCR counts refugees in the camp with financial products, including bank accounts, and their number rose from 2,400 in 2022 to 5,600 in 2023. In February 2024 it counted 128,000 registered refugees and asylum-seekers. A World Bank project is piloting continuous updating of the social registry, open to refugee households. In the last twelve months, UNHCR's factsheet of January 2026 says around 185,000 refugees were in the national population registry by December 2025.

MUS.short: Refugees or displaced people were registered and documented in 2024; their access to digital services is not on record.
MUS.summary: UNHCR's 2024 results report covers Mauritius from its South Africa office. It says 79 refugees and asylum-seekers were registered individually in Mauritius in 2024. The registration was done remotely, and protection documents were issued to them. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found since October 2023 says refugees may use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID, or counts those who do. Operating would need a source showing that they may register SIM cards, open mobile money or bank accounts, or enrol in the national digital ID.

MWI.short: Over 1,100 asylum-seekers were registered in Nsanje in 2024; no source found says refugees may use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID.
MWI.summary: UNHCR reports more than 1,100 asylum-seekers from Mozambique registered in Nsanje District by the end of December 2024. In June 2023 the National Registration Bureau's principal secretary said nine national IDs issued illegally to refugees were confiscated, and that the Registration Act gives no mandate to register refugees. In December 2019 UNHCR reported that the Bureau had announced plans to register refugees and asylum-seekers and issue them ID cards. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found since October 2023 says refugees in Malawi may use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID. Operating would need a source showing that they may, by law or in practice.

NAM.short: Namibia issued 682 identity cards to refugees in 2025; no source found says whether refugees may hold SIM cards or accounts in their own name.
NAM.summary: The Home Affairs minister said 682 African guest identity cards were issued to refugees in 2025, easing refugees' access to education, employment and financial services. In October 2024 Home Affairs began registering refugees in Osire to issue them ID cards, capturing the biometrics of 238 refugees. In February 2025 UNHCR and the government began cash transfers to refugees and asylum-seekers in Osire settlement, paid through MTC Namibia's mobile money service to about 6,000 people. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found says refugees may hold a SIM, an account or a national ID. Operating would need a source showing that they may, by law or in practice.

NER.short: Refugees received 1,542 certificates and ID cards in 2025; their access to digital services is not on record.
NER.summary: UNHCR says 2,237 refugees and displaced people were registered or verified in 2025, and 1,542 refugee certificates and ID cards were distributed. Since 2019 Niger has issued 2,700 national identity cards to displaced people. In January 2024 the humanitarian action minister launched biometric registration of about 160,000 displaced people in Diffa. In the last twelve months, on 15 September 2026, the Interior Ministry began biometric enrolment for the AES e-passport range, which includes a refugee travel document. No source found since October 2023 says refugees or displaced people may use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID. Operating would need a source showing that they may, by law or in practice.

NGA.short: The number of refugees or displaced people using digital services was published in 2026.
NGA.summary: In May 2026 NIMC's director-general said over 206,000 refugees and displaced people had been enrolled in the national identity database. UNHCR figures relayed by the EU asylum agency put bank account holding in 2024 at 29% of refugees and asylum seekers and 0.4% of displaced people. In 2024 about 1,950 refugees in the South-South were enrolled in state social registers. In the last twelve months, in November 2026, the government, UNHCR and Germany gave 10 states mobile one-stop-shop vehicles. They register SIM cards and open bank accounts for displaced people.

RWA.short: In 2024, 76% of adult refugees held a registered mobile money account, and refugees may enrol in the digital ID.
RWA.summary: Access to Finance Rwanda presented the FinScope 2024 refugees survey, which found 76% of adult refugees with a registered mobile money account and 37% using a bank account. Digital ID registration began on 28 October 2025, with cards due from June 2026. In the last twelve months, in Kigali, refugees and asylum seekers registered from 7 to 15 February 2026. In June 2026 MINEMA said 93% of eligible refugees had been issued refugee identity cards.

SDN.short: Sudan held a registry of over 950,000 refugees in 2026; no source found says displaced people may hold SIM cards or accounts as a rule.
SDN.summary: In May 2026 Sudan's Commission for Refugees announced a review of refugee records and a return of the Foreign Number from June. It says its UNHCR-approved registry holds over 950,000 refugees, and it had run a Foreign Number system before. In the last twelve months the Red Crescent piloted offline registration for cash aid, paying 200 displaced people in White Nile in 2026. In 2024 Forced Migration Review reported that Sudanese refugee ID cards did not meet the ID requirement for registering a SIM card. No source found since October 2023 says refugees may hold SIM cards, mobile money or bank accounts. Operating would need a source showing that they may.

SEN.short: Registration or a digital service for refugees or displaced people was under way in 2026; documents issued are not on record.
SEN.summary: Under a decree of 17 September 2025, asylum claims may be filed electronically and are recorded in the refugee and stateless database, and a refugee identity card is issued on admission. A second decree says a biometric ID card and travel document is to be introduced for recognised refugees and stateless people. UNHCR says an applicant lodges a claim with the Commission Nationale d'Eligibilite in Dakar and receives a receipt, valid for six months. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found says how many refugees are registered and documented. Establishing would need refugees registered and issued identity documents, with a number stated.

SLE.short: Nothing found names registration of refugees and displaced people or says there is none, so no stage is set.
SLE.summary: Not found. Nothing found says whether refugees or displaced people are registered or can use digital services.

SOM.short: The number of refugees or displaced people using digital services was published in 2026.
SOM.summary: A one-month NIRA pilot in Baidoa registered 38,026 displaced people with biometrics, against a target of 25,000, and they obtained the national ID. UNDP says 38,026 is of over 500,000 displaced people there. From January 2026 the ID is required for services such as opening a bank account. In the last twelve months, in June 2026, NIRA launched a national ID registration initiative for displaced people, funded by Switzerland and carried out by the Norwegian Refugee Council. The count covers the Baidoa pilot only, and no national count of displaced people with the national ID has been found.

SSD.short: 448,243 refugees were registered by 2024 and most in refugee-hosting areas held SIMs in 2026; refugees alone with a SIM are not counted.
SSD.summary: A World Bank paper counts 448,243 refugees and asylum-seekers registered in South Sudan in March 2024. In the last twelve months a 2026 GSMA, REACH and UNHCR survey of 2,135 households in four refugee-hosting areas found about 78% of respondents had a SIM card registered in their own name. The figure joins refugees and their hosts. In 2026 a World Bank review found nearly 90% of South Sudan's people lack government-recognised ID. No source found counts refugees, apart from their hosts, with a SIM, an account or a digital ID. Mature would need a published number or share of refugees or displaced people with a registered SIM, an account or a national digital ID.

STP.short: Nothing found names registration of refugees and displaced people or says there is none, so no stage is set.
STP.summary: Not found. Nothing found says whether refugees or displaced people are registered or can use digital services.

SWZ.short: Refugees or displaced people could use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID in 2026; how many do is not counted.
SWZ.summary: Eswatini hosts 5,058 registered refugees and asylum seekers. In the last twelve months, from April to June 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs dispatched 70 refugee status permits and sent out 77 machine-readable Convention Travel Documents. It says refugee status permits let holders obtain personal identification numbers and national identity cards. In March 2025 the central bank and the Commissioner for Refugees prepared a know-your-customer pack for refugees. No source found since October 2023 counts refugees or displaced people with a SIM, an account or a digital ID. Mature would need a published number or share of them with a registered SIM, an account or a national digital ID.

SYC.short: Nothing found names registration of refugees and displaced people or says there is none, so no stage is set.
SYC.summary: Not found. Nothing found says whether refugees or displaced people are registered or can use digital services.

TCD.short: Since 2025 refugees in Chad with a refugee ID number can open bank accounts and register SIM cards; no source found says how many have.
TCD.summary: UNHCR said in May 2025 that refugees given a National Refugee Identification Number can open bank accounts and register SIM cards. By September 2025 the World Bank counted 25,000 secure identity documents issued to refugees, against a target of 80,000. In the last twelve months, in December 2025, the World Bank reported that every eligible refugee held an identity document issued by the refugee commission, CNARR. The social registry then held 283,448 refugees. No source found publishes how many refugees hold a SIM card, an account or a national digital ID. Mature would need that number or share published.

TGO.short: Refugees or displaced people were registered and documented in 2025; their access to digital services is not on record.
TGO.summary: From 22 May to 16 July 2025 a decentralised operation produced and distributed 10,972 refugee identity cards in the Savanes region. In the last twelve months, since 24 May 2026, CNAR has run biometric registration in the Savanes, registering 3,999 people by the end of June. At that date 1,958 were still unregistered, and card issue had stalled for lack of materials. In August 2026 the African Development Bank approved a $1 million grant to register and document 5,000 new arrivals there. No source found since October 2023 says refugees may use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID. Operating would need a source showing that they may, by law or in practice.

TUN.short: UNHCR renewed 560 refugee registration cards in 2026, though new registration was suspended in 2024; no source found reports access to digital services.
TUN.summary: UNHCR says 7,812 refugees and asylum-seekers were registered with it at 30 September 2025. In the last twelve months, in January 2026, it renewed 560 registration cards. Amnesty International says the authorities ordered UNHCR in June 2024 to suspend asylum registration and refugee status decisions. No source found says that suspension has ended, or that refugees may use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID. Operating would need a source showing that they may register SIM cards, open mobile money or bank accounts, or enrol in the national digital ID.

TZA.short: A 2026 source says refugees or displaced people are not registered or are barred from digital services.
TZA.summary: In 2026 GSMA research on refugee women's use of mobile phones in Tanzania found that national identity rules lead many to register SIMs through local citizens or intermediaries. Biometric Update reported that women are more likely than men to rely on relatives or citizens for SIMs in other people's names. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source found since October 2023 says refugees are being registered or documented in Tanzania. None says they may use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID. Preparing would need a source showing that registration of refugees was planned, begun or resumed.

UGA.short: Refugees or displaced people were registered and documented in 2026; their access to digital services is not on record.
UGA.summary: In October 2025 an official of the Office of the Prime Minister said registration of new asylum seekers from Somalia, Ethiopia and Eritrea had closed. In the last twelve months UNHCR registered 30,220 new arrivals in the first quarter of 2026. On 7 September 2026 the office and UNHCR began a nationwide refugee verification at Nakivale, to count refugees estimated at about 2.3 million. NIRA says refugees and asylum seekers cannot apply for Ugandan national ID cards. No source found since October 2023 says refugees may use SIM cards or mobile money. Operating would need a source showing that they may, by law or in practice.

ZAF.short: 57,288 refugees and 80,803 asylum seekers held active permits in 2026; their access to digital services is not on record.
ZAF.summary: In September 2026 the Minister of Home Affairs reported 57,288 refugees and 80,803 asylum seekers holding active permits. At the end of 2024 the counts were 62,649 refugee permits and 92,657 asylum seeker permits. In the last twelve months, in November 2026, Home Affairs launched the first phase of its Digital Asylum System. The portal records asylum seekers' intention to apply, with facial biometrics and documents, and is live for test cases. It confers no status. No source found since October 2023 says refugees may use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID. Operating would need a source showing that they may, by law or in practice.

ZMB.short: The government registered 10,194 refugees in 2024; no source found says refugees may use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID.
ZMB.summary: From January to August 2024 the government registered 10,194 refugees, including births and 6,485 new arrivals. In October 2025 Zambia's Ministry of Home Affairs was launching a refugee and host communities project, which the World Bank funds with $30 million. Under it refugees and former refugees will get biometric national registration cards. In the last twelve months, in December 2025, the minister said refugee travel documents could be applied for online, through ZamPortal. No source found since October 2023 says refugees may use SIM cards, mobile money or digital ID. Operating would need a source showing that they may, by law or in practice.

ZWE.short: Zimbabwe said in 2024 that refugees can register for national identity cards; no source found says whether any are registered, so no stage is set.
ZWE.summary: No stage is set. In October 2024 Zimbabwe told UNHCR that refugees can register for birth certificates and national identity cards. No source found since October 2023 says refugees or displaced people are being registered or documented. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Preparing would need a source showing that the government or UNHCR planned, began or resumed registering or documenting refugees or internally displaced people, or piloted a digital service for them.

AGO.short: Angola's state operator carried services over a fibre link with Namibia's in 2026; no shared exchange or data centre is known.
AGO.summary: Angola Telecom's executive director said in July 2026 that a terrestrial fibre link joins Santa Clara in Angola to Namibia and carries services of Angola Telecom and Telecom Namibia in both directions. In the last twelve months, the two companies also signed a memorandum in March 2026 for the SARSSy sea cable. Angola's and Mozambique's ministers signed one on 22 June 2026 for a Nacala to Lobito cable. In November 2026 the communications minister put the SARSSy cable at the study and preparation stage. No exchange point or data centre shared with another country has been found. Mature would need a second kind of shared infrastructure in service: a traffic exchange or data storage.

BDI.short: Burundi agreed fibre links with the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Zambia in 2024; no source says building has started.
BDI.summary: Burundi's Council of Ministers adopted a memorandum on 8 May 2024 for a fibre interconnection with the Democratic Republic of the Congo, which the government calls a joint initiative. Burundi's and Zambia's ministers signed a memorandum in Lusaka in October 2024 for a fibre cable under Lake Tanganyika. No change has been found in the last twelve months. The report on the Zambia cable says an unnamed private firm was contracted, and no source names a contract or a start of works on either link. No shared link, exchange point or data facility has been found in service. Establishing would need a contract awarded, works begun or cable being laid in the past three years.

BEN.short: Benin's SBIN agreed a Lagos to Accra fibre route with Nigerian and Ghanaian partners in 2025; no source found says it is in service.
BEN.summary: Benin's state infrastructure company SBIN, with CSquared and the Nigerian operator Phase3, announced a fibre route from Lagos to Accra in May 2025, running through Benin, Togo and Ghana. The partners said it was configured, activated and tested, and gave no date for it to enter service. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Benin lies on a Lagos to Dakar route that Phase3 and Sonatel activated in 2025, but no Beninese party to it has been found. No source found says the Lagos to Accra route has entered service. Establishing would need a contract awarded, works begun or cable being laid in the past three years.

BFA.short: The national research network was partly connected to the West African research backbone in 2025; no shared exchange or data centre was found.
BFA.summary: WACREN, the regional research and education network, said in 2025 that FasoREN's connection to its regional network was still partial. FasoREN is Burkina Faso's national research network, and the connection runs over national fibre laid by ANPTIC, the state digital agency. In November 2025 WACREN held a workshop in Ouagadougou to set a roadmap and timetable for joining FasoREN fully to the regional backbone. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No exchange point or data facility run with another country has been found, and no source says the research network connection is complete. Mature would need a second kind of shared infrastructure in service: a traffic exchange or data storage.

BWA.short: Botswana's state fibre company and Namibia's MTC completed cross-border fibre in 2026; no source found reports it to carry traffic.
BWA.summary: In May 2025 BoFiNet's acting chief executive said it has fibre connections to all of Botswana's neighbours. The source names no party in those countries. In the last twelve months, Namibia's MTC and BoFiNet signed a memorandum in February 2026 on cross-border fibre interconnection, IP transit and wholesale capacity. BoFiNet says the two had recently completed cross-border fibre interconnections at Mamuno to Charles Hill and at Ngoma. No source found says those interconnections carry traffic, or that a shared link, exchange point or data facility is in service. Operating would need one kind of shared infrastructure in service under an arrangement both countries are party to.

CAF.short: The Central African Backbone has joined the country to Cameroon and Congo since 2023; no shared exchange or data centre was found.
CAF.summary: The Central African Republic inaugurated its national backbone on 6 February 2023, with links to Cameroon at Gamboula and to Congo at Bomassa. The African Development Bank closed the project in September 2023 with both links built. In the last twelve months, vandalism in March 2026 partly cut national service, and in October 2026 the two routes were still the country's fibre links abroad. No exchange point or data facility run with another country has been found. Mature would need a second kind of shared infrastructure in service: a traffic exchange or data storage.

CIV.short: The state broadcaster used RASCOM, the African states' shared satellite, in 2023; no shared exchange or data centre was found.
CIV.summary: Côte d'Ivoire's and Guinea's digital ministers signed a protocol in Conakry on 11 October 2024 to interconnect the two countries' fibre networks. No source reports works begun on it. In the last twelve months, the country's use of RASCOM, the satellite organisation of African states, was cited and not changed: its director general said on 31 July 2026 that its services are already used in Côte d'Ivoire. He cited the state broadcaster RTI, which used RASCOM capacity during the 2023 Africa Cup of Nations. No Ivorian party to a cross-border fibre link in service has been found. Mature would need a second kind of shared infrastructure in service: a traffic exchange or data storage.

CMR.short: Cameroon's backbone has been linked to the Central African Republic since 2023; no shared exchange or data centre was found.
CMR.summary: The Central African Republic inaugurated its backbone in February 2023, interconnected with Cameroon at Gamboula. Chad told ITU-D in March 2026 that its link to CAMTEL's network is working. In the last twelve months, Gabon's SPIN and Cameroon's CAMTEL signed a memorandum on CAB-Corridor, published in October 2026, that would join Cameroon, Gabon and Congo. Chad's regulator suspended a planned operator route from N'Djamena in February 2026. No exchange point or data facility run with another country has been found. Mature would need a second kind of shared infrastructure in service: a traffic exchange or data storage.

COD.short: The country agreed a fibre link with Burundi in 2024; no source found says shared infrastructure is in service under an agreement.
COD.summary: Congo's SOCOF and Tanzania's TTCL made the Kalemie to Kigoma lake cable official on 20 October 2025, with works due in early 2026. In the last twelve months, the ministries of the country and Uganda signed a memorandum on 11 May 2026 that includes joining Uganda's backbone to Congolese fibre. Tanzania reaffirmed the lake cable in September 2026. Burundi's Council of Ministers adopted a memorandum on 8 May 2024 for a fibre interconnection. No source found says building has started on the links with Burundi, Tanzania or Uganda. Establishing would need a contract awarded, works begun or cable being laid in the past three years.

COG.short: The Central African Backbone has joined Congo to Gabon since 2018 and to Cameroon since 2022; no shared exchange or data centre was found.
COG.summary: Under the Central African Backbone, Congo has been interconnected with Gabon since 2018, a French Treasury sheet says. The Central African Republic inaugurated its interconnection with Congo at Bomassa in February 2023. In the last twelve months, ADIAC said in August 2026 that the backbone's link to Cameroon was still being built. Gabon's SPIN and Cameroon's CAMTEL signed a memorandum on CAB-Corridor, published in October 2026, and no Congolese party to it has been found. No exchange point or data facility run with another country has been found. Mature would need a second kind of shared infrastructure in service: a traffic exchange or data storage.

COM.short: Nothing found names infrastructure Comoros shares with another African country under an agreement, so no stage is set.
COM.summary: Not found. Nothing found names digital infrastructure Comoros shares with another African country under an agreement. Nothing found says it has none.

CPV.short: Cabo Verde's 2024 cable loan is from a European lender; no agreement with another African country was found, so no stage is set.
CPV.summary: Not found. Nothing found names digital infrastructure Cabo Verde shares with another African country under an agreement. Nothing found says it has none.

DJI.short: Djibouti agreed the Horizon fibre corridor with Ethiopia and Sudan in 2026; no source found names a partner on its working cables.
DJI.summary: Djibouti Telecom, Ethio telecom and Sudatel signed a memorandum in Addis Ababa in December 2024. In the last twelve months, the three signed an agreement in Djibouti on 4 February 2026 to build and maintain Horizon, a fibre corridor of about 2,800 km to Ethiopia and Sudan. In September 2026 they presented Horizon to carriers before deployment. It is not yet in service. No source found says building has started. None names a Somali, Kenyan or Ethiopian party to a cable already working. Establishing would need a contract awarded, works begun or cable being laid in the past three years.

DZA.short: Algeria and Niger opened their trans-Saharan fibre link in October 2026; no shared exchange or data centre was found.
DZA.summary: Algeria's ministry said in July 2024 that works on its 2,600 km section of the trans-Saharan backbone, from Algiers to In Guezzam, were complete. In the last twelve months, Algérie Télécom and Niger Telecom signed a convention in Niamey on 8 September 2026 for a 100 gigabit link. The ministers of Algeria and Niger opened the trans-Saharan fibre link at Assamaka on 6 October 2026. Niger's ministry declared it officially in service. No exchange point or data facility run with another country has been found. Mature would need a second kind of shared infrastructure in service: a traffic exchange or data storage.

EGY.short: Egypt's fibre link to Sudan, opened in 2004, runs under a 2021 operator agreement with Sudatel; no shared exchange or data centre was found.
EGY.summary: Egypt's telecommunications minister launched a 400 km fibre cable to Sudan on 26 October 2004, built to carry calls and internet between the two countries. Telecom Egypt and Sudatel signed a cooperation agreement in April 2021 to make better use of that fibre. They also planned to join Sudatel's Port Sudan landing to Telecom Egypt's Red Sea landings. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No agreement, memorandum or financing for new shared infrastructure dated in the last three years has been found, nor any exchange point or data facility run with another country. Mature would need a second kind of shared infrastructure in service: a traffic exchange or data storage.

ERI.short: A 2026 source says Eritrea still has no international fibre connection; no shared infrastructure with a neighbour was found.
ERI.summary: A commentary published on 16 April 2026 says Eritrea still has no international fibre connection. A 2021 World Bank overview said the planned regional sea cable and data projects lacked a commitment to serve the whole region, Asmara included. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No agreement, financing or start of works on any link to a neighbour has been found, and no regional programme's plans name Eritrea. No link, exchange point or data facility shared with another African country has been found. Preparing would need an agreement made in the past three years, with another African country or through a regional body, to build, join or run shared digital infrastructure.

ETH.short: Ethio telecom began deploying the Horizon fibre corridor to Djibouti and Sudan in 2026; no shared link is yet in service.
ETH.summary: Ethio telecom, Djibouti Telecom and Sudatel signed a tripartite agreement on 4 February 2026 for Horizon, a fibre corridor from Djibouti's cable landings across Ethiopia to Sudan's. It builds on a memorandum signed in Addis Ababa on 3 December 2024. In the last twelve months, in August 2026 Ethio telecom moved from planning into active deployment, with its design final and site materials delivered. In September 2026 the three operators presented Horizon to carriers ahead of commercial launch. No source found says a shared link, exchange point or data centre is in service. Operating would need one kind of shared infrastructure in service under an arrangement both countries are party to.

GAB.short: Gabon and Equatorial Guinea inaugurated their backbone interconnection in 2025; no shared exchange or data centre was found.
GAB.summary: Gabon's and Equatorial Guinea's ministers inaugurated the interconnection of the Gabonese and Equatoguinean backbones on 10 November 2025, at Meyo-Kyé and Ebebeyin, after signing an agreement at Mongomo. Tests confirmed traffic flowing between Bitam and Ebebeyin, and between Libreville and Bata. In the last twelve months, Gabon's backbone company SPIN and Cameroon's CAMTEL signed a memorandum on CAB-Corridor, published in October 2026, that would join Cameroon, Gabon and Congo. No exchange point or data facility run with another country has been found. Mature would need a second kind of shared infrastructure in service: a traffic exchange or data storage.

GHA.short: A Lagos to Accra fibre route was agreed with Nigerian and Beninese partners in 2025; no source found says it is in service.
GHA.summary: CSquared, the Nigerian operator Phase3 and Benin's state infrastructure company SBIN announced a fibre route from Lagos to Accra in May 2025, running through Benin and Togo into Ghana. The partners said it was configured, activated and tested, and gave no date for it to enter service. No change has been found in the last twelve months. GVA of Côte d'Ivoire holds a 100 Gbps port at Accra-IX, routing data of August 2026 show, and CSquared runs its own network from Accra to Lagos. Neither is an arrangement between bodies of two countries. No source found says the route is in service. Establishing would need a contract awarded, works begun or cable being laid in the past three years.

GIN.short: Guinea's backbone links to Mali and Sierra Leone, agreed in 2024 and 2025, were working in 2025; no shared exchange or data centre was found.
GIN.summary: Guinea's telecoms ministry says four cross-border interconnections were working in 2025, with Mali, Senegal, Côte d'Ivoire and Sierra Leone. Guinea and Sierra Leone signed an agreement in November 2024 to interconnect their national backbones. Guinea's SOGEB and Sierra Leone's Leoncom then signed an interconnection agreement in Conakry, published in June 2025. In June 2024 SOGEB and Mali's SMTD agreed to interconnect the two countries' networks. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No exchange point or data facility run with another country has been found. Mature would need a second kind of shared infrastructure in service: a traffic exchange or data storage.

GMB.short: Gamtel held 28 Gbps with Senegal's Free on a cross-border backup link in 2026; no shared exchange or data centre was found.
GMB.summary: Gamtel's company profile, captured in September 2026, says the state operator holds 28 Gbps with the Senegalese operator Free on Cross Gambia, a backup link. The page is undated. Traffic moves onto the link automatically when the ACE sea cable fails. The Gambia also joined the backbone of WACREN, the regional research and education network, in 2025. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No agreement for new shared infrastructure dated in the last three years has been found, nor any exchange point or data facility run with another country. Mature would need a second kind of shared infrastructure in service: a traffic exchange or data storage.

GNB.short: Guinea-Bissau joined the West African research network's backbone in 2025; no shared exchange or data centre was found.
GNB.summary: Guinea-Bissau joined the backbone of WACREN, the regional research and education network, in 2025, with five other West African countries. AfricaConnect projects co-funded by the European Commission support the expansion. An ECOWAS commissioner said a protocol of April 2023 consolidated commitment to the Amilcar Cabral sea cable, whose study and construction were still unfunded in June 2024. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No agreement for new shared infrastructure dated in the last three years has been found, nor any exchange point or data facility run with another country. Mature would need a second kind of shared infrastructure in service: a traffic exchange or data storage.

GNQ.short: Equatorial Guinea and Gabon inaugurated their backbone interconnection in 2025; no shared exchange or data centre was found.
GNQ.summary: Equatorial Guinea's and Gabon's ministers inaugurated the interconnection of the Gabonese and Equatoguinean backbones on 10 November 2025, at Meyo-Kyé and Ebebeyin. Tests confirmed traffic flowing between Bitam and Ebebeyin, and between Libreville and Bata. In the last twelve months, Nigeria's Backbone Connectivity Network and Equatorial Guinea's transport minister signed a sea cable agreement in Malabo in February 2026 for a direct link between the two countries. Specifications, investment and a timetable were not disclosed. No exchange point or data facility run with another country has been found, and no source says work on the cable to Nigeria has begun. Mature would need a second kind of shared infrastructure in service: a traffic exchange or data storage.

KEN.short: Kenya and Tanzania launched a fibre link between their state networks in 2025; no shared exchange or data centre was found.
KEN.summary: TTCL and Kenya's ICT Authority launched a fibre link between Dar es Salaam and Mombasa in July 2025. Tanzania's Daily News reported it running at 1.6 terabits a second, with Kenyan companies using it. In the last twelve months, Uganda and Kenya completed a fibre connection at Busia, PML Daily reported in August 2026. An agreement between NITA-U and the ICT Authority is still to be finalised there. A World Bank report counts a cross-border connectivity memorandum between Kenya and South Sudan as signed by June 2026. No exchange point or data centre shared with another country under an agreement has been found. Mature would need a second kind of shared infrastructure in service: a traffic exchange or data storage.

LBR.short: Nothing found names infrastructure Liberia shares with another African country under an agreement, so no stage is set.
